process.notes: The spine of the Learn library. Stages and steps are data; lessons, templates and style guides attach to steps by slug. `inputs` and `outputs` are named artifacts: every input must be produced by an earlier step in the full track. `uses` lists library or MCP tools relevant to the step. `sources` are ids in content/learn/sources.json. `loops` record where the process is expected to go back. `tracks` are shorter paths through the same steps; a track may skip steps, in which case their artifacts are marked not applicable. A track may also list `replaces`: for each step it runs, an input the track skips is named with the artifact that carries it in this track (`by`, one artifact or a list, produced by an earlier step of the track or by the step itself) or with `by: null` when the input is dropped, and `how` says what to write instead. validate-process.mjs checks that every input of a track step is produced in the track or listed in `replaces`.

stages.name: Need
stages.question: What problem are we solving, for whom, under which limits?

steps.name: Define the need and the goal
steps.goal: State the business goal, the visitor goal and how success will be recognized.

steps.name: Understand the audience
steps.goal: Talk to and observe real people. Describe who visits the homepage, what they came for, how aware they are and on which devices.

steps.name: Frame the job to be done
steps.goal: Write the job story: the situation, the motivation and the progress the visitor wants to make.

steps.name: List the constraints
steps.goal: Capture brand assets, budget, deadline, platform, content, legal and accessibility limits.

steps.name: Audit the landscape
steps.goal: Look at how comparable companies present themselves, and what is overused in the niche.

steps.name: Align with stakeholders
steps.goal: Run a kickoff with the right questions and agree who decides.

stages.name: Brief
stages.question: What exactly are we making, and how will we judge it?

steps.name: Write the brief
steps.goal: Turn the need into a one-page brief: purpose, audience, message, tone, scope, constraints.

steps.name: Set positioning and tone
steps.goal: Choose the value proposition and 3–5 tone words with their opposites.

steps.name: Plan the content and page goal
steps.goal: List what the homepage must say and do, in priority order, and pick one primary action.

steps.name: Define success criteria
steps.goal: Write measurable and qualitative criteria that decide between options later.

steps.name: Review and sign off
steps.goal: Check the brief against a checklist and get agreement before design starts.

stages.name: References
stages.question: What already exists that points the way?

steps.name: Gather references
steps.goal: Collect 15–30 references by niche, style and mood, not only from direct competitors.

steps.name: Analyze references
steps.goal: Annotate what exactly works in each reference: structure, type, color, motion, copy.

steps.name: Write design principles
steps.goal: Distill 3–5 principles and 3 anti-goals that guide every later decision.

stages.name: Explore
stages.question: What are the genuinely different ways to do this?

steps.name: Pick library sections
steps.goal: Choose, with the owner, the 2 to 4 finished library sections the page is built from, and say for each what changes in its adaptation slots.

steps.name: Sketch many ideas
steps.goal: Generate many rough ideas quickly without judging them. Quantity first, selection later.

steps.name: Frame three directions
steps.goal: Combine art style, mood, typography and color into three distinct directions with a one-line north star each.

steps.name: Explore type and color
steps.goal: Try type pairings and palettes with defined roles for each direction, and check text contrast against WCAG AA from the start.

steps.name: Explore structure
steps.goal: Choose a page skeleton and sketch the section order for each direction.

steps.name: Draft headlines and copy
steps.goal: Write headline and subhead options for each direction before polishing visuals.

steps.name: Design hero concepts
steps.goal: Design the first screen for each direction, using the real headlines.

steps.name: Explore motion and interaction
steps.goal: Decide where motion earns its place and which triggers and techniques fit the direction.

steps.name: Critique against the brief
steps.goal: Review each direction against the brief with a rubric built from the principles and success criteria. Critique asks whether it works, not whether anyone likes it.

steps.name: Check inclusion and accessibility early
steps.goal: Check the leading directions for contrast, motion, readability and who might be excluded, before investing in detail.

steps.name: Prototype the strongest candidates
steps.goal: Make a realistic clickable or coded version of the best one or two directions, with real content.

steps.name: Test quickly
steps.goal: Test with about five people per audience group, fix what you find and test again. Several small rounds beat one big one.

steps.name: Choose and document
steps.goal: Pick a direction and write down why, what was rejected, and what to carry over.

steps.name: Define the tokens
steps.goal: Fix color roles, type scale, spacing, radius and elevation; write them as a DESIGN.md.

stages.name: Realize
stages.question: How do we turn the chosen direction into a real page?

steps.name: Design the homepage in full
steps.goal: Design every section, state and breakpoint with real content.

steps.name: Build the component set
steps.goal: Define the small set of reusable components the page needs.

steps.name: Specify motion
steps.goal: Write motion specs: triggers, durations, easing, reduced-motion behavior.

steps.name: Prepare imagery and assets
steps.goal: Produce or source images, icons, video and fonts with licenses and performance in mind.

steps.name: Build it
steps.goal: Choose the platform and build so the core content works first and effects layer on top. Use an AI agent that reads the DESIGN.md if helpful.

steps.name: Remove what the build does not need
steps.goal: Take out the extra copy, lines, icons, metadata and decoration that building added, until every element earns its place.

steps.name: Look at every state and keep a papercut log
steps.goal: Capture every state of every section and breakpoint, review the build's own trail for surprises, and record small issues in a log that carries into the next round.

steps.name: Check accessibility, performance and SEO
steps.goal: Test contrast (WCAG 2.2 AA: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large), keyboard use, reduced-motion behavior, Core Web Vitals (LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 at the 75th percentile), metadata and responsiveness.

steps.name: Hand off and launch
steps.goal: Release, redirect, monitor and hand over the files and guidelines.

stages.name: Reflect
stages.question: Did it work, and what do we keep?

steps.name: Measure
steps.goal: Compare real results with the success criteria.

steps.name: Iterate and run a retro
steps.goal: Decide what to change next and what the process taught.

steps.name: Archive as a case study
steps.goal: Write up the project: brief, directions, decision, result. Add the site to the library.

loops.reason: Exploring solutions changes how the problem is understood. Treat the brief as a versioned hypothesis, not a contract.
If no direction passes critique and tests, return to exploration with what you learned.
Build and QA findings can force changes to the direction or the tokens.
Results reframe the need. Digital work is never finished.

tracks.name: Full process
tracks.description: Every step, with time for real research and several test rounds. Weeks.

tracks.name: Five-day sprint
tracks.description: A compressed path modeled on the GV Design Sprint: Map, Sketch, Decide, Prototype, Test. After Day 5 it continues with realize-build and realize-qa (listed under `after`): the prototype is the first draft of the build. Inputs of skipped steps are folded into the artifacts the track does produce (see `replaces`); skipped steps are noted, not ignored.

days.name: Decide
days.note: Decide holds the critique and the inclusion check, not the decision: decide-choose records the decision on Day 5, after the test, and the owner confirms it there.

days.name: Prototype
days.note: The prototype is the first draft of the build (build once). Build it where the site will live, or promote it to the site root in realize-build; do not rebuild it.

days.name: Test
days.note: With no people to test with, write the script in test-results.md and record UNTESTED; decide-choose then decides on the critique and the inclusion check alone.

after.name: Build and QA
after.note: Not optional: the prototype has had only a blocker review. Promote the prototype to the site, finish it (states, motion, assets, copy) and run realize-qa. realize-launch is not part of the sprint; if the owner deploys, run it first (it refuses while unconfirmed facts remain).

tracks.description: The default since 2026-11-16 (a client pilot pilot: owner 9/10 against 5 to 7.5 for the rule-driven rounds). The page is assembled from finished, spec-pinned library sections (content/sections, MCP list_library_sections and get_library_section) and adapted only in their slots; rules and audits run last as checks. Inputs of skipped steps are folded into the artifacts the track does produce (see `replaces`).

success-criteria.how: The Success section of the brief: the primary action and how it is counted.

need-goal.role: Pin down what the homepage is for before any design thinking. You are framing a problem, not proposing a solution.
procedure: Redesigning an existing site? Before you restate anything or ask the owner a question, read what exists (the code, the content, the analytics events) and write down what the site actually does today and which action it really serves. A brief can describe a site that does not exist: a first test found a request for a 'booking site' on a site with no booking at all, whose real action was 'follow'. Where the request and the code disagree, say so and let the code set the primary action unless the owner decides otherwise.

Redesigning an existing site? Ask the scope once, first, as the first ask_user question (three multiple-choice lines with the recommended answer first) and write the answer as a `## Scope` block at the top of need-statement.md; every later step reads it. Structure: rebuild from scratch, or keep the current sections. Content: rework key parts (the hero and 2 or 3 key sections; everything else is kept and moved into the new sections), keep verbatim, full rework, or none supplied (you write draft copy marked unconfirmed). SEO: keep URL, title, meta description, canonical, structured data, heading text and internal links, or free to change. For a "make it stylish" job on an existing site the recommended answer is rebuild, rework key parts, keep SEO: the owner's own words were "from scratch ... respect the content, but not the structure ... repurpose the content across the new sections ... keep it for SEO". Owner away: use the recommended answers, mark the block `ASSUMED, not owner-approved`, and list it in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.

Existing content with a scope that keeps any of it: write design/01-need/content-map.md before designing: every text block of the current page (heading, paragraph, list, button, FAQ item) with an id, marked `SEO` when it is the title, meta description, h1 or h2 text, structured data or an internal link; the new section it moves into; and `keep`, `rework` or `drop (owner)`. Nothing is dropped without the owner's word. realize-qa checks the build against it with the audit's `coverage` command.

Outside the scope's rework parts the content is the owner's. Content problems you find (unsourced claims, odd copy, missing sections) are findings for the owner, listed in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md and the QA report; do not fix, remove or rewrite them yourself, and do not add claims of your own. In a test the first build rewrote copy outside its scope and dropped sections, and had to be reverted. Also ask whether the done bar may touch shared chrome (header, footer, shared components): it moves the work from one file to many.

Open the pages the primary action sends people to (the three main destinations) and check their claims and sources too: a homepage inherits their honesty. In a real run the homepage's own claims were fixable, but 99 of the 124 pages its main action led to might still cite fabricated papers, and the repo's own commit messages said so. Check also the people the content names as authors or reviewers: a name, title or credential is shown only if the person exists and can be reached (protocol 3.2). Read the git log for words such as `fabricated`, `placeholder`, `fake`, `TODO` and `unverified`.
Restate the user's request in one sentence without solution words (no 'with a video', 'in dark mode').
Write the business goal, the visitor goal and ONE primary action the page asks for (a single verb phrase: buy, book a demo, join the waitlist...). [Craft]
Define how success will be recognized: at least one measurable signal (a rate, a count, a task success) and one observable signal (a five-second test result, a stakeholder reaction).

No baseline? Do not invent one. Set a relative target (for example `+X% against the first four weeks after launch`, or `more enquiries per 100 visits than the old page`) and name the measure, or write the absolute number and mark it `ASSUMED, no baseline`. Record the missing baseline as an open question: a target with no baseline is a hypothesis, not a result. [Our take]

The owner names two actions ('book or buy')? Pick the one with the higher value or the higher frequency as the primary action, name the other as a secondary action, and record the call and the reason as an open question for the owner. Do not write both as primary. If you cannot tell which is more valuable, default to the more frequent one and mark it ASSUMED. [Our take]
List what is unknown. Mark every statement that is an assumption, not a fact the user gave you.
Stop. Do not start designing. Hand the unknowns to the next steps or ask the user.
lean: Need-audience, need-constraints and need-alignment are skipped, so this file carries them. Add three short sections to need-statement.md after the assumptions: `## Audience` (who arrives, in what situation, on which device, what could stop them, access needs; each claim tagged evidence or assumption; plus the audience flags and COGA escalation from need-audience), `## Constraints` (brand assets, stack, deadline, content that exists, legal, must-not, accessibility WCAG 2.2 AA and performance defaults, and which shared components render on the page and whether you may change them: header, footer, global styles) and `## Owner's words` (three feeling adjectives, sites liked and disliked; if the owner is unavailable, write your defaults and mark them `ASSUMED, not owner-approved`).
Keep each section to five lines or fewer. A fact you do not have is an open question in design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, not a reason to stop.
sprint: need-constraints and need-alignment are skipped in the sprint, so this file carries them. need-audience is not skipped: the audience keeps its own file. After the assumptions add two short sections to need-statement.md: `## Constraints` (brand assets, stack, deadline, content that exists, legal, must-not, accessibility WCAG 2.2 AA and performance defaults, and which shared components render on the page and whether you may change them: header, footer, global styles) and `## Owner's words` (three feeling adjectives, sites liked and disliked; if the owner is unavailable on Day 1, write your defaults and mark them `ASSUMED, not owner-approved`). brief-write reads them from there.

Keep each section to five lines or fewer. A fact you do not have is an open question in design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, not a reason to stop. Day 1 is the best time to ask the owner: batch the questions in one message with a default for each.
ask_user: Scope (redesign of an existing site; one letter per line, recommended first). Structure: (a) rebuild from scratch (recommended) (b) keep the current sections and order. Content: (a) rework key parts: hero plus 2 or 3 key sections, the rest kept and moved into the new sections (recommended) (b) keep every text verbatim (c) full rework (d) none supplied: I write draft copy marked unconfirmed. SEO: (a) keep URL, title, meta description, canonical, structured data, heading text and internal links (recommended) (b) free to change.
What does the company or product do, in one sentence? (a) my draft from the current site: [one sentence] (recommended) (b) your own sentence.
Who should use the page, and what should they do on it? (a) my reading of the site: [audience] should [primary action] (recommended) (b) a different audience or action: say which.
How will you know the homepage worked? (a) more [primary action] per 100 visits than the first four weeks after launch (recommended) (b) a number you already track: say which.

checks: The primary action is a single verb phrase.
At least one measurable success signal is stated.
No sentence in the need statement describes a visual or a feature.

done_when: Every field is filled or explicitly marked unknown.
Assumptions are listed separately from facts.
pitfalls: Writing the solution into the need ('a homepage with a hero video').
Two or three primary actions: pick one, move the rest to secondary and record the choice as an open question when the owner named both.
A success target with an invented baseline: use a relative target or mark it ASSUMED.

need-audience.role: Describe the real people the page serves, from evidence where it exists. Do not invent personas.
procedure: List up to three audience groups. For each write: the situation they arrive in, what they already know about the company, the decision they must make, the device and setting, and what could stop them (doubt, risk, time).
Use only evidence the user has given you (interviews, analytics, support questions, sales notes). Mark everything else 'assumption'. [Evidence: start from user data, not assumptions]
If there is no evidence, say so in the file and recommend the owner run 3 to 5 short conversations before launch; continue with clearly marked assumptions.

Add access needs for each group: screen reader or keyboard use, low vision or zoom, motor limits, cognitive load, slow networks, small screens, one-handed use. [Craft: designing for the margins improves the page for everyone]

Flag the groups that need cognitive accessibility first: people under stress (a crisis, a deadline, a frightening letter), with low literacy, reading in a second language (ESL), with cognitive or learning disabilities, or who use a screen reader or have dyslexia. If any group has a flag, write `COGA escalation: yes` in the file: the 15 `a11y-coga-*` rules are then treated as major for this project, and brief-write says so. Also note the reading level to aim for (see `copy-reading-grade`: a lower target for ESL, low-literacy and UK public-service audiences) and whether a translation or interpreter offer is needed. [Our take]
ask_user: Do you have real customer evidence? (a) no: I mark audience claims as assumptions (recommended if none exists) (b) yes: send interviews, analytics or sales notes.
Which groups matter most? (a) my proposal: [group 1], [group 2] (recommended) (b) a different order or group: say which.

Each claim is tagged evidence or assumption.

done_when: Two or three groups, each with situation, decision, device, access needs and an evidence tag.
pitfalls: Demographic personas ('Sarah, 34, loves coffee').
Omitting assistive technology and small-screen use.
Leaving a stressed, low-literacy or ESL audience unflagged, so the COGA rules stay minor and get missed.

need-jobs.role: Describe what each visitor is trying to get done, in their words, without naming a product or feature.
procedure: For each audience group write one to three job stories: 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].' [Craft: the job-story format comes from Intercom's practitioners, not from Christensen, Moesta or Ulwick, whose definitions of a job differ; treat the format as a convenience]
A job statement must not contain a solution (no product, page type or feature). Rewrite until it does not.
Rank the jobs by how often they occur and how costly failure is. The top job drives the primary action.
lean: audience-profile is replaced by the Audience section of need-statement.md. Write one to three job stories from it and rank them; the top one must match the primary action.

done_when: Each group has at least one ranked job story.
pitfalls: Smuggling the solution into the job ('I want a dashboard').

need-constraints.role: Record everything that limits the design so later steps treat limits as inputs, not surprises.
procedure: Ask for or find: brand assets (logo, colors, fonts, voice), existing site and its analytics, stack and hosting, CMS, deadline and budget, content that exists, legal needs (cookie consent, claims, regulated language), languages.

Set defaults unless the user says otherwise and write them down: accessibility target WCAG 2.2 Level AA [Standard]; Core Web Vitals targets LCP at most 2.5 s, INP at most 200 ms, CLS at most 0.1 at the 75th percentile [Standard]; support the current evergreen browsers and common mobile sizes (320 to 1920 px wide).
List explicit 'must not' items (words, colors, competitors' looks, technologies).

Shared chrome: list the shared components that render on this page (header, footer, navigation, cookie banner, region or language switcher, global tokens and base styles) and ask whether you may change them. The homepage's done bar (zero blockers) often cannot be met without them: in a real run the failures were a low-contrast button in the footer, 12 to 14 px footer text, an icon-only switcher with no name and a light input border token, all shared. Record the answer as `Shared chrome: may change [list] / must not change [list]`, and in realize-qa report their failures as inherited, not new.
ask_user: Brand assets I must use? (a) the logo, colours and fonts on the current site (recommended) (b) new or different ones: send them.
Stack and deadline? (a) the current project's stack, no fixed deadline (recommended) (b) another stack or a date: say which.
Anything the page must not say or look like? (a) nothing beyond the brief's anti-goals (recommended) (b) yes: list it.
May I change the shared header, footer and global styles to fix problems on this page? (a) yes, and I audit one inner page too (recommended) (b) no, this page only.

pitfalls: Leaving accessibility and performance unstated so they become optional.

need-landscape.role: See how comparable companies present themselves, and what the niche has made generic.
procedure: Query the library: search_sites with the industry and site-type tags that fit the need; also one or two adjacent industries.

Review at least 6 sites. If the library has fewer than 6 that fit the industry, add sites found on the web (open and view each) and mark them `not in library`. For each note the art style, hero type, page skeleton, how the primary action is presented, and anything the audit says not to copy (get_site returns audit failures).
Name the niche's default look in one sentence ('white, blue gradient, three icon cards'). That is what to avoid being indistinguishable from, unless the brief says otherwise. [Our take]
Note what nobody does that the audience might want.

need-alignment.role: Confirm the framing with the owner before the brief. This is the main point to ask, not assume.
procedure: Summarize the need statement, audience groups, top job, constraints and the landscape's default look in under one page.

Ask the owner these five questions in one message: confirm the primary action; rank the audience groups; confirm or correct constraints; give three adjectives for the feeling; name two sites they like and one they dislike, with why.
Record the answers verbatim. Update earlier artifacts where answers change them and say so.
ask_user: Is the primary action right? (a) yes: [primary action] (recommended) (b) no: say which.
Which audience group matters most? (a) [group 1] (recommended) (b) [group 2].
Are the constraints right? (a) yes, as listed in constraints.md (recommended) (b) change: say what.
How should the page feel? (a) [three adjectives I propose from the brand] (recommended) (b) three words of your own.
Sites you like and dislike? (a) skip: the taste intake at ref-gather shows library screenshots (recommended) (b) name two you like and one you dislike, with why.

output.template:
# Kickoff notes
## Summary sent
## Owner's answers (verbatim)
## Changes made to earlier artifacts
## Decision rights (who signs off the brief, the direction)

checks: The owner's own words are recorded, not paraphrased.

done_when: All five questions are answered or explicitly deferred with a default.
pitfalls: Proceeding on assumptions when the owner is available to answer.

brief-write.role: Turn the need into a one-page brief that says what and why, not how. Treat it as a hypothesis you will revise.
procedure: Write the brief from the need statement, audience profile, job stories, constraints and kickoff notes. Keep it to one page.

Sections: problem and why now; audience and situation; goal and primary action; message; tone (filled in by the next step); scope (what the homepage contains and what it does not); constraints as inputs; deliverables and what 'done' means.
State the version (v1). The brief changes if exploration reframes the problem; record each change with the reason. [Evidence: problem and solution develop together]
Do not describe visuals or technology. If a sentence says how, move it to the constraints or delete it.

Audience flags: if the audience profile flags people under stress, with low literacy, ESL, cognitive or learning disabilities, or screen-reader or dyslexia users, write under `Audience and situation`: `COGA escalation: the a11y-coga-* rules are major for this project` and name the reading level to aim for. Those rules (all fifteen are in `rules/build.md`) are then part of the brief's definition of done. [Our take]
sections: audience-profile, job-story, constraints and kickoff-notes are replaced by the Audience, Jobs, Constraints and Owner's words sections of need-statement.md. Read them from there.

Fill the Success section for real: the one primary action (a lead, a sign-up, a booking) and how it is counted. realize-qa checks it, and the picked sections must give it a place (a form slot in the hero or the close).
Keep the brief to one page. Its job in this track is to say what the page must do and say, not what it looks like: the look comes from the library sections picked next.
lean: Audience, constraints and kickoff notes are replaced by the Audience, Constraints and Owner's words sections of need-statement.md. Read them from there.

Positioning and design-principles are skipped, so fill the `Tone` section for real instead of leaving a placeholder: a one-sentence value proposition (who, what, why different), proof points with sources or `no proof yet`, three to five tone words each with its opposite, and three anti-goals (one derived from the niche's default look). Later lean steps read these lines from brief-draft.md as positioning and principles.
The brief stays v1 and is not reviewed by the owner in lean: mark it `ASSUMED, not owner-approved` unless the owner has read it. It still must fit one page.
sprint: constraints and kickoff-notes are replaced by the Constraints and Owner's words sections of need-statement.md. audience-profile and job-story exist as their own files in the sprint.

positioning and the content inventory are skipped, so brief-draft carries them. Fill `Tone` as in lean: a one-sentence value proposition (who, what, why different), proof points with sources or `no proof yet`, three to five tone words each with its opposite, a swap-test line and three anti-goals (one from the niche's default look). Add a `## Content inventory` section: a table with one row per block the page needs (block, the visitor question it answers, priority must/should/could, source provided/to write/to produce, status) and the primary action's place. Twelve rows or fewer. Facts the owner has not confirmed get status `unconfirmed` and go in design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md. Any block that gives legal, medical, financial or safety advice is also marked `needs expert review` (`copy-expert-review-before-launch`).
ref-principles later refines the tone words and anti-goals into design principles; keep them in the brief as well. brief-review turns this file plus success-criteria into brief.md.

output.template:
# Design brief (v1)
## Problem and why now
## Audience and situation
## Goal and primary action
## Message (what the page must make people understand)
## Tone (placeholder, completed in positioning; in lean and sprint fill it here: value proposition, proof or 'no proof yet', tone words with opposites, three anti-goals)
## Scope: includes / excludes
## Constraints (inputs, not obstacles)
## Deliverables and what done means
## Content inventory (sprint only; in full and lean see brief-content)
## Change log

checks: One page or less.
No visual or technical solution is prescribed.
Success criteria and constraints appear (full criteria are written in brief-success).

done_when: All sections exist; the brief is versioned.
pitfalls: A brief that is a feature list or a mood board in words.

brief-positioning.role: Decide what the page claims and in what voice, specifically enough that a competitor could not say it.
procedure: Write a value proposition in one sentence: who it is for, what it does, why it is different. Use the audience's words, not internal jargon. [Evidence: say who you are, what you offer and how you differ]

List three to five proof points that are facts (numbers, names, results), each with its source. If there is no proof yet (new product, no customers), write `no proof yet`, lead with what the product does and how it works instead, and never fill the gap with invented numbers, logos or quotes; list what proof the owner should collect first.
Choose three to five tone words, each with its opposite ('direct, not curt'). Add words and phrases to avoid.
Run the swap test: replace the company name with a competitor's. If the claim still reads true, rewrite it. [Our take]
ask_user: What can you prove with a number, a name or a result? (a) only what is already public on the site: [list] (recommended) (b) more: send it with its source.

tools.use: optional: read competitor headlines in the landscape audit to check the swap test

output.template:
# Positioning
- Value proposition (one sentence):
- Differentiator:
- Proof points (with source):
- Tone words (and their opposites):
- Words and phrases to avoid:
- Swap test result:

checks: The value proposition passes the swap test only if it is specific: with a competitor's name swapped in it becomes false or absurd.
Each proof point has a source.

done_when: Value proposition, proof, tone words and swap test result are written.
pitfalls: Superlatives with no evidence.
Generic claims ('seamless', 'powerful', 'next-generation') that any company could write.

brief-content.role: Decide what the homepage must say and do, in priority order, with one primary action.
procedure: List every block of content the page needs (headline, what it is, proof, how it works, pricing, FAQ, contact...). For each: priority (must, should, could), source (provided, to be written, to be produced), and the visitor question it answers.
Order by importance to the top job. Put the primary action in the first screen and repeat it where it is natural.
Flag missing content now. Use real content in designs; if it does not exist, write plausible real copy and mark it 'draft'. Never use lorem ipsum. [Craft: content-first]

Facts the owner has not confirmed (prices, hours, sizes, policies, addresses, dates, contact details) get status `unconfirmed` in the inventory and are listed in design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md. Inside a prototype page they carry the visible marker from the protocol (section 3.2: the `.assumed` dotted-underline convention with a legend), never brackets and never a silent invention. Invented proof (customers, numbers, quotes, press) is not a fact you may mark and ship: leave it out. [Our take]

A status or count derived from history (git commits, a changelog, old notes: "25 of 124 pages have sources matched to PubMed") is an assumption until the owner confirms the list: status `unconfirmed`, `.assumed` on the page, listed in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md. Named reviewers and their credentials are facts too: check the person exists before you show the name (protocol 3.2).

After you compute a number from content (counts per category, pages per type), open the list it counts and read ten rows before the number goes on the page: in a test a count doubled because two category pages shared one product type, and some items were dropped by a schema error.
Map the content to likely section types (hero, features, proof, pricing, FAQ, CTA, footer).

Mark every block that gives legal, medical, financial or safety advice `needs expert review` and add the reviewer you need (a solicitor, a clinician, an adviser) to design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md. Until a qualified person has reviewed it, the copy ships only as a visible draft (the `.assumed`-style marker and legend, protocol 3.2) and realize-launch stays closed. [Our take: `copy-expert-review-before-launch`]

Forms: if the page takes personal data (a callback, an enquiry, a booking), list the form, the fields it needs (three required at most), where the data goes (a backend, or email) and who can answer for it; the recipe `form-no-backend-and-privacy` covers the no-backend case and the privacy line.
ask_user: Which content exists? (a) the current site's text and images, mapped in content-map.md (recommended) (b) new material: send it.

output.template:
# Content inventory
| Block | Visitor question it answers | Priority | Source | Section type | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
## Primary action and where it appears

checks: Every must-have block has a source.
The primary action appears in the first screen.
Every block that gives legal, medical, financial or safety advice is marked `needs expert review` with the reviewer named.

done_when: All blocks are prioritized and sourced; gaps are listed.
pitfalls: Designing with placeholder text that hides copy problems.
Inventing a plausible fact and shipping it unmarked: mark it, list it in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, and let realize-launch refuse while it remains.

brief-success.role: Fix the criteria that will decide between options later, so taste does not decide alone.
procedure: Write measurable criteria (for example a conversion target, a task success rate in a test, a load-time target) and qualitative criteria (a five-second test: at least 4 of 5 people can say what the page is for).

For each measurable criterion find the event, query or report that produces the number, and check that it fires today (read the tracking code and trigger it once). A criterion nothing records will read zero: if the event does not exist or is declared but never sent, building it is part of the work, so add it to the brief's scope and to the build plan.

Conversion: name what the page captures (an email, a booking, a sign-up, a purchase) and the value the visitor gets in exchange (a plan, a checklist, reminders, a quote). A page that has a form must use it to capture, with that exchange stated next to it; copy that promises the opposite ("no email") needs the owner's say-so. Write where the capture appears: in the first screen, repeated after each major section, and in a closing band. In a real run the owner's verdict on a stylish page was "very little conversion potential" because its only action captured nothing. [Our take]
Add the quality bar: zero blocker failures from the Quality Bar, WCAG 2.2 AA, Web Vitals targets from the constraints.
Write the decision rule: how directions will be compared and who decides (usually the owner).
ask_user: What would make you call the homepage a success? (a) [primary action] per 100 visits up against the first four weeks (recommended) (b) another number or event: say which.

tools.use: topic 'blockers' to cite the quality bar

output.template:
# Success criteria
## Measurable
## Qualitative (five-second test and others)
## Quality bar (blockers = 0, WCAG 2.2 AA, Web Vitals)
## Decision rule and decider

checks: At least one criterion can be measured without opinion.
Quality-bar line is present.

done_when: Criteria and the decision rule are written.
pitfalls: Only subjective criteria ('feels modern').

brief-review.role: Check the brief against a checklist and get the owner's agreement before design starts.
procedure: Run the checklist below on the draft and fix failures.
Assemble brief.md: the one-page brief plus positioning, content inventory and success criteria as linked sections.
Ask the owner to approve. Record the approval and the version.

Owner unavailable: do not stop and do not write `approved`. Use the heading `# Brief v1 (NOT owner-approved, ASSUMED)`, tick the approval box as `requested, open` and list the approval as the first line of design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md. Every later artifact then inherits the label `ASSUMED, not owner-approved` (protocol 4).
sprint: positioning and content-inventory are replaced by the Tone and Content inventory sections of brief-draft.md. Assemble brief.md from brief-draft.md and success-criteria.md; the checklist below then also asks that both sections exist.
ask_user: Do you approve this brief (v1)? (a) yes, approved as written (recommended) (b) approve with changes: list them.

output.template:
# Brief v1 (approved [date] by [name])
(owner unavailable: write the heading as "# Brief v1 (NOT owner-approved, ASSUMED)")
(links to positioning, content inventory and success criteria; sprint: the Tone and Content inventory sections of brief-draft)
## Checklist
- [ ] One page
- [ ] What and why, not how
- [ ] Measurable success criteria
- [ ] Constraints as inputs
- [ ] Assumptions flagged
- [ ] Owner approval recorded (or, owner unavailable: heading says NOT owner-approved, ASSUMED; approval listed as open)

checks: All checklist boxes ticked.
Approval recorded; owner unavailable: the heading says NOT owner-approved, ASSUMED and the approval is listed as an open question.

done_when: The owner has approved and the version is recorded, or the brief is headed `NOT owner-approved, ASSUMED` and the approval is an open question.
pitfalls: Moving on without approval; the brief then cannot arbitrate later disputes.

ref-gather.role: Collect references that point the way. References are evidence for decisions, not things to copy.
procedure: Gate 1, taste intake, before any search: call taste_intake (brief text, tag slugs; lean and sprint ask for 3 bundles, full 4). It returns style bundles: each named after two library sites, with three feeling words, why it could fit and what it takes from each site. Rewrite each `why` in one line for this project. Make one cheap hero sketch per bundle on the base kit (get_base: header plus one hero skeleton, with the bundle's tokens): the real headline and primary action in the bundle's type, colour and lead object, about fifteen lines of your own on top of the kit, the widths check passed, drawn fresh (when the scope says rebuild, never on the old layout), with the graphic from the asset plan below. Put them on one labelled sheet (`pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit cli sheet design/03-references/bundles <sketch>="Bundle name|three feeling words" ...`) and send it with the bundle sites' screenshots. Ask the ref-gather question (proposed answers as letters, your recommended bundle first). These sketches become the explore-hero concepts: refine them there, do not start over.

Asset and motion plan at gate 1: for each bundle say what the hero's visual is and its one lead motion (from the bundle sites' motion, get_craft gives their timing), made in code first (a data graph or diagram from the real content, type as image, an SVG motif in the bundle's colours; plan_graphics proposes one per section). A paid generated image appears only as a marked placeholder with its proposed prompt; it is generated later and only after the owner's yes (protocol 6).

The library is the owner's taste profile: every site in it is liked, the plain ones included, so include the most visually ambitious sites (art-style, standout and motion tags) alongside the quiet ones and do not pre-filter to what looks safe for the niche. Record the answer as the first line of the board: `Owner taste: bundle [n] ([slugs]), not for this project [slugs], why: ...`; library rows the owner picked are `taste anchor` rows. Record the answer with record_taste (type pick, gate 1, the project folder, picked and notFor slugs, their words, the project's industry slugs). Pass the project (and industry) to taste_intake so the client's earlier answers, or earlier clients in the same niche, pick your recommended bundle. A client new to this can do the faster intake first: 8 to 10 A-vs-B pairs (taste_pairs with the project), answered as letters and recorded as type ab. Owner away: send the question, draft the board meanwhile, and write `Owner taste: waiting for the owner`; explore-directions cannot finish without it (protocol 4).

Look at the pictures, not only the text: every library site has fold screenshots and section crops under `storage/sites/<slug>/` (get_site and get_design_brief give the paths; get_sections and get_section give per-section crops). Open the images for every library row you keep; a text brief alone does not tell you whether a site is visually ambitious.

Call list_tags first (facets art-style, mood, industry, site-type) and pass tag slugs (recommend takes them in `tags`, search_sites in `allOf`/`anyOf`), not sentences: a natural-language brief often matches no tag and returns only a fallback. Then call recommend with the brief plus those slugs, and the owner's liked slugs from the taste intake as `taste` (they come first and sites that look like them rank higher), and search_sites across at least three art-style families that fit the tone words. recommend can return references from an unrelated niche because it matches on style tags (a playful ceramics brief can return a software product): read why each one was returned before you keep it.

See how big the library is before you search for niche matches: search_sites with `{}` returns the library total. An empty result for a niche (for example `text: "ceramics"`) usually means the library has nothing there, not that your query is wrong; go to the thin-library step below instead of retrying variants.

Gather 15 to 30 references: about a third from the same niche, a third from adjacent niches, a third chosen purely for style, type or motion. [Our take: diverse references prevent copying the niche's default]
Use find_similar from your strongest reference.

Include the library's strongest visual sites even when their niche is unrelated, and say for each what it would give this project (a type move, a hero object, a palette mood, a motion idea). With a thin library the shortfall is easily filled with utilitarian sites from the niche (evidence hubs, clinics, directories); they show the niche default, which is useful as a landscape note but not as a direction. [Our take]

Niche the library does not cover (fewer than three library sites with the project's industry tag): web references are required, not optional. See at least three sites from the niche in a browser and write the visual vocabulary they share (motifs, palette, shapes, materials, type): it is where the niche cue in explore-directions comes from. Skipping them to save time left a wedding page with nothing that said wedding.

Thin library: if the library holds fewer than 15 sites that fit (recommend and search_sites will tell you), fill the shortfall with web research (awards listings, competitor sites, the owner's likes) and mark those rows `not in library`. Open each one in a browser and look; do not list a site you did not view. Say in the file how many came from the library and how many from outside.

A text-only fetch (WebFetch, a page-to-text tool) is not looking: it returns a model's text summary of the page, not the design. Open the site in a browser or take a screenshot. A site you could only read as text may stay on the board only if its row says `read as text, not seen`, and it is not used for any visual decision (type, colour, layout, motion) and not counted as seen. Say in the file how many rows were seen and how many were read as text. [Our take]

For each reference record why it is here (one specific thing), what to take, what not to take. Read each site's audit failures before deciding what to take (get_site): do not copy what fails a blocker rule.
lean: brief is replaced by brief-draft.md (v1); an unreviewed brief is fine in lean.

Lower the minimum to about 8 references (library plus web) from at least three art-style families, with some from adjacent niches. First-screen notes are enough: open each site, say what the first screen does, what to take, what not to take. Do not list a site you did not open; if a site fails to load or hides behind a cookie wall, say so and drop it.

Audit column: write the get_site audit failures for library rows; write `UNKNOWN` for every `not in library` row and do not spend audits on them in lean. Do not copy anything from an UNKNOWN row that touches accessibility.

Landscape: need-landscape is skipped, so put a five-line landscape note at the top of reference-board.md: (1) the niche's default look in one sentence, (2) the default hero, (3) the default skeleton, (4) what nobody does that this audience might want, (5) how many sites you looked at, from the library and from outside. explore-directions reads it as the landscape audit.
sprint: brief is the reviewed brief.md here (brief-review runs on Day 1), so no replacement is needed for it.

Thin-library minimum: when the library holds fewer than 15 sites that fit, about 8 references (library plus web) from at least three art-style families are enough, with some from adjacent niches, exactly as in lean. First-screen notes are enough: what the first screen does, what to take, what not to take. Audit column: the get_site failures for library rows, `UNKNOWN` for every `not in library` row; copy nothing from an UNKNOWN row that touches accessibility. ref-analyze then annotates the six or so you looked at most closely (get_site only works for library rows; for the rest annotate from your own first-screen notes).

need-landscape is skipped, so put a five-line landscape note at the top of reference-board.md: (1) the niche's default look in one sentence, (2) the default hero, (3) the default skeleton, (4) what nobody does that this audience might want, (5) how many sites you saw, read as text, and took from the library. explore-directions reads it as the landscape audit.
ask_user: (Taste intake, with the bundle sheet) Which style bundle fits this project? (a) bundle [n], my pick from the brief (recommended) (b) another bundle number, or a mix ("1's type with 3's colour") (c) none: say why.
Any other sites to include or exclude? (a) no, the library is enough (recommended) (b) yes: name them.

first: the canonical slugs for art-style, mood, industry and site-type
brief text plus tag slugs, and `taste` (the owner's liked slugs); returns art direction and references; may include an unrelated niche, so check each
allOf by art-style/mood/type; passesBlockers true when you only want safe-to-copy references; call with {} to see the library size
slug of the strongest reference

(lean and sprint: five-line landscape note first: default look, default hero, default skeleton, gap nobody fills, counts of seen / read as text / from the library)
| Slug | Why it is here (one specific thing) | Take | Do not take (audit / taste) | Art style | Niche |

checks: The board opens with an `Owner taste` line recorded from the owner's answer to the screenshots (or `waiting for the owner`, which blocks explore-directions).
The library's most visually ambitious sites were looked at (images, not only briefs) and the board says what each would give this project.

15 or more references (library plus web research; lean and sprint with a thin library: about 8), at least three art-style families; the file states how many are from the library and how many were seen rather than read as text.
Each reference has a specific reason, not 'looks good'.
No reference with a known blocker failure is listed as something to copy in that respect.

done_when: The board has 15 or more references (lean, or sprint with a thin library: about 8) with take and do-not-take columns filled.
pitfalls: Skipping the taste intake because the owner is away: ask anyway and wait at the directions sheet.
Filling a thin library with the niche's plainest sites and calling it a reference set.
Reading the text briefs of library sites without opening their screenshots.
Only collecting direct competitors.
Recording 'nice' instead of a reason.
Retrying a niche query that returned nothing instead of checking the library size.
Passing a whole brief sentence to search_sites or recommend and treating the fallback as a real match.
Writing an audit result for a site you never audited: use UNKNOWN.
Counting sites a text-only fetch summarised as if you had seen them.

ref-analyze.role: Find out exactly what works in the strongest references so you can reuse the idea, not the surface.
procedure: Pick the 6 to 10 most useful references. For each call get_site and read its style record, palette roles, fonts, tags and audit.

Get the numbers before the impressions: get_craft with the slugs gives each site's scale contrast (headline over body), type scale step, section whitespace in body units, lead-object share of the first screen and motion timing, and the library's quartiles. Write them in the notes; they are what makes a page feel agency-grade, and compare_to_library checks your concepts against them later.

Annotate: page skeleton and section order, hero type, navigation, type scale and pairing, color roles and contrast, motion (what, when, how long), copy approach (headline structure, proof, CTA wording).
Write a 'why it works' sentence for each notable move and the reusable principle behind it. For motion use phases: trigger, start, move, settle. [Craft]
Use compare for two to four references that look alike on the surface to find what actually differs.

tools.use: style record, palette roles, fonts, audit summary and failing rules
slugs; scale contrast, type step, whitespace, lead-object share and motion timing per site, with the library quartiles
format markdown for the DESIGN.md of a reference
tokens, components, section map, image files and audit failures of a reference: enough to study or rebuild its structure without a screenshot
slugs of 2 to 4 references

# Reference notes
## [slug]
- Skeleton and section order:
- Hero and navigation:
- Type and color:
- Motion (trigger, start, move, settle):
- Copy approach:
- Why it works:
- Reusable principle:
- Do not copy (audit failures):

checks: Every note states a reusable principle, not a surface feature.
Audit failures are named, not ignored.

done_when: 6 to 10 references annotated with a principle each.
pitfalls: Describing the look instead of explaining why it works.
Treating a reference's accessibility failures as part of its style.

ref-principles.role: Distill the project's own design principles, short and testable, so later choices have a rule to be judged against.
procedure: From the brief and reference notes write 3 to 5 principles. Each one must be a positive, testable sentence that can decide between two options ('Evidence before ornament', 'One idea per screen').
Add 3 anti-goals: things the design must not be. Include one derived from the niche's default look.
Trace each principle back to a brief line or a reference note. Use established principle sets (Rams, Nielsen, Norman, POUR) as a lens to check for gaps; do not copy them in. [Craft]
Write one tension the design will have to manage (for example calm versus bold) and which side wins when they conflict.
ask_user: Do these principles fit the project? (a) yes, as written (recommended) (b) change: say which.

tools.use: the library of named principles with how to apply and check them

output.template:
# Design principles
## Principles (each can decide between two options)
1. [principle] : traces to [brief line / reference]
## Anti-goals
## The main tension and which side wins

checks: Each principle can be used to reject an option.
No principle is a platitude ('be user-friendly').

done_when: 3 to 5 principles, 3 anti-goals and one stated tension.
pitfalls: Vague principles that never reject anything.

explore-sections.role: Choose the page's sections from the library: finished, spec-pinned sections from sites the owner curated. The look comes from them; this step decides which ones, in what order, and what goes in their slots.
procedure: Call list_library_sections. Match sections to the brief's jobs: a hero that carries the primary action, then the sections that answer the visitor's top questions, then a close that captures (the Success section of the brief).

Propose 2 to 4 sections, plus one alternative for the hero. For each: why it fits this brief, which slots change and with what (words, pictures, the client's product UI, the canvas within the spec's range, one niche accent), and which of its bans matter here.

The option gate (protocol 4) applies here too: the sheet of library sources and rebuilds comes from list_library_sections, but any adapted section or mock-up you show as an option passes review_design with zero blockers and none of `distinct-hero-not-template`, `distinct-no-decorative-glow`, `distinct-no-accent-word-headline`, `distinct-eyebrow-restraint`, is scored by one fresh critic from screenshots only (get_critic_brief), and the owner's 1 to 10 score per option is recorded with record_taste (type score).

Show the owner one sheet: per section a row with the source (get_library_section's sourceFold, or the live sourceUrl for a lower section) and the rebuild, labelled with the section id. An owner who is not at your keyboard needs the sheet as image files, not links.
Write the media plan: for every picture slot, the real photo, video or product UI it will hold and where it comes from. No code-drawn stand-ins for photographs.

Write the design system before any section is adapted (content/sections/TOKENS.md): every --ds-* token, one ground, one ink, two greys, one accent, two families plus mono, one h2 size, one h3 style, two buttons, two radii, one container and gutter, one section rhythm. Sections keep their source geometry and motion; their paint and type come from these tokens through content/sections/roles.css (class ds on the page root). Skipping this ships a page where every section brings its source's fonts and colours (a client pilot, 2026-11-16: 41 type styles, 13 text colours, 8 radii, 8 button styles).
No section fits a need the brief has: pin a new one from a library site first (content/sections/HOW-TO-ADD.md), or ask the owner for a site to take it from. Do not design that part from scratch.

explore-directions.role: Converge the sketches into three genuinely different directions the owner could choose between.
procedure: The option gate (protocol 4) comes before the owner sees anything: draft the three with propose_directions and show them only as render_sheet sheets; each concept passes review_design with zero blockers and none of `distinct-hero-not-template`, `distinct-no-decorative-glow`, `distinct-no-accent-word-headline`, `distinct-eyebrow-restraint`; one fresh critic scores each from its screenshots only (get_critic_brief), recorded as a model's scores beside the sheet; and the owner's 1 to 10 score for every option is recorded with record_taste (type score, round `gate 2: <direction>`). Hand-made mock-ups never go to the owner, whata.design's own pages included. [Our take]

Show the directions to an owner who is not at your keyboard as one side-by-side sheet per size (desktop and mobile, the three concepts in a row, each labelled with its name and one-line north star) saved as image files, plus the north-star lines in your message. That worked better than links or prose.
Cluster the sketches and pick three directions that differ in at least two of: art-style family, mood, type class (serif, grotesque, mono, display), palette mood, page skeleton.

Concept first (studio method, get_studio concepts): write three concepts from different territories (the subject's name or story, its material, its place or culture, a metaphor for how it works, a formal or typographic system). Each has one sentence, its anchor (the specific fact about this subject it depends on), the signature moment, the emotion of the first 3 seconds, the motion verb and the frame people would screenshot; score originality, fit, feasibility and portability (could it move to another brand? lower is better). Each direction below is one concept dressed in an art direction from the library; a library style alone is not a direction. [Our take, from the awwwards method]

Span a range of ambition: one **safe** direction (closest to the owner's taste anchors from the reference board), one **stretch** (a visibly stronger look taken from the library's most distinctive sites), one **wildcard** (an unexpected combination). Anchor each on named library sites with one stated take per site ("butter-video's type scale with makingsoftware-com's ledger"). propose_directions drafts this from the brief and the owner's taste slugs and checks the spread; it is a starting point, not the answer. Three variations of one idea fail the gate.

For each, write a one-line north star ('Calm editorial finance with serif display type'), the taxonomy tags (art style up to 3, mood up to 2), the page skeleton, hero type, and the reference sites it draws on.

For each direction call get_recipe for its art styles (at most 3 tags per call, canonical slugs from list_tags such as `hand-drawn`, not invented ones such as `illustration-hand-drawn`: with 8 tags a pilot got over 60 KB of JSON, and unknown tags come back with empty rule lists) to learn upfront which Quality Bar rules it collides with and how to keep the look and pass the rules. Write those risks in the matrix. [Our take: surface accessibility risk before falling in love with a direction]
Check the three against the swap test and the niche's default look from the landscape audit: at least one direction must clearly depart from the default.

Name each direction's niche cue: what in the look says, in one second, which kind of site this is (a motif, a palette, a shape, a material). Avoiding the niche's clichés (blush, florals, script for weddings) is not the same as dropping its legitimate vocabulary: in a real run an elegant editorial direction with a timeline said nothing about weddings, and the owner asked for "more pink, patterns and graphics". Draw the cue from the niche references on the board. [Our take]

Pick each direction's lead element from the catalogue of recurring moves where one fits (get_moves: oversized type plus object, pinned scene, chaptered story, data as image, product showcase, 3D hero ...): each move lists the library sites that show it, so study them with get_section before you draw. One lead move per direction.

Name each direction's lead element: the one thing (a hero object, a layout idea, a type move, an interaction) that the niche's default page does not have and that carries the brief's message. A new skeleton is not required, but a lead element is. Read the slop versions in `trends.md` and the rules in `rules/distinct.md` (get_guidelines distinct) before you fix the three directions, so none of them is the probable default (for example cream and terracotta, a split hero with a product card, a three-column icon grid). Copy that is specific on a generic skeleton still reads as generic. [Our take]

A lead element above the fold is not enough. Write down where the lead element recurs or is answered lower on the page (a second moment: the same object in a new state, the same type move as a section break, the same interaction as the close), and make the sections below the hero differ in structure from each other (not a run of heading plus paragraphs, not the same card repeated). A page with a strong hero and a plain typographic sequence below it is still the default page. [Our take]

No photography exists (physical goods with no photos yet: a studio, a shop, a food or craft business; or a service with no photographs, or none you may use: advice, a clinic, a helpline, a firm)? The imagery rules were written with software in mind, which has an interface to show. Choose one of three, in this order, and write it in the matrix (graphics drawn in code from the page's real content, such as a data graph or a process diagram in the tokens, can serve any of them; see protocol 6 and plan_graphics): (1) the offer itself is the live object: price, seats, dates, sizes or a booking interactive built from real HTML controls with real states and real numbers (it works only when the offer has state to show: seats, slots, sizes, bundles); (2) type as image: a measurement, a date, a price or a name set large as the visual, as real text, not as an image of text; (3) leave imagery out and mark the gap in the matrix and in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, because real photographs have to be commissioned before launch. A pieces-only catalogue has no state to show: say that, and treat the missing photographs as a launch risk. Illustrations assembled from shapes in code (a drawn bowl, a cross-section) stay out (`distinct-real-imagery-and-icons`). For a service the live object is something it really has state for (opening hours, free slots, a waiting time, a self-check or calculator), and type as image can be the fact that answers the first question (a phone number and its hours, a fee, "free and independent"); photographs of people need their consent. Which recipe steps apply to a service: `np-offer-live-object` (when there is state to show), `np-live-object-accessible` (if you build one), `np-type-as-image`, `np-mark-the-gap` and `np-commission-later`; `np-menu-and-run-sheet` only when the service has rows to list (a fee table, opening hours, the steps of a process); `np-pieces-only-limit` is for goods. Recipe: `no-photography-physical-goods`. [Our take]

Public service, advice or crisis audience (people who may be in danger, in debt, ill or facing a deadline)? Decide before you design the hero what the urgent route is and where it sits: read the recipe `urgent-help-route` (what goes first, a phone number as a `tel:` link with hours and an out-of-hours route, the emergency-services boundary stated once, not relying on red alone, and how the band stacks with the primary action at 390x844) and write the choice in the matrix. If the page also takes personal data in a form, read `form-no-backend-and-privacy`. An audience with these flags usually also means the COGA rules are major (protocol 5). Read the trend records `plain-language-public-service-pages`, `charity-emotional-template` and `law-firm-authority-template` in `trends.md`: the last two are the slop versions to depart from. [Our take]

Three directions are still required, but three short columns are enough: north star, art style, type class, palette mood, skeleton and hero, lead element and its second moment, recipe and the rules it collides with. Choose the recipe with get_recipe (at most 3 tags per call).

explore-type-color.role: Make type and color concrete for each direction, with roles and proven contrast.
procedure: For each direction choose at most two type families with roles (display, body), a scale with named steps, and a measure for body text. Follow the craft rules for size, line length and line height. [Craft]

Define the palette as named roles (background, surface, text, text-muted, accent, border, focus, and state colors). Compute contrast for every text/background pair and every UI/background pair with check_contrast; fix pairs that fail: normal text 4.5:1, large text and UI parts 3:1. [Standard]

Set the display headline's line height and letter spacing from the anchors, not by eye: get_craft lists each library site's displayLeading and displayTrackingEm, and compare_to_library flags a sketch whose titles are set looser than its anchors. Large type almost always wants tighter leading and slightly negative tracking than the body; owners notice loose titles before anything else (whata.design's owner asked twice in one evening). [Our take]
State what the accent is for (one job) and keep the palette small. Reserve semantic colors for meaning. [Craft]

Fonts: use only fonts you can ship. If the owner gave brand fonts, use them. Otherwise choose one of two, and write which and why. (a) A deliberate system stack is an allowed default (for example a native transitional serif, humanist or grotesque stack): name the stack and the reason, and warn that it renders differently per operating system (a stack that begins with Charter shows Charter on Apple devices, Cambria on Windows and something else on Android or Linux): check size, line length and line breaks with the fallback face too, and state which systems you did not see. (b) An open-licence web font, saved locally and self-hosted: look in places such as Fontsource, Google Fonts (download and self-host, do not link), or Open Foundry; these are names to look in, not endorsements, and licences differ per family, so read the licence file that comes with the font and record it in assets.md before relying on it. Check that the font file is present before you rely on it. Build-time self-hosting counts as self-hosting and needs no separate download approval: in a Next.js project `next/font/google` (or `next/font/local`) downloads an open-licence family at build and serves it from the site, with no runtime link; the same goes for a Fontsource package. A system stack is a last resort, not the owner-away default: in a real run the safe reading (dropping a web serif for Charter and Georgia) made the page look generic. Show the font on the directions sheet so the owner picks it with the look. Never link a font from a CDN you cannot reach offline, and never design with a font that will silently fall back to a different one. Check the fallback in the browser at the chosen sizes. [Craft]
Do not use a reflex palette or font without a stated reason (see the distinctiveness rules). If you choose a common font or hue, write why.
ask_user: Brand fonts or colours that fix some choices? (a) keep the current logo colour and fonts where the direction allows (recommended) (b) free to change everything.

explore-copy.role: Write real headlines and calls to action before polishing visuals. Copy shapes layout, not the other way round.
procedure: For each direction write three headline options, a subhead, and the label of the primary action. Use the value proposition and tone words; be specific and plain. [Evidence: plain objective language outperformed promotional language; Craft: specific over abstract]

Scope keeps the copy (need-statement `## Scope`: keep verbatim)? Do not write new headlines. Write a placement map in headline-drafts.md instead: each existing heading, paragraph and action from content-map.md, and the new section and position it moves into; the only new words allowed are labels the new structure needs, marked as new. coverage checks it later.
Button and link labels name the result ('Book a demo', not 'Submit' or 'Learn more').
Run the swap test on every headline (replace the company name; if it still reads true for a competitor, rewrite). Strike buzzwords and filler openers. [Our take]
Check length: headline readable in two lines on mobile; paragraph and sentence length per the copy rules.

Reading level: `copy-reading-grade` targets US grade 6 to 8 for a general audience. For ESL or low-literacy audiences, or a UK public service, aim at grade 5 or lower, or CEFR B1 and GOV.UK-style plain language (short common words, one idea per sentence, the action first) and say the target in headline-drafts. [Our take: the tighter target is ours; the rule's own number is grade 6 to 8] An ESL group also gets: an offer of a translation or an interpreter (links to translated pages with `lang` and `hreflang`, the passage language marked with `lang`; say what the service can really offer, never promise an interpreter you do not have), no idioms or phrasal-verb puns, dates and numbers written out in one unambiguous format, and a plain statement of what happens next.

Legal, medical, financial or safety advice in the copy: write it as a draft, list the reviewer you need in design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, and mark it with the visible draft marker and legend until a qualified person has signed it off (`copy-expert-review-before-launch`). Do not write a claim you cannot attribute.

Forms and urgent routes: write the form's labels, the hint under each, the privacy line, the error and success messages and the phone line together (recipes `form-no-backend-and-privacy` and `urgent-help-route`): plain words, the action first, the hours as text, and "do not write bank details here" wherever a free-text box could collect sensitive data.

Facts the owner has not confirmed (a price, an opening hour, a size, a policy) stay in the copy only with the visible `.assumed` marker from the protocol (dotted underline plus a legend on the page), listed in design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md. No brackets, no bare invention, and no invented customers, numbers, quotes or press at all.

explore-hero.role: Design the first screen of each direction as something you can look at, with real copy, type and color.
procedure: Build each hero on the base kit (get_base: skip link, header, a hero skeleton) as a small HTML/CSS page using the direction's tokens, the real headline and the real action label; your own CSS adds only the lead idea. Run `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit cli widths <file>` and fix every problem before the sheet. Render it at 1440×900 and 390×844 and look at the screenshots.
The first screen must show: who/what, why it differs, the primary action, a cue that more follows, navigation. [Evidence: homepage principles]
Apply the direction's recipe steps while building (focus ring, reduced motion, contrast, media handling). [Standard + Craft]

Start from the gate 1 bundle sketches (design/03-references/bundles/): the concept for the owner's bundle and two others are refined here, not drawn again. With scope `Structure: rebuild`, draw each hero fresh: nothing of the old layout carries over except content.

Make each concept look like its references, not like a template with their colours. Two ways, pick per concept: (1) **Critique loop:** run compare_to_library on the concept with its anchor slugs (it measures scale contrast, section whitespace, lead-object share and motion against the anchors and lists the gaps), then put the concept beside its main reference at the same viewport (`cli sheet` with both files, or the reference's fold screenshot from storage/sites/), list the gaps in scale (display size against body, the largest element against the viewport), whitespace, imagery and the lead object, fix them, and repeat once more: two rounds before the owner sees it. Keep the two gap lists in notes.md. (2) **Reference rebuild:** when the owner picked a library site at gate 1, rebuild its hero as a structural re-skin (same grid, scale steps, spacing and object placement from get_design_brief and get_section), check the structure with `pnpm site score <slug> <file:// or http URL of your hero>` (the rebuild score compares section by section; read the hero section's score, the rest of the page is not built yet), then swap in this project's content, colours and imagery. Copy structure only: no text, logo, images or brand colours of the reference, and none of its audit failures. [Our take]

Presence of style, not only absence of slop: each concept needs a clear scale contrast (the display size several times the body size, or one element that fills much of the first screen), one lead object that carries the message, and deliberate whitespace. A concept that is type plus colour on an even grid is flat: fix it before the sheet. The library's heroes fill most of the first screen with their lead object, usually as a full-bleed backdrop (an image, video or code-made SVG behind the text); the kit's `hero-bleed` part does this with a scrim so text contrast holds, and get_backdrop draws the backdrop in code from the palette and the project's own content (aurora, a field of one mark per real item, contours, the brand word set huge; see content/kit/backdrops.html). An object in a column is fine when the brief needs it, but then say on the sheet that it is smaller than the references' and why. compare_to_library counts full-bleed backgrounds and judges a hero-only sketch on its first screen only. [Our take]

Order in the first screen: one clear headline, one line, one action and one lead object, with the niche cue and atmosphere around them; separate elements that compete for attention need a reason. Richness (pattern, motif, backdrop, texture) is not competition and stays. Check each concept with `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit cli types <file>`: every role takes one style and peers in a list match; the style and element counts it prints are information, not a target. [Our take]
Keep the heroes small; do not build the whole page yet.

Show each concept beside its library anchors: the concept's key frame and the fold screenshots of the two or three library sites it takes its visual language from, on one sheet (`imageSheet` in @whata/audit, or put the anchor folds from storage/sites/ next to the concept in `cli sheet`). Name what each anchor gives (canvas, type, the object, the motion). If the frame does not visibly belong next to them, it is not in the library's language yet: change the canvas, type, spacing or object, not the concept. [Our take]

Every frame a poster: the first frame of each concept is its best, with type, space and image composed on purpose; motion may only amplify it. Rough the signature moment in at least the concept you recommend (a still of its key frame is enough for the sheet), so the owner judges the idea, not a layout. [Our take, from the awwwards method]

Before the sheet, the option gate (protocol 4): each concept passes review_design with zero blockers and none of `distinct-hero-not-template`, `distinct-no-decorative-glow`, `distinct-no-accent-word-headline`, `distinct-eyebrow-restraint`, and one fresh critic scores each from its screenshots only (get_critic_brief). Fix and re-run a concept that fails; do not send it with a note.

Make the sheets and stop: render_sheet (or the audit CLI's `sheet` command) puts the three concepts side by side, labelled with name and north star, one image per size (1440x900 and 390x844), with review_design run on each concept first. Send both sheets to the owner and ask gate 2's question (explore-directions). Nothing from decide-tokens onward starts, and nothing is built in the site tree, until the owner's pick is recorded. Screenshots of a single concept: `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit cli shot <file|url> <out.png> <width> <height>`.

No photographs of a physical product? Follow the imagery plan in the direction matrix: build the live object (price, seats, dates, a calculator or booking control made of real HTML with real states and real numbers), or set a measurement, date or price large as real text, or leave the image out and mark the gap. Do not draw the product from shapes in code. A faint decorative gradient or texture that does not depict the product is ornament; one that starts to depict it (grooves that read as a wheel, a glaze) is an illustration and counts under `distinct-real-imagery-and-icons`. [Our take]
lean: type-color-studies and structure-wireframes are replaced by the draft tokens and the skeleton and hero rows of direction-matrix.md. Build every hero from those draft tokens.

A lower bar: three concepts, each a small page of about fifteen lines is enough, but each is rendered at 1440x900 and 390x844 and looked at. Run review_design on all three concepts when each audit takes under five minutes (it usually does): reviewing only the concept you expect to choose biases the comparison, and in a test the owner chose the one with the most blocker risk. Fix blocker findings on the one chosen. If time is short, say in notes.md which concept got the full review.
Check the lead element and the primary action are inside the first viewport at both sizes by screenshot: the audit does not check that.
sprint: type-color-studies and structure-wireframes are replaced by the draft tokens and the skeleton and hero rows of direction-matrix.md. Build every hero from those draft tokens.

The same lighter bar as lean: three concepts, each a small page of about fifteen lines is enough, each rendered at 1440x900 and 390x844 and looked at. Run review_design on all three when each audit takes under five minutes; the concept you expect to choose is built on the real tokens, and decide-critique on Day 3 runs review_design on the others, whose findings are then about a small page, not a finished one. Record in notes.md which concepts got the full review.

Check the lead element and the primary action are inside the first viewport at both sizes by screenshot; with an urgent-help band (recipe `urgent-help-route`) check that the band does not push the primary action below the fold at 390x844.

explore-motion.role: Decide where motion earns its place. Motion supports meaning; it is not decoration for its own sake.
procedure: List candidate motions with the purpose of each (orient, give feedback, show relationship, express brand). Drop any without a purpose.

Motion follows the concept's motion verb (get_studio motion): one micro-interaction treatment per role (primary actions, navigation, work or product images) chosen from the verb, the signature moment, the continuity between states (intro, page to page), and an idle state that keeps the concept breathing at rest. Primary targets answer in the verb, not with a colour swap alone. One clock, one easing family; big things move slower than small things. [Our take, from the awwwards method]
Pick one lead motion idea for the direction and at most two supporting ones. Name triggers (scroll, hover, click, load) and techniques. [Our take: one lead idea beats five effects]
For each, define the reduced-motion variant (replace large movement with fades; keep what it conveyed) and the pause control for anything that starts automatically. [Standard]
Set budgets: animate transform and opacity only; no layout shift; no long main-thread tasks. [Craft]
