decide-critique.role: Judge each direction against the brief, not against taste. Critique asks whether it works toward the goals.
procedure: Build a rubric from the brief's success criteria, the design principles and the anti-goals, plus one row for resemblance to the library's strongest references and the owner's taste anchors (name the sites). Give each row a weight, state it in the table, and make the resemblance row weigh at least as much as the heaviest message row: a rubric made only of message and compliance rows favours the safest direction by construction. Score each direction 1 to 5 per row with a one-sentence reason, multiply by the weight, and check that the totals equal the sum of the rows before you write them down.
Run review_design on each hero concept and add its blocker and major findings to the rubric.

Ask questions rather than proposing fixes: What problem does this solve? Who is it for? What would make it fail? Park fixes for a later pass. [Craft: critique rules: everyone is a critic, avoid problem-solving, do not rush]
Write down which strengths to carry over from each direction, even the ones you will not choose.

decide-test.role: Get evidence from people. You cannot be the test participant; plan the test and ask the owner to run it.
procedure: Write a short test script: a five-second test (show the first screen, ask what the page is for and what they would do), a preference question between directions, and one task (find X).

Ask the owner to run it with about five people per audience group and to send you the answers. Do not substitute model opinions for participants; label any model review as such. [Evidence: five users per group per round find most problems; test, fix, test again]

When the owner's score falls after a round, first put the two rounds side by side and list what the new one removed or flattened; restore that before changing anything else. "Clustered" or "too busy" asks for order (consistent styles, spacing, hierarchy, no collisions), not for fewer motifs: ask which parts feel busy, with proposed answers, before cutting. [Our take]

Between rounds, the owner's score out of 10 with one sentence of why is cheap, honest evidence and moved a real project more than any audit did. Keep an owner round log in design/05-decide/owner-rounds.md as a table `| Round | Date | Shown | Score | Owner's words | What changed |` (name library slugs in Shown when a concept was anchored on them); `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/mcp taste import --project <project>` copies the scores into this client's taste record. Label it `UNTESTED` evidence about one person's view: it is not approval and not a user test.
Run automated checks as a supplement (axe, lab Web Vitals via review_design).
Summarize results, fix what you can, and say what remains unproven.

decide-choose.role: Choose a direction and record why, so the decision can be revisited with the same facts.
procedure: An early pick: when the owner already picked one bundle or sketch at gate 1, record it here (`Owner pick:`, gate 1) at that moment and say so; gate 2 then confirms it with the built concepts instead of asking again from scratch.

Start from the owner's pick. The owner chose from the directions sheet (gate 2, explore-directions); record their words as `Owner pick: ...` at the top of the decision, with any mix they asked for, and record it with record_taste (type pick, gate 2, the project folder, the anchor slugs of the picked concept, their words). No pick recorded means this step is not done: do not decide for them (protocol 4).

Record the owner's scores too: a 1 to 10 score for every option on the sheet, one record_taste call each (type score, round `gate 2: <option>`, score, their words, slugs shown), so a rejected option's score is kept as well as the pick. If the owner gave only a pick, ask for the scores in the same message as the next question; do not infer them. The critic's scores from the option gate (protocol 4) sit beside them, labelled a model's.

Apply the decision rule from the success criteria to the critique, inclusion check and test results, and write your own scoring as advice under the heading `The model's ranking, for what it is worth`. If your ranking disagrees with the owner's pick, say so in one line and follow the pick.
Write the decision log: chosen direction, scores, reasons, rejected directions and why, what to carry over from rejected ones, and open risks.

Name the crux surfaces: the one or two parts of the page it stands or falls on (for example the hero and the booking path). They get the longest polish in realize-sweep. Choose them from the need and the brief, not from what is easiest to make beautiful.
The final choice of taste is the owner's: nothing here overrides the pick.

decide-tokens.role: Freeze the design decisions as tokens so building is mechanical and consistent.
procedure: Write the tokens: color roles with a verified contrast table, type scale (rem), spacing scale, radii, borders, elevation, motion durations and easing, container widths, breakpoints. [Craft]

Write a role table in DESIGN.md: every text role on the page (h1, section heading, card or item title, lead, body, label, numeral or stat, button, nav, caption, small print) gets exactly one token (family, size step, weight, case). Every element of a role uses that token; peers in one list or row (all values of a readout, all phase names) are one role, and an override for one member is a defect. Keep the hero to about four styles and the page to about eight. In a real run the owner's first complaint was "too many font variations, same-level things don't have the same font". `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit cli types <file>` checks it. [Our take]
Produce three files: DESIGN.md (the agent-readable summary with dos and don'ts), tokens.json in the W3C design-tokens format, tokens.css (CSS custom properties).
Verify every contrast pair again with check_contrast and put the ratios in DESIGN.md. Include the recipe steps that apply to this direction.
State the anti-slop decisions: which defaults you chose deliberately and why.

Fonts: use the family shown on the sheet the owner picked from. Build-time self-hosting of an open-licence family (`next/font/google` or `next/font/local` in Next.js, a Fontsource package) is self-hosting and needs no separate download approval. A system stack remains allowed but only as a choice the owner saw on the sheet, never as a silent default; name it and warn that it renders as a different face per operating system (Charter on Apple devices, Cambria on Windows, another face on Android or Linux), and keep the same stack in tokens.json, tokens.css and DESIGN.md. For a web font, open-licence places to look are Fontsource, Google Fonts (download and self-host, never link) and Open Foundry, as names only: read the licence file that comes with the font and record it in assets. realize-components.role: Define the small set of components the page needs and build them accessibly from established patterns.
procedure: List only the components the page uses (navigation, button, link, card, form field, accordion, dialog, tabs, carousel...). Each gets: purpose, states, tokens, and the accessibility pattern it follows.

Form errors: `comp-alert-no-focus-no-autodismiss` forbids moving focus to a message, while the common accessible error-summary pattern moves focus to the summary. Resolve it this way: an empty `role=alert` region exists at load (`comp-live-region-exists-before-content`); on a failed submit fill it with the summary text and do not call `focus()` on it; move focus to the first invalid field; keep each error in text next to its field and keep what the user typed. procedure: List each asset: purpose, source, license, format, size, responsive variants. Prefer modern formats; set width and height; never lazy-load the likely LCP image; give it fetchpriority high. [Standard + Craft]

A creator's own videos and photos often contain other people (photos pinned on a board, a friend in frame, a screenshot of a follower). Rules about consent for photographs of people cover strangers; here, choose frames or crops that show only the person who owns the page, by eye, because automated frame selection does not see the others. Note each exception in the asset list.

Graphics made in code: for each section, decide the graphic with plan_graphics (pass the sections and tokens.css). Draw data graphs and diagrams as SVG or HTML from the real content in the project's tokens (colour roles, type scale, one stroke width), give each a text equivalent (the numbers as text or a table, the steps as a list) and check every stroke and label with check_contrast (ui 3:1, text 4.5:1). A number still marked `.assumed` stays marked inside the graph. A graph or diagram encodes content and is allowed; a scene, product, person or place drawn from shapes is not (`distinct-real-imagery-and-icons`). realize-build.role: Build the page. Meaning first, then presentation, then behavior; content must work when the enhancements fail.
procedure: Do not build in the site tree before the owner has picked a direction (direction-decision.md has `Owner pick:`). If you find unpicked work there (a build of a direction the owner did not choose), do not carry it forward: say so and ask whether to discard it.

Restyling an existing site that uses a component library (for example shadcn with Tailwind)? Do not rebuild the components. Map the design's colour roles onto the library's own role variables inside one scoped class (such as a theme class on the section or header), keep new CSS in a cascade layer (`@layer components`) so the library's utilities still win (unlayered custom CSS beat Tailwind's `hidden` in a test). First grep the global CSS for unlayered `*`, `html` and `body` rules: an unlayered `* { border-color: ... }` beats every layered border colour and stops the library's own border utilities from applying, so where such a rule sets border-color or colour, do not layer that CSS, and change the library's component files only where a role cannot express the change.

After every CSS change, confirm the new rule is in the stylesheet the server actually sends (fetch it, or read the computed style in the browser) before trusting a review: a dev server that missed three edits made the audit judge stale CSS without any warning.

Re-theming library components (shadcn and similar) breaks text at 200% in the same few places: badges that clip text, `line-clamp`, fixed-height bars and rows, `grid-cols-N` without a mobile fallback, and flex rows that cannot wrap. Check those five before the first audit.
Write control borders and other colours the audit must read as plain hex or rgb; the audit cannot always read modern colour functions (`oklch()`, `lab()`) and may report a border that is not there.

Name your own classes so they cannot collide with the project's utility framework: in Tailwind projects a section class `table` became `display: table` and shrank every such section to its content, and a `spine` class restyled every list. Prefix page classes or scope them under one page class.

Studio build (get_studio engine, nextjs or astro, patterns, layout): compose each section with a different layout family and make the static page complete and beautiful with motion off; then add motion through the studio engine (one clock, page lifecycle, data attributes; copy it, do not rewrite it) and build the concept as one driver module (one variable, such as scroll progress or time, drives every visual that carries the concept). Design the reduced-motion and no-JS versions on purpose. Avoid, unless the concept demands it: an eyebrow label above every heading, glass everywhere, decorative 01/02/03 when the content is not a sequence, three equal cards.

New page or a rebuilt structure: start from the base kit parts (get_base) in the project's tokens, and adapt them to the stack (components in a framework, partials in a static site); keep their accessibility details (menu button states, form error wiring, 44 px targets, wrapping rows).

Choose the stack from the constraints. Write semantic HTML first (landmarks, headings, real links and buttons), then CSS from the tokens (no raw hex in components), then behavior as enhancement. [Craft: layers; progressive enhancement]
Apply the direction's recipe steps and the component patterns. Keep the DOM order equal to the reading order; add a skip link; keep focus visible.
Read the rule list for the build once before starting (get_guidelines topic: build) and keep generate_hints in mind; re-run review_design after each section and fix blockers immediately.
Commit in small steps (if the project allows version control); keep a CHANGELOG of decisions that deviate from the tokens.

Rebuilding a page after a reference the owner names ("duplicate X", "make it like X"): measure X into the library first (get_sections and get_section give its order, sizes and motion beats) and copy those numbers; take nothing of its brand (`distinct-reference-not-brand`): its object becomes one made from the subject's world, its pictures come from the subject or the library with credit, and a paid font is replaced by a free one in the same role. Put the rebuild beside X at both sizes before the owner sees it.

Several agents building one site at once (a home and a wiki in parallel, say): before either writes styles, one of them puts every shared value in one tokens file (colours with their contrast, type, radii, container, gutter, section gap, header offset) loaded after the global CSS, and both read only those variables, never raw values. Agree in writing who owns which files and shared classes; a shared class is changed only by its owner, and a look the owner wants on one page only is scoped to that page. Each agent stages only its own files. Before any commit, the full build must pass with everyone's uncommitted edits in the tree (a type error in the other agent's file still breaks your deploy). A push deploys every local commit on the branch, the other agent's too: ask the owner before pushing work that is not yours, and tell the other agent the commit you pushed.

Unconfirmed facts shown on the page (see protocol 3.2): mark each with the visible `.assumed` marker, never brackets, add a legend on the page, and list each in design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md. For a marked phone number or address inside a link, follow the `<Assumed>` pattern in `rules/build.md` (a solid link underline plus an inner marker; one legend plus `aria-describedby`).

Public-service or crisis audience: build the urgent route from the recipe `urgent-help-route` (the emergency-services line once, a `tel:` link with hours and an out-of-hours route, contrast and text instead of red alone) and check at 390x844 that it does not push the primary action below the first screen. Forms: build every form from `form-no-backend-and-privacy` (labels, `type`, `inputmode` and `autocomplete`, native `required`, the no-backend `mailto:` fallback with its honest success text, the privacy line, and no promise that anything was sent). If the audience flags the COGA rules, build to them as majors (`rules/build.md` lists all fifteen). [Our take]

Legal, medical, financial or safety advice on the page: it stays under the draft marker and legend until a qualified person has reviewed it (`copy-expert-review-before-launch`); record the reviewer and the date or the open question in design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.
sections: homepage-design, component-set, motion-spec, assets and design-tokens do not exist in this track. section-pick.md replaces all five: build from the picked library sections (get_library_section for each), in the picked order.

Copy sections.css, roles.css and sections.js unchanged, then each section's markup. Put the design system's --ds-* tokens from section-pick.md on the page root together with the class ds, so every section takes its type, colour, buttons, radii, container and rhythm from the one system. A longer headline or a different object may need a slot the spec allows (for example the h1 stepping down until it fits one line). A change the spec does not allow is a change to the section: stop and ask the owner, or pin a new section (content/sections/HOW-TO-ADD.md).
Every picture slot gets real media from the media plan. Code-drawn stand-ins for photos read as cheap.

realize-subtract.role: Remove what the build does not need. Agents and first drafts add; this step only takes away.
procedure: List every element in each section of the built page at desktop and mobile: headings, lines of copy, icons, dividers, badges, labels, metadata, decorative shapes, hover effects, animations.

For each element ask: what job does it do for the visitor or the goal, and what is lost if it goes? Remove it if the answer is nothing, if another element already does the job, or if it only fills space. Prefer removing to restyling.

Watch for what builders add by habit: a second line of explanation under a clear heading, an icon on every list item, a divider between sections that already differ, metadata (dates, counts, tags) nobody asked for, a third button next to the primary action, repeated claims in different words.
Keep what the brief, the recipe or the quality bar requires (skip link, labels, alt text, legal lines), even if it looks like clutter. Removing a required element is a regression.

Never subtract the style. The lead object, the niche cue (motifs, pattern, palette), the atmosphere (backdrop, glow, texture) and the display type are what make the page look designed; they are not clutter. Remove habit-added extras and inconsistencies (a second style in one role, colliding parts, duplicate explanations), not richness. After subtracting, run compare_to_library and put the page beside its previous round: if the lead object shrank or the motifs went, put them back. In a real run a subtract-and-simplify round removed the florals, pattern and glow, and the owner's score fell from 6.5 to 5: "too simple, no style". [Our take]
Write the subtract log: each removal with a reason, and each element kept on the edge with the job it does. Re-run review_design: the removals must not have introduced failures.

realize-sweep.role: Look at every state of the page once, on purpose, and keep a log of the small issues so they are fixed together instead of one reaction at a time.
procedure: Review the build's own trail first: the commit list, the build notes, the changelog of deviations, and any screenshots or logs the build produced. Look for anything you did not expect (a component you did not plan, a dependency, a new section, a changed token). A surprise means the brief or the direction was not understood: go back to the decision and the brief before polishing.

List every state the page can be in: each section; hover, focus, active and disabled controls; menus and dialogs opened; forms empty, filled, with an error, and submitted; loading and empty content; reduced motion; no JavaScript; dark scheme if present; widths 320, 390, 768, 1440; text at 200%.

Capture a screenshot of each state, grouped by section, and note any bug met on the way (broken link, overflow, wrong state, console error). Use a browser tool or Playwright; a state you cannot reach is listed as not seen, not skipped silently.
Skim the set once for surprises (not details): are these the screens you expected? Then go through it marking small, obvious fixes and fix them at once.

Anything small that is not obvious, or that touches the design (spacing rhythm, label wording, a colour that is a little off), goes in the papercut log instead of a spot fix. Spot fixes made one at a time drift the page away from its constraints.

Shared chrome changed (header, footer, navigation, a theme applied site-wide)? It touches every page and moves the done bar from one file to many (in a test, eleven edits outside the homepage): confirm with the owner up front that the done bar may touch it. Also audit one inner page, and list the accessibility problems that were already in the shared chrome (focus ring, small targets, controls dead without JavaScript) separately from the ones this work introduced, so old debts are visible and not mistaken for regressions. Compare with the baseline audit.

Detail pass (what separates agency-grade from cheap): no default-looking controls (style native date, select and file inputs; buttons with a clear primary, secondary and text hierarchy), small labels set deliberately (small caps or tracked caps, numerals for steps), hairline rules and frames that give structure, real images framed or cropped on purpose, illustration with fills and layers rather than single thin strokes, hover and focus states designed rather than inherited, and secondary text large enough to hold its own beside the display type. Compare each section with its anchor's section crop (get_section) and list the details the anchor has that the page lacks. In a real run the owner scored a page with restored richness 7/10 and said "still feels cheap, lack of details". [Our take]

Conversion pass: the capture named in the brief is in the first screen, repeated after each major section and in a closing band; the value exchange sits next to each form; the success and error states are honest; any proof is real (unconfirmed counts stay marked). [Our take]
Density check: count words and links per screen at 1440 and 390. More than about 150 words or 30 links in one screen is overloaded: move, group or cut, and say what you moved. [Our take]

Choose the crux surfaces named in direction-decision.md (the one or two the page stands or falls on, for example the hero and the booking path) and give them a longer pass: other variants, other copy, the details.

realize-qa.role: Prove the build against the Quality Bar. Automated results are a baseline, not a verdict.
procedure: Measure a production build behind compression: a static export served by a plain local server sends files uncompressed, and on a throttled phone that read as a 5 to 6 s first paint for a page that paints in 1.4 s with gzip. Serve it with `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit serve <out dir> [port]` (gzip, like a CDN), or measure the deployed preview.

Critic pass (get_critic_brief): build for production, shoot desktop, mobile, reduced motion and keyboard states, and give a fresh subagent the critic brief and the screenshots only. Every category (Design, Usability, Creativity, Content) must reach 8 with evidence; its fix list is the next pass, and its one-line reading of the idea must match the concept. At least two passes; a new critic each time. Finish with 'remove one accessory'. Record the scores in design/06-realize/critic.md as a model's scores.

Run review_design (or the audit CLI) on desktop and mobile; list every failure and every rule that needs a person. A rule the audit did not evaluate is not a pass: the audit lists the rules it skipped, and '0 failures' only means none of the rules it did check failed. Serve the build over http (not file://) so stylesheets load.

State and keyboard checks are owned by realize-sweep when it ran (states, widths, 200% text, reduced motion, no-JS): link to its state-sweep.md instead of repeating them, and do here only the checks the sweep does not cover (screen reader or accessibility tree, forced colours, performance, the rest of this list).

Do the manual list. Owned by realize-sweep when it ran, so link and do not repeat: keyboard-only pass, text at 200%, 320 px reflow, reduced motion, dark mode, no-JS load. Owned here: a screen reader smoke test (VoiceOver: headings, landmarks, links, forms, dialogs; if you cannot run a screen reader, read the accessibility tree with Playwright's `page.accessibility.snapshot()` or `locator.ariaSnapshot()` for headings, landmarks, names, roles and states, and record the result as `accessibility tree only, not a screen reader test`: it is not a substitute and the owner should have someone run VoiceOver or NVDA); zoom 400%; text spacing override; forced colors; slow network. When the sweep did not run, do the owned-by-sweep checks here as well. [Standard + Craft]

Give the audit an absolute path for a local file (in the pilot a relative path was resolved from the audit package folder, not from the working folder, the page did not load, and fake findings were printed); if the report says the page failed to load, its findings are not about your page: fix the path and run again.

Reflow and text stress: if the audit lists a 320 px or 200% text overflow (a sideways scroll at 320 px, at 200% text size or with text spacing) as `check` ("needs a person"), do not read it as a pass: a measured overflow is a failure of `a11y-reflow`. Fix it (grid `minmax(0, 1fr)`, `overflow-wrap`, wrapping flex rows) or justify the exception in writing with the measured width, then run the audit again. [Our take]

Reflow culprit: the audit names the first element that overflows, not the cause, and the named element can change while the overflow width stays the same. Find the cause by bisecting: hide sections one at a time until the overflow drops, then hide inside that section. Typical culprits are a long word in a footer paragraph, a heading in a wide display face, a table and a field row.

Audit a production build when one is possible: the dev server's overlay or indicator can widen the page at 200% text and show up as a false overflow. If the build cannot run (no disk, no secrets), say so, run typecheck, lint and a dev-server render, name any dev-only indicator as a known false source, and mark performance `unmeasured`.

Gaps the audit may leave: read the audit's `not evaluated` list. If it lists `ux-primary-cta-above-fold` (a major rule), check the first viewport by screenshot at 390x844 and 1440x900 and confirm the primary action is fully visible without scrolling at both: a page can pass every automated check and still have its button below the fold on a phone. Do the same by hand for any of these the audit lists as not evaluated: `craft-body-size-min` (computed font size of running text, at 320 and 1280 px; 14 px is our review threshold, not a standard) and `craft-breakpoints-content-based` (sweep the width from 320 to 1920 px in steps of about 40 px and look for horizontal scroll, overlaps and clipped text). Record each as a manual check with the method.

`--verified` entries: say in `by` whether a person or a model verified the rule (for example `model: <name>` or `person: <name>`). A model's check is a model review, not a person's; rules that need real people (screen reader, test with people) cannot honestly be verified this way and stay open.

Lead element and the page below it: confirm the lead element is in the first viewport at both sizes, and describe in two or three sentences what the page looks like below the hero. The lead element must also recur or be answered lower on the page (a second moment), and the sections below the hero must differ in structure from each other (not a plain run of headings and paragraphs, not the same card repeated). If the page below the hero is a plain sequence, say so and fix it or record it as an open issue. Automated checks cannot see this. [Our take]
Check performance (lab Web Vitals: LCP 2.5 s, CLS 0.1; INP needs field data), page weight, fonts, images.

Frequency and absolute words ('every week', 'daily', 'always', 'never', 'all') are claims too: check each against the data (post dates, release logs, order counts) and use the measured wording ('most weeks', 'about 1.5 a week').
Check copy against the copy rules (specific, plain, consistent) and distinctiveness (swap test, defaults justified).

Inherited or new: before you change anything, save an audit of the current page (`pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit cli <url> --out design/00-baseline/audit.json`), then run review_design with `baseline` set to that file so the report splits failures into new, inherited and fixed. Inherited failures in shared chrome (header, footer, global tokens) are listed separately with whether need-constraints allows you to change them; they are not passes, and new failures are yours to fix.

Type census and header: run `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit cli types <url>` (one style per role, peers in a list alike, first-screen counts) and `cli widths <url>` (now 320, 390, 768, 1024, 1280, 1440 and 320 at 200% text, with overlapping text caught). Look at screenshots of the header at 1440, 1280, 1100, 1024 and 390: shared chrome that passes every rule can still collide between breakpoints. When the chrome is in scope and broken, the kit header (get_base) is the replacement.

Content coverage (when need-statement's scope keeps any content): run `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit cli coverage <old url> <new url>`. Every block it lists as missing or partly kept must be explained by content-map.md (moved, reworked in scope, or dropped by the owner); with `SEO: keep`, every SEO field must be `same` and no internal link lost. Paste the summary line into the QA report.
Count the unconfirmed facts still on the page (the `.assumed` marks) and list them in the QA report; they are open issues, not passes.
Fix blockers and majors; list the rest with owners.
Say honestly what the result is. With no owner sign-off, no user test and no screen-reader run, the status is `built, audited, not approved`, with the list of what was not done.
sections: success-criteria is replaced by the Success section of the brief.

Check the design system held: `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/audit cli types <url>` reports no mixed role group (a display-size closing line is the one allowed exception), and the page uses one section ground, at most two corner radii for controls and media, and only the primary and secondary buttons. Fix through tokens or roles.css, never per section.

The audits are checks on a finished look, not a source of it. Fix every blocker. Where a fix would change a section's pinned design, prefer the accessible version and record the deviation in that section's spec under 'Accessibility changes from the source'; where the design is the source's and the rule is a heuristic (small text inside decorative product UI, a nested panel), record it as justified with the reason.

Close with the owner's score (record_taste type score, round = the section ids). Below the previous round: compare section by section with the sources before changing anything; never add rules to rescue a section.

reflect-iterate.role: Decide what to change next and what the project taught about the process.
procedure: Copy the owner's round scores into this client's taste record: `pnpm --silent --filter @whata/mcp taste import --project <project dir>` (reads design/05-decide/owner-rounds.md), then `taste profile --project <project dir>`: it also adds the project's line to the shared clients record, so the next client in the same niche starts from a better recommended answer.

Turn findings (metrics, QA leftovers, owner feedback, and the papercut log from realize-sweep, handled together as one design pass, not one by one) into a prioritized list of changes with expected impact and effort.
Run a short retrospective: what helped, what wasted time, which assumptions were wrong, which rules or recipes needed correcting.
If exploration changed the problem, update the brief version and note why (the brief is a hypothesis). [Evidence]

output.template:
# Retro and next changes
## Prioritized changes
## What helped / what wasted time
## Assumptions proven wrong
## Corrections needed in the guide (rules, recipes, steps)

checks: Corrections to the guide are listed, not forgotten.

done_when: A prioritized list and retro notes exist.
pitfalls: Treating launch as the end.

reflect-archive.role: Write the case study and teach the library: add the finished site so future projects can use it as a reference.
procedure: Write a one-page case study: need, brief, the three directions, the decision, results, what you would do differently.

Add the live site to the gallery (skip if you may not write to the library; then write the entry as a ready-to-run command list for the owner): pnpm site add <url>, capture and audit run automatically; write the tags with its facts and apply them with status review.
Write its style record from the design tokens and the decision log (pnpm site style).

output.template:
# Case study
Need > brief > directions > decision > result > lessons.

checks: The site is in the library with tags and a style record.

done_when: The case study exists and the site is in the library.
pitfalls: Skipping the archive: the library only improves if finished work goes back in.

rules.statement: Every informative image has a text alternative that serves the same purpose; purely decorative images have an empty alt so they are skipped. (WCAG 1.1.1, A)
rules.why: People who cannot see an image still need what it conveys. Missing alt text appears on 53.1% of analyzed home pages.

check.how: Automated check finds missing alt (axe `image-alt`); a person judges whether the text actually matches the purpose.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Give every informative image alt text that states what it conveys; use alt="" for decorative images; never leave alt missing.

rules.statement: Prerecorded video with sound has captions. (WCAG 1.2.2, A)
rules.why: Deaf and hard-of-hearing people, and people watching without sound.

check.how: Play every video with sound off; check captions exist and are accurate.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Caption every video that has speech or meaningful sound; decorative silent loops need no captions but must not carry information.

rules.statement: Prerecorded video has audio description or a text alternative covering the visual content. (WCAG 1.2.3 A, 1.2.5 AA)
rules.why: Blind and low-vision people miss information that is only shown.

check.how: Check whether key visual information is described by narration, a description track or a transcript. WCAG 1.2.1 requires an alternative or audio track for prerecorded video-only content and its Understanding page does not exempt decorative or background video; 1.1.1 says pure decoration should be ignorable by assistive technology. Treating a purely decorative loop as decoration is an inference from 1.1.1.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Describe key visual information in video through narration, a description track or a transcript.

rules.statement: Structure that is visible (headings, lists, tables, form labels, regions) is also in the markup, not only in the styling. (WCAG 1.3.1, A)
rules.why: Assistive technology navigates by structure.

check.how: Automated checks for headings, lists, labels and landmarks; read the page outline in a screen reader or the accessibility tree.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Use real headings, lists, tables, labels and landmarks in the markup; never fake structure with styling.

rules.statement: The reading order in the code matches the meaning of the page, even if CSS moves things around visually. (WCAG 1.3.2, A)
rules.why: Screen reader and keyboard users follow the code order.

check.how: Compare DOM order with visual order. Failure F1 is positioning that changes meaning; technique C27 is making DOM order match visual order. MDN: CSS `order` changes only the visual order, not the logical or tab order, which creates a mismatch for screen reader and keyboard users. A check with CSS disabled is a practical test (not described on WCAG's page).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Keep DOM order equal to reading order; do not use CSS order or absolute positioning to rearrange meaningful content.

rules.statement: Instructions do not rely only on shape, color, size, position or sound ("click the green button on the right"). (WCAG 1.3.3, A)
rules.why: People cannot always perceive those characteristics.

check.how: Read all instructions and labels; each must work without seeing the layout.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Write instructions that work without seeing shape, color or position: name the control, not its look or place.

rules.statement: Content works in both portrait and landscape unless one orientation is essential. (WCAG 1.3.4, AA)
rules.why: Some people mount their device in one orientation.

check.how: Rotate a device or emulator and check nothing is locked.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Do not lock the page to portrait or landscape.

rules.statement: Fields that collect personal data (name, email, address...) declare their purpose with the right autocomplete value. (WCAG 1.3.5, AA)
rules.why: Lets browsers and tools fill and present fields predictably.

check.how: Check `autocomplete` attributes on user-data fields (axe `autocomplete-valid`).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Add the correct autocomplete value to fields that collect personal data (name, email, address, phone).

rules.statement: Color is never the only way to show information, state, errors or required fields. (WCAG 1.4.1, A)
rules.why: Color-blind and low-vision people, and monochrome displays.

check.how: Use another cue wherever color carries meaning: text, an icon, underline, weight or pattern (techniques G14, G182). Error and required fields must not rely on color alone (F81); links in text must be distinguishable from surrounding text, for example 3:1 contrast against the text (G183) or another cue (F73). WCAG lists color-vision simulators for checking; grayscale is a quick approximation, not a WCAG test.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Pair every color signal (state, error, link) with text, an icon, an underline or a pattern.

rules.statement: Audio that plays automatically for more than 3 seconds can be paused or stopped, or its volume controlled separately from the system volume. (WCAG 1.4.2, A)
rules.why: Autoplaying sound interferes with screen readers and with people who cannot easily find the source.

check.how: Load the page with sound on; check for autoplaying audio and its controls.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Never autoplay audio; autoplay video muted and provide a control to start sound.

rules.statement: Text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background, or 3:1 for large text (18 pt, or 14 pt bold). (WCAG 1.4.3, AA)
rules.why: Low-contrast text is the most common detected failure: 83.9% of analyzed home pages.

check.how: Automated check (axe `color-contrast`) misses text over images and gradients; check those by hand, in all states and themes.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Keep text at 4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for large text); compute every pair with check_contrast and put text on solid surfaces or scrims, not directly on gradients, images or video.

rules.statement: Text can be enlarged to 200% by the browser without losing content or function. (WCAG 1.4.4, AA)
rules.why: Many people enlarge text.

check.how: WCAG's pass condition: text can be scaled to 200% using at least one scaling mechanism browsers offer (page zoom, text-only zoom, a larger default font size), with no loss of content or function. Text may shrink at smaller breakpoints if 200% is still reachable; the example is 20 px at 100% in a 1280 px window needing to display at twice that size when enlarged. Viewport-unit-only sizing is a listed failure (F94). Measured 2026-11-05: stepped rem sizes doubled under text-only enlargement; vw-only did not change; a clamp() with a vw term grew 1.14× (see content/learn/measurements).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Size text in rem or em; never in viewport units alone; check the page at 200% text size without clipping.

rules.statement: Text is real text, not an image of text, except for logos and cases where the look is essential. (WCAG 1.4.5, AA)
rules.why: Real text can be resized, recolored and read aloud.

check.how: Check headlines, buttons and navigation for text baked into images. Exceptions: the image of text can be customized by the user, the presentation is essential, or it is a logotype.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Use real text for headlines, buttons and navigation; images of text only for logotypes.

rules.statement: At 320 CSS pixels wide (400% zoom at 1280 px) content works without two-dimensional scrolling, apart from exceptions such as maps and wide tables. (WCAG 1.4.10, AA)
rules.why: People with low vision zoom in and rely on a single column.

check.how: Set the viewport to 320 px wide (vertical scrolling content) and 256 px tall (horizontal scrolling content); ordinary content must not need two-dimensional scrolling. Exceptions: maps, diagrams, video, games, presentations, data tables, toolbar-in-view interfaces. A horizontal carousel passes if each panel fits 320 px; a table in its own scroll container passes if the content around it reflows. Also run it at 320 px with the root font size at 200% (and with the WCAG text-spacing overrides applied): fixed rem tracks (minmax(15rem,1fr) is 480 px at 200%), padding that leaves a 96 px column, and display words wider than the viewport are the usual causes. Measured in Chrome on the 2026-11 recipe demos: this extra pass found overflow in 11 of 18 demos that passed the plain 320 px check.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Make the layout work at 320 CSS px wide without sideways scrolling, also when the root text size is 200%: write grid tracks as minmax(min(Nrem, 100%), 1fr), give headings and long strings overflow-wrap: anywhere, step display sizes down in a rem media query (max-width: 30rem) instead of clamp() with vw, cut container padding under 30rem, let flex rows wrap (inputs and buttons in a row: flex: 1 1 6rem; min-width: 0, not a 12rem basis that cannot shrink; nav and pill lists get flex-wrap: wrap), and put wide tables or galleries in their own focusable scroll region (role=region, aria-label, tabindex=0).

rules.statement: UI components and graphics needed to understand the content have at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors. (WCAG 1.4.11, AA)
rules.why: Buttons, inputs, focus rings and icons must be perceivable.

check.how: Check borders of inputs, icon buttons, toggles and focus indicators; automated tools cover only part.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Give input borders, icon buttons, toggles and focus indicators at least 3:1 contrast against their surroundings.

rules.statement: Content still works when users override line height, paragraph, letter and word spacing. (WCAG 1.4.12, AA)
rules.why: People with dyslexia and low vision change spacing.

check.how: Apply a text-spacing bookmarklet or user stylesheet; check for clipped or overlapping text.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Do not clip text in fixed-height containers; test with line height 1.5, letter spacing 0.12em, word spacing 0.16em.

rules.statement: Content that appears on hover or focus can be dismissed without moving the pointer, can be hovered over, and stays until dismissed. (WCAG 1.4.13, AA)
rules.why: Magnifier users and keyboard users trigger tooltips and menus differently.

check.how: Test every tooltip, mega menu and hover card with mouse, keyboard and zoom.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Make hover or focus content (tooltips, menus) dismissible with Escape, hoverable, and persistent until dismissed.

rules.statement: All functionality can be operated with a keyboard alone. (WCAG 2.1.1, A)
rules.why: Keyboard, switch and voice users.

check.how: Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space and arrow keys through the whole page, including menus and dialogs.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Make every function work with the keyboard using native controls; test with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space and arrows.

rules.statement: Keyboard focus can always be moved away from any component. (WCAG 2.1.2, A)
rules.why: A trap locks users in.

check.how: Tab through every widget, including embeds, modals and 3D canvases. Deliberately restricting focus (a modal dialog) is allowed if users can leave by Esc or buttons; any non-standard exit method must be explained to the user.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Ensure focus can always leave a component; modals close with Escape and return focus.

rules.statement: Single-character keyboard shortcuts can be turned off, remapped, or only work when the component has focus. (WCAG 2.1.4, A)
rules.why: Speech-input users trigger shortcuts by accident.

check.how: List all single-key shortcuts (letters, numbers, punctuation, symbols, also those needing Shift, and key sequences such as G then A). Each must be turn-off-able, remappable to include a non-printable key, or active only while its component has focus. Exceptions: listbox type-ahead, menus opened with a modified key, access keys.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Avoid single-key shortcuts, or let users turn them off or remap them, or make them work only while their component has focus.

rules.statement: Time limits can be turned off, adjusted or extended, unless an exception applies. (WCAG 2.2.1, A)
rules.why: People need different amounts of time.

check.how: Look for timeouts, auto-advancing content and expiring sessions.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Avoid time limits; if one is needed let the user turn it off, adjust or extend it.

rules.statement: Moving, blinking, scrolling or auto-updating content that starts automatically and runs alongside other content can be paused, stopped or hidden. (WCAG 2.2.2, A)
rules.why: Motion distracts and can make content unreadable. WCAG 2.2.2 (see the Understanding page) sets the five-second threshold for automatically starting moving content.

check.how: Applies to moving, blinking or scrolling content that starts automatically (including by hover, focus or scrolling into view), lasts more than five seconds and runs alongside other content; auto-updating content has no five-second exception. A control that pauses only while focused does not qualify. Best practice is one control for all moving content. Check carousels, background video, marquees and ambient animations.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Give a visible, keyboard-reachable control to pause anything that moves automatically for more than five seconds (video, loops, tickers, carousels).

rules.statement: Nothing flashes more than three times per second unless below the defined thresholds. (WCAG 2.3.1, A)
rules.why: Flashing can trigger seizures.

check.how: Pass if no more than three general or red flashes occur in any one second (content within that limit passes without a tool), or the flashes stay below the thresholds: a general flash is an opposing luminance change of at least 10% with the darker state below 0.80, and the flashing area stays within 0.006 steradians of a 10-degree field (WCAG estimates 341×256 px at 1024×768).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Never flash content more than three times per second; keep glows static or slow.

rules.statement: A mechanism, such as a skip link or correct landmarks and headings, lets users skip repeated blocks. (WCAG 2.4.1, A)
rules.why: Keyboard and screen reader users should not tab through the full navigation every time.

check.how: The skip link should be the first focusable control and may be visible only on focus; WCAG does not require it to be visible when it lacks focus (G1). Landmarks (ARIA11) or headings (H69) are also sufficient. WebAIM: a hidden skip link must become prominently visible on focus; do not use display:none or the hidden attribute; a skip link is not strictly required where a starting h1 or a main region meets the criterion.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Put a skip link first in the DOM with a z-index above hero layers, and use landmarks (header, nav, main, footer).

rules.statement: The page has a title that describes its purpose. (WCAG 2.4.2, A)
rules.why: The title is the first thing a screen reader says and what appears in tabs and history.

check.how: Check `<title>` is present, specific and different from other pages (axe `document-title`).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Give the page a specific <title> that names its purpose.

rules.statement: Keyboard focus moves in an order that keeps meaning and operability. (WCAG 2.4.3, A)
rules.why: Random jumps disorient.

check.how: Tab through the page and compare focus order with the visual and logical order.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Keep focus order equal to the reading order; avoid positive tabindex.

rules.statement: The purpose of each link can be understood from its text, or from its text with its context. (WCAG 2.4.4, A)
rules.why: Screen reader users list links out of context. Empty links appear on 46.3% of analyzed home pages.

check.how: List all links; flag "click here", "more", and links with no name (axe `link-name`).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Make every link's text meaningful on its own; no 'click here' or 'read more' without context.

rules.statement: Headings and labels describe their topic or purpose. (WCAG 2.4.6, AA)
rules.why: Helps people scan and navigate.

check.how: Read the headings list; each should make sense on its own.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Write headings and labels that describe their topic; keep one h1 and a logical heading order.

rules.statement: Every keyboard-operable element shows a visible focus indicator. (WCAG 2.4.7, AA)
rules.why: Keyboard users must see where they are.

check.how: Tab through the page; the focus indicator is always visible with 3:1 contrast against what it sits on, and `outline: none` is never left without a replacement. In forced-colors mode outline and border colors are forced to system colors and stay visible, while box-shadow is removed, so draw focus with outline or border, not box-shadow alone.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Style :focus-visible with a solid, high-contrast outline and offset; never remove the outline without a replacement; use outline rather than box-shadow alone.

rules.statement: A focused element is not entirely hidden behind sticky headers, cookie banners or chat widgets. (WCAG 2.4.11, AA, new in 2.2)
rules.why: Keyboard users lose their place when focus lands under an overlay.

check.how: Tab through the page with sticky elements and banners present, at several viewport sizes. A focused item may be partly covered but not entirely (failure F110). Technique C43 (CSS scroll-padding) is the sufficient technique listed; a banner can also pass by being modal or closing when it loses focus.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Add scroll-padding for sticky headers and avoid banners or widgets that cover focused elements.

rules.statement: Anything that needs a multi-point or path-based gesture (pinch, swipe) can also be done with a single pointer, unless essential. (WCAG 2.5.1, A)
rules.why: People with motor impairments cannot always do complex gestures.

check.how: Check swipers, maps and sliders for single-tap alternatives.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Offer a single-tap or button alternative for every swipe, pinch or path gesture.

rules.statement: Single-pointer actions can be cancelled or undone, or do not fire on the down event. (WCAG 2.5.2, A)
rules.why: Prevents accidental activation.

check.how: Check that buttons act on release, and drag-start actions can be aborted.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Trigger actions on release (click), not on press, so they can be cancelled.

rules.statement: The accessible name of a control contains its visible label text. (WCAG 2.5.3, A)
rules.why: Speech-input users say what they see.

check.how: Compare visible labels with aria-label and names in the accessibility tree.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Make a control's accessible name start with or include its visible label text.

rules.statement: Functions triggered by device motion also have a normal control and can be turned off. (WCAG 2.5.4, A)
rules.why: Not everyone can shake or tilt a device.

check.how: Look for shake, tilt and gyroscope effects.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Do not rely on device motion; provide a normal control and let users disable motion triggers.

rules.statement: Anything that needs dragging can also be done with a single press, without dragging. (WCAG 2.5.7, AA, new in 2.2)
rules.why: Dragging is hard or impossible for some people.

check.how: Check sliders, sortable lists and reveal-on-drag effects for a single-pointer alternative (buttons, tap-to-place, direct selection, typed value; technique G219). A keyboard alternative alone does not satisfy this criterion; controls must work with a pointer, though they may be visually hidden.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Offer a single-pointer alternative (buttons, tap-to-place, typed value) for every drag interaction.

rules.statement: Pointer targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have enough spacing around them, with listed exceptions. (WCAG 2.5.8, AA, new in 2.2)
rules.why: Small targets are hard to hit with a finger, a tremor or a pointer.

check.how: Measure icon buttons, close buttons, footer links and inline controls. axe `target-size` is disabled by default, so enable it. Exceptions: spacing (a 24 px circle centered on an undersized target must not touch another target or its circle; 20×20 px buttons with a 4 px gap pass, with no gap they fail), equivalent control, inline text, user-agent controls, essential.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Make pointer targets at least 24 by 24 CSS px, or space undersized ones so a 24 px circle around each does not overlap another; use 44 px for primary actions.

rules.statement: The page declares its main language, and passages in another language are marked. (WCAG 3.1.1 A, 3.1.2 AA)
rules.why: Screen readers pronounce text using the declared language. 13.5% of analyzed home pages lack it.

check.how: Check `<html lang>` and `lang` on foreign phrases (axe `html-has-lang`, `html-lang-valid`).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Set <html lang> and mark passages in another language with lang.

rules.statement: Moving focus to, or changing the value of, a control does not by itself cause a major change of context such as navigation or opening a new window. (WCAG 3.2.1 A, 3.2.2 A)
rules.why: Unexpected changes disorient keyboard and screen reader users.

check.how: Tab through selects, radios and inputs; nothing submits or navigates without a deliberate action.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Never change context (navigate, submit, open windows) just because an element received focus or changed value.

rules.statement: Repeated navigation keeps the same relative order, components with the same function are labeled the same way, and help mechanisms appear in the same place. (WCAG 3.2.3 AA, 3.2.4 AA, 3.2.6 A)
rules.why: Predictability helps everyone, especially people with cognitive disabilities.

check.how: Compare header, footer, help links and component labels across several pages.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Keep navigation order, component names and help links consistent across pages.

rules.statement: Detected input errors are identified and described in text, and where possible a correction is suggested. (WCAG 3.3.1 A, 3.3.3 AA)
rules.why: People need to know what went wrong and how to fix it.

check.how: Submit forms with bad and empty input; each error is announced, specific and linked to its field.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Describe each error in text next to its field, say what is wrong and how to fix it, and keep what the user typed.

rules.statement: Every input has a visible label or instructions, and format requirements are stated before the user hits an error. (WCAG 3.3.2, A)
rules.why: Missing form labels occur on 51% of analyzed home pages.

check.how: Check every field for a programmatic label (axe `label`); placeholders do not count as labels.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Give every field a visible, persistent label; state format requirements before the user makes a mistake.

rules.statement: Submissions that have legal or financial effect, or change data, can be reversed, checked or confirmed. (WCAG 3.3.4, AA)
rules.why: Prevents costly mistakes.

check.how: Walk through checkout, signup with payment, and deletion flows.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Let users review, confirm or undo submissions with legal, financial or data effects.

rules.statement: Information already given in a process is filled in automatically or can be selected, not asked again. (WCAG 3.3.7, A, new in 2.2)
rules.why: Re-entering data is hard for people with memory or motor difficulties.

check.how: Walk through multi-step forms; check for repeated fields.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Do not ask for information the user already gave in the same process; prefill or let them select it.

rules.statement: Login does not require remembering, solving puzzles or transcribing, unless an alternative or helper exists (password managers, paste, passkeys). (WCAG 3.3.8, AA, new in 2.2)
rules.why: Cognitive tests block many people.

check.how: Check that password fields allow paste and autofill, and that CAPTCHAs have alternatives.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Allow password managers, paste and passkeys; do not require memory, puzzles or transcription to log in.

rules.statement: Every interface component exposes its name, role, state and value to assistive technology. (WCAG 4.1.2, A)
rules.why: Custom widgets are invisible or confusing otherwise. Empty buttons appear on 30.6% of analyzed home pages.

check.how: Inspect the accessibility tree; check icon buttons for names (axe `button-name`); test custom controls in a screen reader.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Use native elements; give custom controls a name, role and state; label icon-only buttons.

rules.statement: Status messages (success, errors, progress, results counts) are announced by assistive technology without moving focus. (WCAG 4.1.3, AA)
rules.why: Without it, screen reader users miss feedback.

check.how: Trigger form confirmations, loading and search-result updates with a screen reader running.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Announce success, error and progress messages through a live region without moving focus.

rules.statement: Use native HTML elements before ARIA. No ARIA is better than bad ARIA.
rules.why: Incorrect ARIA misrepresents the interface and can seriously harm screen reader users.

check.how: Review custom widgets; replace `div role="button"` with `<button>`, and remove ARIA that duplicates or contradicts native semantics.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Use native HTML elements before ARIA; no ARIA is better than bad ARIA.

rules.statement: If you add an ARIA role, implement the keyboard behavior and states that role promises, following the matching APG pattern.
rules.why: A role without its behavior breaks the user's expectations.

check.how: Compare each custom component with its pattern in the APG (tabs, dialog, menu button, carousel, disclosure...) and test with a screen reader.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: If you add an ARIA role, implement its keyboard behavior and states from the matching APG pattern.

rules.statement: Test accessibility manually as well as with automated tools: keyboard-only, a screen reader, zoom and text-size changes, and color checks.
rules.why: Automated tools do not catch all errors; GOV.UK states this explicitly.

check.how: Run axe or Lighthouse for a baseline, then do the manual checklist above.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Run automated checks, then test by keyboard, screen reader, zoom and text spacing; automated tools miss errors.

rules.statement: Test with people who use assistive technology, including disabled and older users, and get a formal audit before launch for significant services.
rules.why: Only real use shows what actually works.

check.how: Recruit participants with different needs; include assistive technology in usability sessions.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Include people who use assistive technology in testing; plan an audit before launch.

rules.statement: Respect the user's reduced-motion setting: provide a way to reduce or remove non-essential animation, and keep the logo, tagline and headline static.
rules.why: Motion can cause discomfort for people with vestibular disorders and can distract. MDN: honor the setting by replacing large-scale motion (scaling, panning) with gentler effects such as fades, without losing what the animation conveys. NN/g also recommends controls to reduce motion.

check.how: Enable "reduce motion" in the operating system and check that animations respond: large movement is replaced by fades or removed, and information the animation conveyed remains. WCAG 2.3.3 (Level AAA, Animation from Interactions) names parallax and scroll-triggered motion and points to the CSS media query (technique C39) and its JavaScript equivalent (SCR40).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Under prefers-reduced-motion replace large movement with fades or stills and keep what the motion conveyed; keep logo, tagline and headline static.

rules.statement: A tabbed interface uses role=tablist containing role=tab elements, each tab has aria-selected (true on exactly one) and aria-controls pointing at a role=tabpanel that has aria-labelledby pointing back to its tab, and the tablist has an accessible name.
rules.why: The APG tabs pattern requires these roles and properties so assistive technology announces the set, the selected tab and the panel relationship.

check.how: Query the DOM: every [role=tab] is a child of [role=tablist]; exactly one tab has aria-selected=true; each tab aria-controls resolves to a [role=tabpanel] whose aria-labelledby resolves to that tab; tablist has aria-label or aria-labelledby. Confirm with a screen reader that the selected state is announced.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Give the tablist an aria-label, link every tab to its panel with aria-controls and aria-labelledby, and keep aria-selected in sync with the visible active state.

rules.statement: In a tab list only the active tab is in the Tab order (others tabindex=-1), Left/Right arrows move focus between tabs with wrap, Home and End jump to first and last, and a tabpanel whose first content is not focusable has tabindex=0.
rules.why: The APG gives this as the keyboard model; the single tab stop keeps long tab lists from trapping keyboard users, and the focusable panel lets Tab reach the content.

check.how: Press Tab into the tablist: focus lands on the active tab. Press Right/Left/Home/End and verify focus moves; press Tab and verify focus lands in the panel (or its first focusable element). Check inactive tabs have tabindex=-1.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Implement tabs with roving tabindex and arrow, Home and End keys, and set tabindex=0 on a panel that starts with non-focusable content.

rules.statement: Tabs are not used for site-wide navigation or for an unknown or large number of sections; links that go to other pages are not styled or marked up as tabs.
rules.why: Inclusive Components says users who see tabs expect in-page panel switching, not page navigation, and recommends an accordion when the number of tabs is large or unknown. Single practitioner source for this point.

check.how: Find every tab-looking control. If activating it loads another URL or it is part of the primary nav, flag it. Count tabs: more than about five on mobile widths, or generated from data, should be an accordion or a list of links.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Use a plain nav list for pages and a table of contents for page sections; reach for tabs only for a few peer panels of one topic.

rules.statement: Each accordion header is a native button that is the only child of a heading element, with aria-expanded reflecting the panel state, and the button's accessible name is the visible title.
rules.why: APG accordion and Inclusive Components agree: put the button inside the heading so the heading keeps its structure role; do not give the heading role=button. Progressive enhancement: when content must also work without JavaScript (perf-core-first, a11y-native-first), write plain heading + div markup (the content is visible) and let the script insert the button inside the heading and set the hidden state; this is the pattern the 2026-11 pilot used. Native details/summary is an acceptable no-JS alternative where the design allows it.

check.how: For each toggle: tagName is BUTTON, parent is h1-h6 (or role=heading with aria-level), the button is the heading's only child, aria-expanded is 'true' or 'false' and flips on click, the hidden panel is display:none or [hidden] when collapsed.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write accordions as h3 > button[aria-expanded] followed by a div that gets the hidden attribute when collapsed; if content must show without JS, ship plain h3 + div and let the script add the button and the hidden state.

rules.statement: Content inside a collapsed accordion panel cannot receive keyboard focus (hidden attribute or display:none, not just zero height or opacity).
rules.why: Inclusive Components notes collapsed content is removed from the tab order when hidden; focus on invisible controls fails WCAG focus visibility and confuses keyboard users.

check.how: With all panels collapsed, tab through the page and assert no focus lands on an element inside a collapsed panel; or query focusable elements inside collapsed panels and assert none are rendered.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Collapse panels with the hidden attribute (or display:none), never by height:0 alone.

rules.statement: Accordion panels carry role=region with aria-labelledby only when the accordion has fewer than about six panels; larger accordions leave panels unlabeled as regions.
rules.why: APG warns that region on many panels (it cites roughly six or more) creates landmark clutter. The number is approximate in the source.

check.how: Count [role=region] / named section elements that are accordion panels on the page; flag if 6 or more per accordion.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Skip role=region on FAQ-style accordions with six or more items.

rules.statement: The open or closed state of a disclosure control is shown by a shape or icon change (such as plus to minus or a rotating chevron) that is hidden from assistive technology, never by color alone, and the icon uses currentColor.
rules.why: Inclusive Components hides the decorative icon with aria-hidden because state is carried by aria-expanded, and uses currentColor so high-contrast modes recolor it. COGA 4.3.2 asks for consistent, clear indicators for expandable content. Primarily one practitioner plus COGA Note.

check.how: Toggle each control and compare screenshots: the indicator shape changes. Inspect the icon SVG for aria-hidden=true and fill/stroke currentColor. Emulate forced-colors and confirm it stays visible.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Pair every expandable header with a plus/minus or chevron SVG marked aria-hidden that changes shape when aria-expanded flips.

rules.statement: A modal dialog has role=dialog (or alertdialog), aria-modal=true, and an accessible name from aria-labelledby pointing at its visible title (or aria-label), and every control needed to operate it is inside the dialog element.
rules.why: The APG makes the label required and the modal flag part of the pattern. Prefer the native dialog element with showModal(), which supplies modality; the APG page itself does not discuss inert or the native element.

check.how: Open each dialog; query [role=dialog],[role=alertdialog],dialog[open]; assert accessible name is non-empty and that no interactive control needed by the dialog sits outside it.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Build modals with a titled dialog element or role=dialog plus aria-labelledby, and keep all its controls inside it.

rules.statement: Opening a modal dialog moves focus into it, Tab and Shift+Tab cycle only within it, Escape closes it, a visible close or Cancel button exists, and closing returns focus to the control that opened it (or to a logical next target if that control is gone).
rules.why: These are the APG keyboard and focus rules for modal dialogs; the close button is 'strongly recommended' there. Initial focus guidance: first focusable by default; a static start element for long or structured content; least destructive action for irreversible steps.

check.how: Keyboard only: activate the opener, verify focus is inside; Tab through the whole dialog and confirm wrap; press Escape and confirm close and focus on the opener; confirm a visible close control exists.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: On open focus the first control (or the start of long content), trap Tab, wire Escape and a visible Close button, and restore focus to the opener on close.

rules.statement: aria-modal=true is set only when code actually blocks interaction with the page behind the dialog and the page behind is visually obscured; otherwise the surface is built as a non-modal popover.
rules.why: The APG says aria-modal can hide outside content from some assistive technology users, so a dialog marked modal that behaves non-modally seriously harms them.

check.how: With the dialog open, try to Tab, click and screen-reader-navigate to background content. If any works, aria-modal must be absent. If aria-modal is present, confirm a dim or blur overlay covers the page.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Make the background inert and dimmed whenever the dialog is modal; for popovers that leave the page usable, do not set aria-modal.

rules.statement: Confirmations of destructive or irreversible actions use role=alertdialog with aria-describedby pointing at the message, and initial focus goes to the least destructive control (Cancel) when undoing is hard.
rules.why: APG alertdialog is for interrupting the workflow to get a response and requires aria-describedby on the message; the modal-dialog page advises focusing the least destructive action for irreversible steps. COGA 4.8.3 asks that consequences of actions are stated.

check.how: Trigger each delete/purchase/discard confirmation: verify the role, aria-describedby target text, and that focus starts on Cancel (not the destructive button).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Write destructive confirmations as alertdialog with a plain-language consequence message and focus Cancel first.

rules.statement: Alerts and notifications do not move keyboard focus, are not removed by a timer shorter than the user needs to read them, and error or action-required messages stay until the user resolves or dismisses them.
rules.why: The APG alert page says alerts must not take focus and should not vanish automatically (it ties this to time-limit criteria). WCAG 2.2.1 already requires adjustable timing.

check.how: Trigger each alert; confirm document.activeElement does not change. Time how long it stays; any auto-dismiss under about 10 seconds or on an error is a finding unless the user can extend or recover the message elsewhere.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Show messages in a live region without calling focus(); keep errors on screen until fixed. Tension with the common error-summary pattern that moves focus to the summary: put the summary in a role=alert region that exists empty at load (no focus call) and move focus to the first invalid field instead.

rules.statement: Live regions (role=status, role=alert or aria-live) exist in the DOM before their message is inserted, and messages that must be announced are injected after page load rather than rendered in the initial HTML.
rules.why: APG says alerts already present at page load are not announced; Inclusive Components says do not add the region and its content at the same moment, leave a short gap.

check.how: Inspect the initial DOM for an empty live-region container; trigger the message and confirm a screen reader announces it (NVDA, VoiceOver). Flag a region created together with its text.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Render an empty role=status container at load and fill it with text when something happens.

rules.statement: Any transient notification (toast, snackbar) refers to something the user can find again elsewhere (list, history, page state), and notifications are not used for information needed to complete a task.
rules.why: Inclusive Components advises that each notification points to something discoverable elsewhere so people who missed it are not stranded. Sources disagree on dismiss buttons and auto-dismiss (see disagreements); this rule takes the safe common ground. Single practitioner source.

check.how: For each toast: after it disappears, can the same information be found on the page (cart count, order list, inline status)? If not, flag.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Mirror every toast in persistent on-page state so missing it loses nothing.

rules.statement: Non-blocking status messages (results count, success, progress, cart updated) use role=status or an equivalent polite live region; role=alert or aria-live=assertive is reserved for important, time-sensitive messages such as errors; none of them take focus.
rules.why: Understanding 4.1.3 maps success/results to role=status (ARIA22) and errors to role=alert (ARIA19), and lists assertive use on unimportant content as a failure. It adds that over-announcing makes apps chatty.

check.how: List every dynamic message on the page. Assert each has a live-region role or property; assert role=alert / assertive appears only on errors or urgent warnings; test with a screen reader that it is announced once.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Default to role=status; use role=alert only for errors the user must act on now.

rules.statement: A breadcrumb trail sits in a nav landmark with an accessible label (for example 'Breadcrumb'), is a list of links to parent pages in hierarchical order, and marks the current page link with aria-current=page.
rules.why: The APG breadcrumb pattern requires the labeled navigation landmark and aria-current on the current-page link. COGA 4.2.1/4.2.4 also lists breadcrumbs as a way to show where the user is.

check.how: Find the breadcrumb: assert nav[aria-label|aria-labelledby], ol/ul of links, last item aria-current=page.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: On any page deeper than one level, add nav[aria-label=Breadcrumb] > ol with aria-current=page on the last item.

rules.statement: A tooltip appears on both hover and keyboard focus, closes with Escape, stays open while the pointer is over it, is linked to its trigger with aria-describedby, and contains no links, buttons or other interactive content; where space allows, a visible text label is used instead.
rules.why: APG: Escape dismisses, focus stays on trigger, hover persistence, aria-describedby (the page says the pattern has no consensus yet). Inclusive Components: tooltips are a last resort and must not hold interactive content, which belongs in a dialog or menu. WCAG 1.4.13 covers dismiss, hover and persist.

check.how: Hover and Tab to each tooltip trigger; press Escape; move the pointer onto the bubble; check aria-describedby; check the bubble DOM for a, button, input.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Prefer visible labels; if a tooltip is unavoidable, trigger on hover and focus, allow Escape, and keep it text only.

rules.statement: Help bubbles that must work on touch (info icons) are click-activated 'toggletips': a button with type=button and a visible or visually hidden name, an adjacent role=status region filled on click, no aria-describedby on the button, and dismissal by Escape, outside click or blur.
rules.why: Inclusive Components: hover and focus tooltips do not work reliably on touch; describedby would read the content before the user asks. This differs from the APG tooltip, which has no click variant (single practitioner source, so hypothesis).

check.how: Tap and keyboard-activate each info button: bubble appears, screen reader announces it, Escape closes. Check the button is a real button with an accessible name and that the bubble text is not exposed before activation.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: For info icons, render a button plus an empty role=status span and write the help text into it on click.

rules.statement: The title attribute is not the only source of an accessible name, instruction or tooltip text; essential information is also available as visible text or a labelled control.
rules.why: Inclusive Components says title fails for keyboard and touch users and has inconsistent screen reader support; COGA 4.5.6 says labels should not depend only on title or ARIA attributes.

check.how: Search for [title] on interactive elements; for each, assert there is also visible text or aria-label/labelledby and that no instruction exists only in title.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Never put meaning in title; show it as text or a labelled control.

rules.statement: A menu button that opens a list of actions is a button with aria-haspopup=menu and aria-expanded, opening role=menu with menuitem children; Enter/Space (and optionally Down/Up) open it and move focus to an item, arrows move between items, Escape closes it and returns focus to the button, and Tab leaves it.
rules.why: APG menu-button and menu pages give this model; if you cannot implement all of it, use a plain button/list instead because role=menu promises these keys.

check.how: Keyboard-test: open with Enter, Space, Down; move with arrows (Home/End); Escape returns focus to the button; Tab closes. Check aria-expanded flips.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Use role=menu only for action menus and implement every key the APG lists, or use a disclosure instead.

rules.statement: Site navigation is a nav landmark containing a list of links; dropdown groups are disclosure buttons with aria-expanded revealing a nested list; role=menu, menuitem and menubar are not used for site navigation.
rules.why: Inclusive Components says ARIA menus are for application behavior and breaks link semantics in navigation. APG offers a Navigation Menubar example but recommends avoiding items that both navigate and open a submenu. Sources partly disagree (see disagreements).

check.how: In header nav: assert no [role=menu|menubar|menuitem]; submenus triggered by button[aria-expanded]; first link of an opened list follows the button in focus order; nav has accessible name when more than one.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Build header menus as nav > ul with a button[aria-expanded] per dropdown and plain links inside.

rules.statement: Anything that navigates is an a element with an href; elements with role=link, onclick-only spans or buttons are not used for navigation, and buttons are used for in-page actions.
rules.why: APG strongly encourages native link elements because role=link does not provide navigation or context-menu behavior; Inclusive Components uses a button, not a link, for in-page state changes.

check.how: Query [role=link] and elements with click handlers that call location/navigation; assert none are non-anchor. Query a without href or with href='#'/javascript: used as buttons.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Use a[href] to go somewhere and button to do something.
