rules.statement: A custom listbox has role=listbox with an accessible name, role=option children each with aria-selected (or aria-checked, never both), aria-multiselectable=true when multi, short option names, and Up/Down, Home/End and type-ahead keys; options contain no interactive controls.
rules.why: APG listbox: names are read as a flat string, long or repetitive names slow screen reader users, interactive content in options is unsupported. Where a native select would do, a11y-native-first applies.

check.how: Inspect roles and states; keyboard test Up/Down/Home/End and typing a letter; scan options for nested a/button/input.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Prefer a native select; build a custom listbox only with full APG keys and short option labels.

rules.statement: An autocomplete input has role=combobox on the input with aria-expanded, aria-controls pointing at the popup, aria-autocomplete matching its behavior, aria-activedescendant naming the highlighted option, and a real label.
rules.why: APG combobox requires these relationships; DOM focus stays on the input while virtual focus moves in the popup (except for dialog popups).

check.how: Open the popup and assert on the input: role=combobox, aria-expanded=true, aria-controls resolves to a visible listbox, aria-activedescendant changes with Down arrow and resolves to an option; label via label/aria-labelledby.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Keep DOM focus in the input and move aria-activedescendant through the options.

rules.statement: In a combobox, Down Arrow opens the popup and moves into it, Enter accepts the highlighted option, Escape closes the popup (restoring the typed value), typing keeps editing the input, and Tab moves on without stopping inside the popup.
rules.why: APG lists these keys; Escape restoring the previous value is named as a distinction from listbox and menu button.

check.how: Type, press Down, Enter, Escape, Tab in order and verify each outcome and that focus never leaves the input.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Implement Down, Up, Enter, Escape and Alt+Down exactly as the APG lists.

rules.statement: An on/off control is a native checkbox, a button with aria-pressed, or role=switch with aria-checked, has a fixed accessible name, toggles with Space, and its name does not change when its state changes.
rules.why: APG switch calls a stable label critical; Inclusive Components says never change the label and the state together (voice users say the visible label), and explicit aria-pressed true/false. Support for role=switch varied in 2017 (ChromeVox, NVDA) per Inclusive Components; check current support.

check.how: Toggle each control and assert its accessible name is identical before and after, aria-checked/aria-pressed/checked is explicit 'true' or 'false', and Space toggles it.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Name toggles after the setting ('Dark mode') and flip only aria-pressed or aria-checked.

rules.statement: A toggle's on/off state is visible through more than color (position of a knob, an icon, or text) and the visual style is driven by the ARIA state attribute so they cannot diverge.
rules.why: Inclusive Components cites WCAG 1.4.1 and styling from [aria-pressed=true]; COGA 4.5.10 says toggles should expose state programmatically and every state change needs visual feedback.

check.how: Grayscale screenshot of both states; confirm still distinguishable. Check CSS selectors key off aria-pressed/aria-checked/:checked.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Style toggles from [aria-pressed=true] and add a knob position or check icon, not only a color change.

rules.statement: If the site offers a light/dark theme control, it is a labelled toggle (button with aria-pressed, or radio group in a fieldset with legend), lives in a landmark (header or footer) in the same place on every page, and the choice persists across visits.
rules.why: Inclusive Components (2017) describes a toggle button, placement in a landmark, same location everywhere and localStorage persistence; it does not cover prefers-color-scheme, so default to the user's OS setting is not from this source. Single practitioner source.

check.how: Toggle, reload, confirm persistence; confirm control is within header/footer landmark and identical on two pages; check name and state announced.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Put one labelled theme toggle in the header, store the choice, and honor prefers-color-scheme as the default.

rules.statement: Related checkboxes or radios are wrapped in a fieldset with a legend (or role=group / radiogroup with aria-labelledby) that names the group, each input has its own label, and a mixed-state parent checkbox uses aria-checked=mixed.
rules.why: APG checkbox, radio and switch pages require a group label for visible group labels; the radiogroup must be labeled; mixed is the third state for tri-state checkboxes.

check.how: For each set of inputs sharing a name or visual group, assert a fieldset>legend or [role=group|radiogroup][aria-labelledby|aria-label]; every input has a label.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Wrap every option set in fieldset and legend and label each input.

rules.statement: A radio group is one Tab stop (landing on the checked radio, else the first) with arrow keys moving and checking the next/previous radio with wrap; use native input type=radio with a shared name so the browser provides this.
rules.why: APG radio keyboard model; the page notes some browsers differ on Shift+Tab landing when none is checked.

check.how: Tab into the group, press arrows, confirm focus and checked state move together and the group is one tab stop.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Use native radio inputs with the same name attribute rather than custom divs.

rules.statement: A slider is a native input type=range or an element with role=slider carrying aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax and an accessible name, uses aria-valuetext when the number is not self-explanatory (a price, a time), and responds to arrow keys, Home and End.
rules.why: APG slider requirements; it also warns touch-based assistive technology may not support slider gestures well, so test on touch screen readers.

check.how: Inspect value attributes; keyboard test arrows/Home/End/PageUp/PageDown; check aria-valuetext shows units; test with VoiceOver on iOS or TalkBack.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Prefer input type=range; add output text next to it and aria-valuetext when units matter.

rules.statement: role=toolbar is used only for a group of 3 or more controls, has an accessible name, exposes a single tab stop with arrow-key navigation among controls, and contains at most one control that needs the same arrow keys (placed last).
rules.why: APG toolbar states the 3-control threshold and the single-tab-stop roving model; otherwise a plain group of buttons with normal Tab order is simpler.

check.how: Find [role=toolbar]; count controls (3 or more); Tab once into it and use arrows; check name.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Do not add role=toolbar to two buttons; use it for three or more and implement roving tabindex.

rules.statement: The page has exactly one main and one top-level banner (header) and one contentinfo (footer), uses nav, aside and search elements for those roles, and all perceivable content is inside some landmark.
rules.why: APG landmarks best practice says all content belongs in a landmark; banner, main and contentinfo are one per page and top-level. header and footer only count as banner/contentinfo in the body context.

check.how: Query landmarks with axe rules landmark-one-main, landmark-no-duplicate-banner, landmark-no-duplicate-contentinfo, region (content outside landmarks).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Wrap the page in header, nav, main and footer, and keep every text block inside one of them.

rules.statement: Landmarks of the same role each have a unique accessible name (except identical-content pairs), section and form elements become landmarks only when named, labels do not repeat the role word, and the page has about seven or fewer landmark regions.
rules.why: APG landmark regions: unique labels, name required for region and form, 'Site' not 'Site navigation'; the landmarks page gives a seven-or-fewer rule of thumb because value drops as the count grows.

check.how: List landmarks with names; flag duplicates of the same role with the same or missing name; flag labels containing their own role word; count landmarks.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Give header and footer navs distinct aria-labels such as 'Main' and 'Footer'.

rules.statement: Each card is one list item with a heading at the same level across the set; the heading text is the only primary link (not a link wrapping the whole card); a whole-card click area, if wanted, is made with a stretched ::after on that link; images that are decorative have alt="".
rules.why: Inclusive Components: whole-card links make screen reader announcements verbose and break with nested links; list markup gives item counts; the heading link has a unique descriptive name. Trade-off: the stretched-link technique prevents text selection, mitigated by a click-duration check.

check.how: For each card: parent is li inside ul/ol; one heading; exactly one a whose text matches the heading; no a ancestor wrapping heading+image+text; images have alt (empty if decorative).

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Mark cards up as li > heading > a with a stretched pseudo-element for the click area, not a wrapper anchor.

rules.statement: A card has one tab stop, or two only when a secondary link is genuinely useful, and 'read more' cues are non-interactive text hidden from assistive technology (aria-hidden) and tied to the link with aria-describedby rather than being a second link.
rules.why: Inclusive Components: extra tab stops slow keyboard users and cards should not be miniature web pages; a visual 'read more' cue helps people recognize interactivity.

check.how: Count focusable elements per card (max 2); flag 'read more' / 'learn more' links duplicated per card.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Give each card one link on its heading and a decorative 'Read more' cue, nothing else focusable.

rules.statement: Tabular data uses table with a caption (or a figure and figcaption), th with scope=col / scope=row, and no layout tables; the grid role is used only for interactive cell-by-cell widgets.
rules.why: Inclusive Components lists these basics; WCAG 1.3.1 requires the structure to be in the markup, which the existing a11y-semantic-structure rule covers.

check.how: Each table has caption or figcaption/heading, header cells are th with scope, no table used purely for layout (role=presentation only as legacy fallback).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Mark pricing and spec tables with caption, th scope and real rows and columns.

rules.statement: A table wider than its container scrolls inside a labelled container (aria-labelledby the caption) that is keyboard focusable (tabindex=0) only when it actually overflows; table display properties are not changed to reflow it.
rules.why: Inclusive Components: keyboard users cannot scroll unfocusable scrollers; tabindex=0 only on overflow avoids useless tab stops; changing display breaks table semantics. Inclusive Components uses role=group for the container.

check.how: At 320 px and 1280 px: for each table container with scrollWidth > clientWidth assert tabindex=0 and an accessible name; for non-overflowing containers assert no tabindex.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Wrap wide tables in a labelled overflow-x:auto container and add tabindex=0 when it scrolls.

rules.statement: Sortable column headers contain a button labelled with the column name, and the th carries aria-sort (ascending, descending or none); sort arrows use currentColor.
rules.why: Inclusive Components: button in each sortable header, aria-sort for state, and clear labels; icons that show current state can mislead about what pressing does, so the button text must say what happens.

check.how: For each sortable column: th[aria-sort] contains button with name; activating it changes aria-sort and row order.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Render sortable headers as th[aria-sort] > button and update aria-sort on click.

rules.statement: A horizontal slider uses native scrolling with a focusable (tabindex=0) labelled region, list markup for slides, labelled previous/next buttons, does not autoplay or move without user action, and slides that are out of view have their links removed from the tab order.
rules.why: Inclusive Components says a slider should never move without the user's say-so and that WCAG 2.2.2 is a minimum; it also recommends native overflow scrolling, a region with aria-label and tabindex=-1 on links in hidden slides. APG carousel (existing source) covers rotating carousels.

check.how: Load the page for 30 seconds without input: nothing moves. Tab through: arrows reachable, scroller focusable with visible focus, hidden slides' links not focusable. Check prev/next buttons have names.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Build sliders as scroll-snap lists with labelled prev/next buttons and no autoplay.

rules.statement: Decorative inline SVG icons inside controls have aria-hidden=true and focusable=false, informative icons have a text alternative (visually hidden text), and icon fills and strokes use currentColor so forced-colors and high-contrast modes recolor them.
rules.why: Inclusive Components repeats this in collapsible sections, notifications and theme switcher; the same author wrote all three, so this is one source. MDN forced-colors (existing source) is the independent place to confirm.

check.how: Query svg inside buttons and links: aria-hidden=true when the control has text; fill/stroke not hard-coded hex; emulate forced-colors: active and verify icons remain visible.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Draw icons with fill=currentColor and hide them from assistive tech when text is next to them.

rules.statement: Each page in a set of pages (other than steps or results of a process) can be reached by at least two of: links from related pages, table of contents, site map, search, a list of links to all pages, or links to all pages from the home page.
rules.why: WCAG 2.4.5 (AA). The Understanding page says very small sites can satisfy this with links from the home page. Example pairings: search plus category list.

check.how: Pick 3 inner pages and show two independent routes to each (nav + search, nav + sitemap, home page links + previous/next). Process pages (checkout steps, search results) are exempt.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Provide main navigation and a second route (search, sitemap or footer index) on every multi-page site.

rules.statement: Live audio in synchronized media (live stream, webinar, event broadcast) has captions that include speech, speaker identification and significant non-speech sounds.
rules.why: WCAG 1.2.4 (AA). It targets broadcasts, not two-way calls in web apps; live means captured from a real event with at most a broadcast delay; fully generated content is not live.

check.how: If the page embeds a live stream, enable captions in the player during the live event and confirm they track speech; otherwise mark not applicable.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: If you embed a live stream, use a player and a captioning service that supply live captions.

rules.statement: Where text needs more than lower-secondary reading ability (roughly school years 7 to 9), a plain summary, illustrations or a simpler version is offered.
rules.why: WCAG 3.1.5 is Level AAA (not required for AA conformance); the Understanding page lists a text summary, illustrations, spoken version and simplified text as techniques. The EAA Annex I sets B2 (CEFR) for consumer banking information specifically.

check.how: Run a readability score (for example Flesch-Kincaid) on main content, ignoring proper names; if above grade 9, check for a summary or simpler version.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Write at roughly grade 8 and add a short summary above long or technical sections.

rules.statement: The one to three key tasks of the site are visually distinct, placed near the top of the page, each under a descriptive heading, and reachable from the top level of the main navigation.
rules.why: COGA patterns 4.3.1 and 4.3.4 ask for key tasks in visually distinct boxes near the top, in top-level navigation and early in the reading order, visible without scrolling or hovering. Overlaps ux-primary-cta-above-fold.

check.how: At 1280x800 and 375x812 without scrolling, identify the key task controls; check each is in the nav and early in DOM order.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Surface the main task as a prominent labelled control in the first screen and in the top navigation.

rules.statement: Links are visually distinguishable from body text (underline or equally strong cue), controls have a clear boundary or fill, non-interactive items do not look clickable, and nothing styled as a control is crowded against its neighbor.
rules.why: COGA 4.2.5 asks for recognizable controls, underlined links, and for non-clickable items not to look like links; 4.2.6 asks that interactive elements are not crowded. Overlaps WCAG 1.4.1 and 1.4.11.

check.how: Screenshot in grayscale: can every link and button be found? List elements with pointer-style hover or link color that are not links.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Underline inline links and give every button a visible fill or border.

rules.statement: Body paragraphs carry one topic each and are about 50 words or fewer (English), with the point stated first; sequences of three or more items use bulleted lists and steps use numbered lists.
rules.why: COGA 4.4.5 gives about 50 words per paragraph as a guide for English, one point per sentence, lists for three or more items. It is a guideline, not a hard limit.

check.how: Count words per p in main content; report paragraphs over about 60; flag long comma-chained runs of 3+ items that should be lists.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Break copy into short single-topic paragraphs and use lists for three or more items.

rules.statement: Headings, labels, buttons and error messages use common words, literal wording, active voice and positive phrasing; acronyms and jargon are expanded or explained on first use; metaphors or idioms in navigation and calls to action are avoided.
rules.why: COGA patterns 4.4.1 to 4.4.4 (clear words, simple tense and voice, no double negatives or nested clauses, literal language) apply to headings, labels, navigation, instructions and error messages.

check.how: Read every nav label, heading, button and error string: list jargon, unexplained acronyms, idioms, double negatives; each must be replaced or explained.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Name nav items and buttons with the literal thing the user gets, not a metaphor.

rules.statement: Text is placed on solid or low-detail backgrounds (or a solid panel/overlay), not directly over photos, video, gradients or patterns with varying luminance.
rules.why: COGA 4.4.11 says not to place words over busy backgrounds, to use solid backgrounds for text blocks and strong contrast. Overlaps WCAG 1.4.3 measurement, which varies across a photo.

check.how: Screenshot hero and banner text; sample background luminance across the text box (min and max) and confirm the worst case still meets 4.5:1; flag text over video.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Put hero text on a solid or scrimmed panel, never straight onto moving or high-detail imagery.

rules.statement: Each screen or section offers about five or fewer main choices, secondary links sit in the footer or under a titled 'more' link, and one feature is visually dominant.
rules.why: COGA 4.6.3 (avoid too much content) gives five or fewer main choices; also suggests one or two relevant images per page. This conflicts with ux-visible-navigation on desktop if read literally (see disagreements).

check.how: Count primary actions/links competing in each viewport-height section of the homepage; flag more than about 5 equal-weight choices.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Limit each section to one main action plus at most four alternatives. Tension: a list of situations or services that is the content is one choice, not many; keep it as one labelled list that is the dominant feature, group a long one under headings, keep other actions visibly secondary and record the call.

rules.statement: Content and controls do not move, open or change on load or without a user action: no layout shift after paint, no auto-opening windows or pop-ups, no auto-submitting forms; a loading indicator shows while content loads.
rules.why: COGA 4.5.1 and 4.9.1 list these. WCAG 3.2.x and the Core Web Vitals CLS limit (0.1) already cover parts of this.

check.how: Record page load; measure CLS (<= 0.1); open page with no input for 10 s and assert no new windows, dialogs or focus changes; check that selecting a control does not submit or navigate.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Reserve space for late content and open dialogs only after a click.

rules.statement: No pop-up, chat widget prompt, subscribe overlay or moving ad-like element interrupts the first task; moving content can be paused; notification settings, if any, are reachable from every screen.
rules.why: COGA 4.6.1 (limit interruptions) says users should control reminders and changing content and that blocking pop-ups such as subscribe prompts should be avoided. Overlaps ux-no-popups and a11y-pause-stop-hide.

check.how: Load the homepage fresh, wait 30 s, scroll to 50%, and record any overlay, auto-opened chat, or banner that takes attention or blocks controls.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Delay any prompt until after the user finishes a task and make it dismissible.

rules.statement: A way to reach a person (contact page, email or phone) is available from every page within one click, and a contact form has at most three required fields.
rules.why: COGA 4.8.1 and 4.8.5: human help easy to find on every page, few steps, not behind complex menus; feedback forms simple with no more than three required fields; chatbots not the only route.

check.how: On five different pages assert a link to contact/help exists in header or footer; open the contact form and count required fields.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Put a Contact link in the footer of every page and keep its form to three required fields.

rules.statement: Every user action produces immediate visible feedback (pressed or loading state, confirmation message after sending), and multi-step flows show completed, current and upcoming steps.
rules.why: COGA 4.5.10 (provide feedback) and 4.2.4 (make each step clear): confirmation after sending a form, visible status per step, buttons with pressed state.

check.how: Submit each form and click each state-changing control; confirm a visible confirmation or state change within about 1 second; in multi-step flows, check a step indicator exists.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Show a visible confirmation after every submit and mark each step as done, current or next.

rules.statement: On e-commerce and booking pages, price, fees, charges and key conditions are shown at the start of the task and the final total matches what was shown earlier; consequences and disadvantages of each option are stated next to it.
rules.why: COGA 4.5.3 (fees at the start) and 4.8.3 (state results and disadvantages of options). Relevant to the EAA e-commerce scope.

check.how: Walk product page to checkout: record each price shown; confirm no new fee appears at the last step; check options list their inclusions and exclusions.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Show the full price with fees on the product page, not only at checkout.

rules.statement: Password and code fields allow pasting and password-manager autofill; fields use correct autocomplete attributes; the site does not block browser extensions or assistive add-ons.
rules.why: COGA 4.7.1 says password fields allow pasting; 4.9.2 says make sure password managers and spell checkers work and do not block extensions; 4.9.4 asks for HTML autocomplete on common fields. Overlaps a11y-accessible-auth and a11y-input-purpose.

check.how: In login/signup: paste into password and confirm it is accepted; check autocomplete tokens (username, current-password, new-password, email, one-time-code); search for onpaste preventDefault handlers.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Never block paste on inputs and set autocomplete tokens on every credential and contact field.

rules.statement: Icons that carry meaning are paired with a visible text label, each icon has one consistent meaning across the site, and no section is crowded with decorative icons.
rules.why: COGA 4.2.7: familiar icons next to content, one meaning per icon, no cluttered pages. Inclusive Components says tooltips are a last resort for icon-only controls.

check.how: List every icon-only control on the homepage; each needs a visible text label or a proven universal meaning; verify the same icon is not reused for different things.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Add a text label beside every icon except the universally understood few (search, close, menu).

rules.statement: Sub-menus and expandable content show a visible indicator that more exists and open on click or tap, not only on hover; heading levels form an outline of the page and same-level headings share a style.
rules.why: COGA 4.3.2 (clear indicators for hidden or expandable text, no hover-only reveal), 4.3.3 (headings as an outline) and 4.2.3 (consistent visual design).

check.how: Tab and click each menu: it opens without hover; indicator present. Extract heading outline and check levels do not skip and same-level headings have the same computed font-size/weight.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Open menus on click, show a chevron on parents, and style each heading level once.

rules.statement: Long video or audio is split into labelled segments of about six minutes or less where there are natural breaks, and a transcript or summary is easy to find next to it.
rules.why: COGA 4.3.5 (break media into chunks: segments generally six minutes or less, unique descriptive labels, transcripts easy to find) and 4.4.8 (summaries).

check.how: For each media item over 6 minutes, check for chapter links or segmentation and a transcript or summary link adjacent.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Add chapter labels and a transcript link under every video longer than six minutes.

rules.statement: No sentence in body copy is longer than 25 words, and the average sentence length across a page's body copy is 20 words or fewer.
rules.why: GOV.UK says to split any sentence over 25 words; NN/g (Loranger, 2017) suggests 15 to 20 words at most. The two sources differ slightly, so the rule uses 25 as the hard cap and 20 as the average. NN/g also reports that users read only about 20 to 28% of the text on a page.

check.how: Automated (apps/audit): extract the visible text of p, li, blockquote and dd elements (headings, navigation, forms, headers, footers and buttons left out), split on sentence terminators and line ends, count words per sentence. Needs 80 words and <html lang> starting with en, otherwise the result is manual. Fail when the mean exceeds 20 words or more than 25% of sentences are over 25 words; needs a person when only some sentences are over 25 (the splitter can join sentences around abbreviations); pass when none is. A person checks the long sentences it lists and any legal text.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write body sentences of about 15 words, split any that pass 25, and read each aloud before keeping it.

rules.statement: Each body paragraph has one idea and at most 5 sentences; marketing and product pages aim for 3 sentences or fewer.
rules.why: GOV.UK sets 5 sentences as the maximum; NN/g (Loranger, 2017) says one idea per paragraph. The 3-sentence marketing target is our choice, not stated by either source.

check.how: Count sentences in each p element. Fail above 5; warn above 3 on landing and product pages. Manual spot check that each paragraph carries one idea.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Start a new paragraph whenever the idea changes and stop at five sentences.

rules.statement: Body copy for a general audience scores at or below US grade 9 on a readability formula (target grade 6 to 8); specialist audiences may go to grade 10 to 12 only when the audience is documented. For ESL, low-literacy or UK public-service audiences the target is lower: grade 5 or below, or CEFR B1 and GOV.UK-style plain language (our take).
rules.why: NN/g says aim for grades 6 to 8 for general audiences and 10 to 12 for experts, and that plain language helps experts too (2017 article; 2026 FAQ). WCAG 3.1.5 uses more than 9 years of school as the trigger for needing a summary. digital.gov says to write for the 8th grade only if the readers are 8th graders, so the target depends on audience. The lower target for ESL, low-literacy and UK public-service readers (grade 5 or below, CEFR B1, GOV.UK plain language) is our take: grades are a US schooling measure and a poor fit for a UK service, so the brief should name the audience's target and how it was checked. ESL group note: offer a translation or an interpreter where the service really can (translated pages linked with lang and hreflang, passages in another language marked with lang), avoid idioms and phrasal-verb puns, write dates and numbers in one unambiguous form, and put the action first.

check.how: Automated (apps/audit): Flesch-Kincaid grade, with an English-only syllable heuristic, on the page's visible p, li, blockquote and dd text (headings, navigation, forms, headers, footers and buttons left out). It needs 80 words and <html lang> starting with en, otherwise the result is manual. Generic thresholds only: fail above grade 10, needs a person from 8 to 10, pass below 8. A pass never shows that a plain-language target (grade 5 or lower, CEFR B1, ESL or low-literacy readers) is met, and proper names and technical terms inflate the score. A person confirms the audience and the target the brief names, and scores the page by hand where the scorer did not run.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Use short, common words and one clause per sentence, then check the grade score before finishing. For ESL, low-literacy or UK public-service readers aim at grade 5 or below (CEFR B1, GOV.UK plain language), offer translations with lang attributes and an interpreter where you really have one, and avoid idioms.

rules.statement: Any text that needs more than lower secondary education (more than 9 years of school) to read has a plain-language summary or an easier version on the same page, or the page records the conscious exception.
rules.why: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.1.5 (AAA) requires a companion for text above lower secondary level; proper names and titles are excluded, and each language that is at least 5% of the content is assessed separately. AAA is not required for conformance, hence advisory.

check.how: Compute grade per page as in copy-reading-grade. For any section above grade 9, confirm a summary at grade 9 or lower exists (technique G86) or an illustration or easier version (G103, G153).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Open any complex section with a two-sentence summary written at a plain reading level.

rules.statement: Copy uses short everyday words (for example 'buy', 'help', 'about') instead of 'purchase', 'assist', 'approximately', and avoids stacking nominalizations (-tion, -ment, -ance nouns) where a verb works.
rules.why: GOV.UK lists those exact swaps and notes that -ion and -ment words lengthen sentences; digital.gov calls hidden verbs a weakness and prefers the strongest verb form; Microsoft says to use short everyday words and prune every excess word.

check.how: Grep body copy for a banned-word list (utilize, leverage, purchase, assist, approximately, commence, facilitate, in order to, prior to, subsequent to, endeavour, numerous) and flag sentences whose main verb is 'make/take/give/have/achieve + -tion noun'. Review flags manually.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Pick the shorter word and the plain verb ('use', not 'utilize'; 'decide', not 'make a decision').

rules.statement: Headings, buttons, error messages and calls to action are written in the active voice, and body sentences use the passive only where the actor is unknown or unimportant.
rules.why: GOV.UK and digital.gov both prefer active voice; digital.gov says passive hides who does what and calls it one of the biggest problems in government writing; Mailchimp and Microsoft also say active. Neither GOV.UK nor digital.gov gives a percentage limit.

check.how: Run a passive-voice detector (be-verb plus past participle) over all copy. Any hit in a heading, button, error or CTA fails; review body hits for a named actor.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Name the actor first: write 'We send your invoice', not 'Your invoice will be sent'.

rules.statement: Every acronym and specialist term that is not universally known is expanded or explained where it appears in headings, navigation and buttons, and at first use in body copy; branded feature names are always accompanied by a plain description.
rules.why: NN/g says to spell out acronyms on every use because readers scan and miss first-use definitions, and to treat branded labels as jargon; GOV.UK says explain at first use and write unfamiliar abbreviations out in titles. The sources differ on 'every use' versus 'first use'; the rule takes the stricter reading only for the places people scan.

check.how: Extract all-caps tokens of 2 or more letters and capitalised product names from headings, nav and buttons; confirm each is expanded or described adjacent. Confirm first body use is expanded. Whitelist PDF, FAQ, URL.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write the full phrase the first time and in every heading or button, and describe each branded name in plain words next to it.

rules.statement: The H1 and hero subhead name a concrete outcome, offer or audience, and fail a swap test: a direct competitor could not publish the same text unchanged without lying; template headlines of the form 'The [adjective] [category] for modern [audience]' are not used.
rules.why: NN/g says to explain what the organisation does and why to choose it, and to replace generic welcome lines with specific taglines (2024). NN/g's headline guidance replaces 'Make better, faster decisions' with a named benefit (2015). Two practitioner write-ups (Superdesign 2026, Landing Doctor) independently flag the mad-lib hero and 'platform for teams' headlines as generic. Overlaps existing ux-tagline-specific, which does not give the swap test or the template pattern.

check.how: Read the H1 and subhead alone. (1) Does it say what is offered and for whom? (2) Paste it with a competitor's name: does it still read true? If yes, fail. (3) Fail if it matches the template 'The [AI-powered|modern|all-in-one] [noun] for [teams|businesses|everyone]'.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write the headline as the result one named buyer gets, using a noun or number only this product can claim.

rules.statement: Each H2 and H3 describes the content beneath it in literal terms, with generic headings ('Introduction', 'Overview', 'Features', 'Our approach', 'Why choose us') replaced by topic-specific ones, and the list of headings read alone summarises the page.
rules.why: NN/g (FAQ 2026) recommends literal, informative headings that summarise what follows; GOV.UK adds that headings must be descriptive, front-loaded and removable without breaking sense, and says not to use questions as headings. Overlaps a11y-headings-labels and ux-scannable-text; this rule adds the generic-heading blocklist and the 'read headings alone' test.

check.how: Extract the heading outline. Fail any heading matching the blocklist (case-insensitive: introduction, overview, features, benefits, our approach, why us, about, welcome). Then read the outline alone: a reader should be able to say what the page offers.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write each heading as the finding of its section, so the headings alone tell the story.

rules.statement: Headlines and headings make sense out of context (in a search result, a link list or a feed), put the key term in the first few words, and drop nonessential words.
rules.why: NN/g (Loranger, 2015) says headlines often appear alone, that readers focus on the first words, and that long headlines get truncated on small screens; GOV.UK says front-load headings. The article gives no study numbers. Overlaps ux-front-load, which covers the idea generally.

check.how: For each H1 and H2, read it with no surrounding text. Fail if the topic cannot be named, if the key term is not within the first 3 words, or if removing a word changes nothing.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Lead each heading with its subject noun and delete any word that does not change its meaning.

rules.statement: Each page's title element is unique, 65 characters or fewer, names what the page offers with the key term first, and meta descriptions are about 160 characters.
rules.why: GOV.UK sets 65 characters including spaces and says titles must be unique and use search terms; NN/g (2026) says page titles over 60 characters tend to be truncated and descriptions should be about 160 characters. The sources differ by 5 characters. Existing a11y-page-title only requires that a title exist and describe purpose.

check.how: Crawl every page; assert title length is 65 or less, titles are unique across the site, and description length is 150 to 160.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write a unique title under 60 characters that starts with the page's main subject.

rules.statement: Headlines, navigation labels and calls to action contain no idioms, puns, slang, pop-culture references or metaphors that need decoding; any playful line sits next to a plain one that states the offer.
rules.why: NN/g (2015) says cute, faddish or idiomatic headlines sound inauthentic and confuse non-native speakers; Google's style guide says to avoid slang, figurative language and pop-culture references; Mailchimp says avoid slang. NN/g's 2026 microcopy article ranks 'character' last, after clarity and concision, so humour is allowed only after clarity.

check.how: Read each headline, nav label and button aloud to someone who does not know the product. Fail where a literal reading misleads or the meaning needs a cultural reference. Confirm one plain statement of the offer is within the first screen.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Say the plain thing in the headline and put any wit in a supporting line.

rules.statement: Every button and primary call to action label starts with a verb, names the outcome in 1 to 4 words, uses sentence case, and is never 'Submit', 'OK', 'Click here', 'Learn more' or 'Get started' on its own.
rules.why: GOV.UK says button text describes the action and gives examples such as 'Start now' and 'Save and continue'; Mailchimp requires a verb in every button; NN/g (2026) says avoid 'Learn More'. Practitioners (Sacks 2024, UX Movement 2019) say 'Get started' hides the next step and suggest 2 to 3 words. The 1 to 4 word range is our synthesis; no source sets a hard limit (GOV.UK: none). Overlaps ux-descriptive-labels, which names only 'click here' and 'learn more'.

check.how: Collect text of button, [role=button], input[type=submit] and .btn-like links. Fail if the first word is not a verb (use a verb list), if the word count is over 4, or if the label matches the blocklist: submit, ok, click here, learn more, get started, go, continue (unless a save step is stated).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Label each button with a verb plus its object ('Book a demo', 'Download the price list').

rules.statement: Each primary call to action is followed within the same viewport by a short line saying what happens next or what it costs (for example 'No card needed' or 'Takes 2 minutes'), and a repeated generic CTA is not used as filler.
rules.why: NN/g (2025) says CTAs should reduce uncertainty and give an easy next step. Landing Doctor lists the repeated decorative 'Get started' with no stated next step as a tell of generic page copy and recommends reassurance under the button. The second source is a vendor and gives no data, so treat the exact pattern as practice, not proof.

check.how: For each primary CTA, check the adjacent text states the next step, cost or commitment truthfully. Fail if the same unexplained CTA label repeats in 3 or more sections.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Put one factual reassurance line under each primary button naming what happens after the click.

rules.statement: Link text makes sense out of context and is brief; identical link text always goes to the same destination, different destinations never share the same text; the word 'link' and 'click here' are not in link text; external, new-window and file links say so, with file format and size for downloads.
rules.why: GOV.UK: do not reuse the same text for different pages, state when a link leaves the site, give file type and size (its example is 'PDF, 19.5KB'). WebAIM: omit 'link', keep it brief, make it understandable out of context, put 'opens in a new window' after the main text. Overlaps a11y-link-purpose (WCAG 2.4.4) and ux-descriptive-labels; this adds the duplicate-text, destination-notice and file-notice checks.

check.how: Collect all anchors with accessible names. Fail if two different hrefs share the same name, if a name matches /^(click here|here|more|read more|link|this)$/i or contains 'link', if an href ends in a document extension without format and size in the name, or if target=_blank lacks a notice placed after the main text.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write link text that names the destination and say 'PDF, 2 MB' or 'opens in a new window' when it applies.

rules.statement: Every error message names the field or problem and tells the user how to fix it in plain words; generic messages such as 'An error occurred', 'This field is required', 'Something went wrong' and raw error codes are not used without a cause and next step.
rules.why: GOV.UK says to say what happened and how to fix it, with the pattern 'Enter your first name' for empty fields and 'Name must be 35 characters or less' for wrong values, and lists 'This field is required' as a generic message to avoid. NN/g (2023) says be specific, offer remedies and hide error codes. Overlaps ux-form-errors and a11y-error-identification, which require specificity but give no wording patterns.

check.how: Trigger every validation and failure state (empty, wrong format, too long, network failure, server error). Fail any message that does not name the problem and a fix, matches the generic list, or shows a raw code. Automated part: grep message strings for the generic list.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Start empty-field errors with a verb ('Enter your email address') and wrong-value errors with the field name plus 'must be'.

rules.statement: Error and warning text contains none of: invalid, illegal, incorrect, forbidden, prohibited, 'you forgot', 'please', 'sorry', 'oops', and uses no jokes; humour is allowed only for a rare complete system failure.
rules.why: GOV.UK lists these as words to avoid (it says 'please' implies a choice and 'sorry' does not help fix the problem); NN/g avoids 'invalid, illegal, incorrect', says humour wears thin on repeated errors, and allows novelty only for rare total failures. Mailchimp's guide also says forced humour can be worse than none. Sources agree.

check.how: Grep all validation, toast and error-page strings for the banned list (case-insensitive) and for exclamation marks. Manually confirm that any jokes appear only on a whole-site failure page.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Describe what the system needs from the user in neutral words, with no apology and no joke.

rules.statement: Instructions and interface text do not use 'please', 'please note', 'simply', 'just', 'easy', 'quickly', 'it's that simple', or exclamation points.
rules.why: GOV.UK: no 'please' or 'please note'. Google: no 'please', no 'simply/easy/quickly/it's that simple', avoid exclamation points, cut filler such as 'please note' and 'at this time'. Two independent guides agree. Marketing headlines are out of scope; this is for instructions and UI text.

check.how: Grep UI strings, form hints, instructions and help text for the banned list; exclude marketing headlines and testimonials.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Give instructions as plain imperatives ('Enter your postcode') with no softeners and no exclamation marks.

rules.statement: Sentences, paragraphs, headings of more than 3 words and button labels are not set in all capitals, either in the source text or with text-transform: uppercase; short eyebrow labels of 3 words or fewer are the only exception.
rules.why: GOV.UK says no block capitals for large amounts of text because they are hard to read and can read as shouting; digital.gov says the same; UX Movement says all caps is loud and harder to read. The 3-word allowance is our threshold; the sources only say 'large amounts of text'.

check.how: Flag text nodes in source with 4+ words entirely uppercase, and elements with computed text-transform: uppercase whose text has more than 3 words, or that are buttons.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Keep headings and buttons in sentence case and use uppercase only for one- to three-word labels.

rules.statement: Buttons, headings and navigation labels use sentence case consistently across the site.
rules.why: Mailchimp, GOV.UK (buttons), Microsoft and UX Movement all prescribe sentence case; Google says to match the page's existing capitalization. Mailchimp itself uses title case for form titles, so sources are not perfectly aligned. Wikipedia's AI-writing guide lists title-case section headings as a possible tell, but that is a single source about encyclopedia articles.

check.how: For headings, buttons and nav items, flag strings where 3 or more words after the first start with a capital letter (excluding proper nouns); confirm the style is the same across all pages.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Capitalise only the first word and proper nouns in every heading, button and nav label.

rules.statement: The site has a written voice sheet (3 to 4 trait words, each with a do and a don't example), and copy sampled from hero, navigation, buttons, errors, footer and 404 page is consistent on person (you/we), contractions, spelling variant and formality.
rules.why: NN/g (2026), Mailchimp and Microsoft all say keep voice constant while tone varies; GOV.UK says address the reader as 'you'. Inconsistent copy is also a sign of copy pasted from different sources, which is a common failure of generated pages (hypothesis; no source measures it).

check.how: Automated: count 'we/our' versus third-person ('users', 'customers') per page, contraction use, and US versus UK spelling pairs (color/colour); fail on mixed spelling. Manual: sample 6 surfaces and compare against the voice sheet.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Fix the voice in four words with examples before writing, then speak to the reader as 'you' throughout.

rules.statement: Tone is adjusted to the reader's situation: payments, errors, legal, security and account-deletion text is neutral and literal, with no jokes, slang or hype.
rules.why: Mailchimp says tone should follow the reader's emotional state and not to force humour; NN/g (2023) says avoid humour in errors; Microsoft says adapt tone from serious to lighthearted to fit context; NN/g (2026) warns AI can approximate tone but cannot predict how it lands.

check.how: List the copy on checkout, error, security, deletion, cancellation and legal surfaces; fail any joke, exclamation point or hype word.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Keep personality in marketing sections and switch to plain neutral wording wherever money, errors or risk appear.

rules.statement: Every article, guide or long section (more than roughly 300 words) opens with a one- or two-sentence summary that states the conclusion, and each section's first sentence carries its main point.
rules.why: GOV.UK says write a summary at the top and put the most important information first; digital.gov says summarize lengthy documents at the start; NN/g (2025, 2026) recommends the inverted pyramid and found AI answers often buried the overview in the conclusion. The 300-word threshold is our choice. Overlaps ux-front-load.

check.how: For each long page or section, read only the first sentence: does it state the main point? Fail if the summary appears last or is missing.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: State the conclusion first and add detail after it.

rules.statement: Sequential steps are a numbered list and 3 or more parallel items are a bulleted list, not a comma-run sentence or a long paragraph.
rules.why: GOV.UK and digital.gov say to use bullets and numbered steps to reduce duplication and aid scanning; NN/g (2017) lists bullets and tables for scanning; NN/g (2025) found AI output often presented lists as plain paragraphs. The '3 or more' threshold is our choice. Overlaps ux-scannable-text.

check.how: Flag paragraphs containing 3 or more comma-separated parallel items or the words 'first, second, third', and steps written in prose. Confirm real ul or ol elements are used.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Turn any list of three or more items or any procedure into a proper list element.

rules.statement: Interface microcopy (button and link labels, form hints, tooltips, error messages, empty states) is under 3 sentences, with the key information in the first words.
rules.why: NN/g defines microcopy as under 3 sentences and ranks clarity first, then concision, then character (2025 and 2026 articles); it warns that key details get truncated when copy is too long. Microsoft says to prune every excess word.

check.how: Collect microcopy elements (labels, hints, tooltips, alerts, empty states) and count sentences; fail at 3 or more.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Cut hint and error text to one or two sentences and move longer explanations to a linked page.

rules.statement: Statistics, testimonials, client logos, awards and superlatives ('#1', 'trusted by 10,000 teams', 'increase conversions 300%') are either backed by a named, checkable source on the page or removed; nothing is invented to fill a layout.
rules.why: Landing Doctor lists fabricated or unsourced proof (invented testimonials, placeholder logos, precise unsourced stats) as a tell of generated pages; Wikipedia's guide lists vague attribution ('experts argue') as a pattern; NN/g (2026) says AI never certifies that a claim is correct, so a human must check. Mailchimp says to keep claims grounded. Overlaps ux-objective-language; this adds the verification step and the ban on invented proof. Plain facts that are given or agreed (a price, an hour) but not yet confirmed are not proof claims: show them in a prototype with the visible assumption marker and legend (guide protocol 3.2) and list them as open questions; this rule still bans invented customers, numbers, quotes and press, which are removed, not marked.

check.how: List every number, quote, logo and superlative on the page. For each, record the source and confirm the customer or study exists and consented. Remove any with no source. Also grep for placeholder names (John Doe, Acme, Company Name).

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Use only claims and customers from the supplied brief, and mark any missing proof as a content gap instead of inventing it. A plain fact the owner has not confirmed may stay in a prototype only with the visible assumption marker and legend, listed in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md; invented proof is removed.

rules.statement: Shipped pages contain no lorem ipsum, bracketed placeholders ('[Company]', 'Your tagline here'), default template text, or chatbot residue such as 'Certainly!', 'I hope this helps', 'Would you like me to', or 'As an AI'.
rules.why: Wikipedia's guide lists chatbot leftovers ('Certainly!', 'I hope this helps') as a sign of pasted output. Landing Doctor lists placeholder logos as a tell. A published placeholder is a functional content failure. No source measures how often this happens. Not a placeholder: a real fact the owner has not confirmed yet, shown in a prototype with the visible, non-bracket assumption marker and legend from the guide protocol (3.2), listed in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md; it is a draft state, not a ship state, and the launch step refuses while any remain.

check.how: Grep rendered text and alt attributes for: lorem ipsum, \[.*\], 'your (company|tagline|text) here', 'certainly!', 'I hope this helps', 'as an AI', 'let me know if', 'sample text', 'placeholder'.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Leave nothing in brackets: ask for the missing fact or write real copy before finishing. If a real fact is still unconfirmed, show it with the visible assumption marker and legend (dotted underline class plus a footer line) and list it in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md; never brackets, and it must be resolved before launch.

rules.statement: Feature and benefit copy replaces abstract adjectives (powerful, seamless, robust, intuitive, innovative, cutting-edge, next-generation, world-class) with a measurable change, a named workflow or a concrete example, and each feature block opens with a concrete detail rather than an icon plus a two-word title.
rules.why: NN/g (2015) turns 'Make better, faster decisions' into a named benefit and warns against hype; NN/g (2024) says avoid feature-driven wording and jargon and prefer concrete examples over umbrella terms. Landing Doctor, Superdesign and Microcopy Secrets independently recommend replacing vague adjectives and 'fits any product' benefit lines with specifics. Overlaps ux-real-content-examples and ux-objective-language.

check.how: Grep for the abstract-adjective list. For each hit, require a number, a named object or a verifiable example in the same sentence, otherwise rewrite. Check that no three feature cards share the same structure of icon, two-word title and filler sentence.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: For every adjective, write the fact that made you choose it and use the fact instead.

rules.statement: Headlines, buttons and subheads contain none of the stock marketing verbs and metaphors (unlock, unleash, empower, supercharge, elevate, revolutionize, transform, harness, leverage, streamline, game-changer, journey, tapestry, landscape, realm, delve), and body copy has no more than 2 distinct ones per page.
rules.why: GOV.UK, Google and Microsoft separately tell writers to avoid buzzwords, jargon and figurative language; Microcopy Secrets (2024) and ContentBeta (2026) list unlock, unleash, empower, supercharge, game-changer as empty; Wisp (2024) and Wikipedia list tapestry, delve, realm, crucial, pivotal as overused. The thresholds (zero in headlines, 2 in body) are ours. Word lists drift by model era (Wikipedia) and single words are weak evidence (Wikipedia, TechCrunch), so this rule is about empty wording, not about detecting AI.

check.how: Grep headings, buttons, hero text and meta descriptions for the list (case-insensitive, word-boundary); fail on any hit. Count distinct hits in body copy; fail above 2 per page.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: State the plain action in ordinary words ('save', 'connect', 'fix') and drop the stock marketing verb.

rules.statement: A page uses at most one negative-parallelism construction ('not X, it's Y', 'not only... but also', 'No X. No Y. Just Z.'), at most one slogan of three parallel short items ('Save time. Work smarter. Scale faster.'), and no self-answered rhetorical question openers ('The result?').
rules.why: Corroborated by two independent sources: Wikipedia's guide lists negative parallelism and the rule of three; ContentBeta (2026) lists 'It's not about X, it's about Y', 'No X. No Y. Just Z.' and 'The result?'. RAXXO and Superdesign add the triad ('works with any product'). Wikipedia warns that humans also write these, so frequency, not presence, is the signal. The 'one per page' limit is ours.

check.how: Regex for /not (just|only|about)? .{3,40}[,;] (it's|but|it is)/i, /\bno \w+\. no \w+\. just/i, sentences of the form 'X. Y. Z.' with each under 4 words, and short-question-then-answer lines (looked for only in headings, paragraphs, list items and quotes, not in form labels, legends or buttons, where a question with a hint such as '(optional)' is not rhetoric). Count hits per page; fail above 1 of each kind.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Say the claim once and directly, and use a list of two or four only when the items really are distinct. A self-answered label such as 'What is happening? (optional)' can be a false positive of the detector (a question with a hint is not rhetoric), but rewrite it anyway as a plain statement label ('What is happening (optional)').

rules.statement: Em dashes are absent from headings, buttons and labels and appear no more than about once per 300 words of body copy.
rules.why: Three sources report em-dash overuse in AI drafts: Wikipedia's guide (heavy use in place of commas, parentheses or colons, formulaic punch-up), Bullock (her own count: about 1 per 130 words in 24 AI-first drafts against about 1 per 850 words in 15 human pieces), and Monteiro (asserted, no data). All are anecdotal or small, Wikipedia says the sign works only with others, and Wikipedia also notes newer models reportedly avoid em dashes. The 300-word threshold is ours.

check.how: Count U+2014 in visible text; fail any in headings, buttons, nav or labels; fail if body density exceeds 1 per 300 words.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Use periods, commas or colons instead of em dashes, and keep them out of headings entirely.

rules.statement: Copy does not open or close with filler framing such as 'In today's fast-paced world', 'In the realm of', 'It is important to note', 'Whether you're a X or a Y', 'In conclusion', 'stands as a testament to', or an inspirational closing line.
rules.why: Wisp (2024) lists 'In the realm of' and 'It is important to understand'; ContentBeta (2026) lists 'in today's world' and 'digital age'; Wikipedia lists 'stands as a testament', 'pivotal', canned 'It's important to note' (2023 to 2024) and 'In conclusion' summaries (about 2023, since less frequent); RAXXO lists inspirational closings. Google says to cut filler like 'please note'. Corroborated by at least three, but the exact phrases date quickly.

check.how: Grep for the phrase list at the start and end of paragraphs and sections; fail on any hit. Manually review any section whose final sentence only restates the heading.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Start each section with its first real fact and stop when the point is made.

rules.statement: The section order and number of feature blocks on a page follow the audience's decisions and objections (documented in the brief), not the default sequence hero, logo bar, three feature cards, testimonial, pricing, FAQ, CTA, and feature cards do not carry emoji as icons.
rules.why: Superdesign (2026) and Landing Doctor independently name the stock section order and three identical feature cards as tells; Superdesign also names emoji or thin-line icons on cards, and Wikipedia lists emoji at the start of headings or list entries as a possible sign. Landing Doctor recommends answering the buyer's top reasons not to convert near each CTA. No data is given by either vendor.

check.how: Write the page's section order and the question each section answers. Fail if the order matches the stock sequence with no documented reason, if three or more cards share identical structure, or if emoji are used as feature icons or heading prefixes.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Order sections by the questions this buyer asks, and vary block sizes to fit the content.

rules.statement: Alt text states the image's purpose in context in about 150 characters or fewer, starts with the key words, does not begin with 'image of' or 'photo of', does not repeat adjacent text, does not contain keyword lists, and is empty for decorative images.
rules.why: NN/g (2024) gives about 150 characters, purpose from context, no leading 'image', empty alt for decorative images and says AI is unreliable at writing alt text from scratch; WebAIM (2021) says brief, no 'image of', no keyword stuffing, no repeat of nearby text, and gives no numeric limit. Overlaps a11y-alt-text; this adds length and wording checks.

check.how: For every img with non-empty alt: fail if length exceeds about 150 characters, starts with /^(image|photo|picture|graphic) of/i, equals the text of a nearby caption or heading, or contains 3 or more comma-separated keywords. Review decorative images for alt="".

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write alt text that says what the image adds here in one short sentence, or leave it empty if it adds nothing.

rules.statement: Where a page offers plans, tiers or products, the differences between them are stated explicitly with units and precise labels (for example 'Up to 5 users' not 'Small team'), and all costs are shown in one place.
rules.why: NN/g (2024) says implicit differences lead to wrong choices, recommends explicit units and precise labels, and says to show all costs together. Only one source (NN/g, updating a 2013 Nielsen article), so this is not marked craft-consensus.

check.how: For each comparison, confirm each plan label states what differs, numbers have units, and the total price including recurring fees can be read without leaving the page.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Name what differs between options in the label and give every number its unit.

rules.statement: Copy that gives legal, medical, financial or safety advice (anything where a wrong or out-of-date sentence could harm the reader) is reviewed by a qualified person before launch; until then each such passage carries a visible draft marker with a legend on the page, and the page does not ship it as final.
rules.why: This is our judgement, often called 'your money or your life' (YMYL) content in search-quality writing; no source was read for this rule. NN/g (2026) says a human must check that AI-written claims are correct, which supports the principle for generated copy but is not specific to advice. A model cannot hold the licence, the jurisdiction or the current law that the advice depends on, so a draft written by a model is a draft. The marker is the same visible, non-bracket convention as for unconfirmed facts (guide protocol 3.2), so the draft is never presented as checked. Severity is major, not blocker, because an our-take rule cannot be a blocker; realize-launch applies it as a launch gate.

check.how: List every passage that advises on law, health, money or safety (rights, deadlines, dosages, eligibility, 'you should', 'you must'). For each, confirm that a named qualified reviewer and a date are recorded (design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md or the QA report), or that the passage carries the visible draft marker and its legend and the launch gate is still closed. Search the built page for the marker before launch.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Write advice as a draft: mark it with the visible draft marker and a legend, list the reviewer you need (solicitor, clinician, adviser) in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, and do not launch it as final until a qualified person has signed it off.

rules.statement: Running-text paragraphs are never wider than 75 characters per line at any viewport width from 320px to 1920px (the target is about 66 characters; in CSS that is about 50ch to 55ch for proportional fonts, because ch is the width of the digit 0).
rules.why: web.dev (citing Bringhurst) calls 45-75 characters satisfactory and about 66 ideal for single-column text; USWDS says 45-90 with a long-text target of 66; Butterick says 45-90; GOV.UK keeps main content in a two-thirds column for no more than about 75; WCAG 1.4.8 (AAA) caps at about 80. The upper edge differs between sources (75, 80, 90), so the rule uses the strictest common figure. Butterick calls missing line-length checks the main flaw of many responsive designs. Our own measurement (Chrome 156, macOS, 2026-11-06): max-inline-size 66ch produced 87 to 96 characters per line with system-ui, Georgia, Arial and Helvetica Neue; 50ch gave 67 to 74. So set the container to about 50ch to 55ch, not 66ch, and count real characters per line.

check.how: At widths 320, 768, 1280 and 1920 px, find every paragraph/list-item/blockquote with more than two lines of text. Compute characters per line (text length divided by rendered line count, or compute container inline-size divided by the width of one '0' glyph, i.e. in ch). Fail if any exceeds 75. For the lower bound, where the viewport allows it (>= 768px), flag single-column text below 45 characters per line for manual review.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Wrap every block of running text in a container with max-inline-size of about 50ch to 55ch (ch is the width of the digit 0, wider than the average letter), never above 60ch, and count characters per line in the browser: it must not exceed 75.

rules.statement: Font sizes are declared in rem or em (not px), the root font-size is not fixed in px, and text containers are width-limited in ch, rem or em.
rules.why: web.dev says to use relative units for line length (66ch rather than 700px) so it scales with user font settings, and for font size so text follows user preferences; Roselli advises not to set the base font size in px but to start from the browser default; MDN defines rem as the root font size, which users can change in preferences.

check.how: Scan CSS for font-size declarations with px units (allow px only in fallback lines inside clamp() bounds that also use rem), for `html { font-size: <n>px }`, and for max-width/max-inline-size on text containers in px.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write every font-size and text max-width in rem, em or ch, leave html font-size at 100%, and treat any px font-size as a bug.

rules.statement: Running text (paragraphs, list items, form text, table cells) computes to at least 16px at every viewport width; only captions, footnotes and legal text may be smaller.
rules.why: USWDS asks for an effective size of at least 16px for most text and reserves smaller sizes for captions and footnotes; GOV.UK sets body at 19px with its smallest style at 16px, to be used sparingly; Butterick gives 15-25 px as the web range for body text. Sources differ on the floor (15 vs 16), so the rule takes 16.

check.how: At the audit's desktop (1440 px) and mobile (390 px) viewports, collect computed font-size of every visible text node inside p, li, td, th, label, button, and of every visible input, textarea and select (invisible and screen-reader-only text is ignored). Fail when any is under 16px, unless the node is inside figcaption, small, footer or a caption. List every such exempt text under 14px for manual review (14px is our review threshold, not from a source).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Set the body size to 1rem (16px) or larger, sized up (17-20px) for long reading, and use smaller sizes only for captions and legal lines.

rules.statement: Body text uses a unitless line-height between 1.3 and 1.7, and long-form reading text uses 1.5 or more.
rules.why: Butterick recommends 120-145% of point size and unitless CSS; web.dev gives 1.65 at a 66ch measure and says shorter lines can take more; USWDS says longer texts need at least 1.5 and gives tokens up to 1.75 for extended reading; GOV.UK body is 19px on 25px (about 1.32); WCAG 1.4.8 (AAA) asks that users can get 1.5. Sources overlap only loosely (1.2 to 1.65+), so the band is wide and the 1.5 floor applies to long-form only.

check.how: For p, li, blockquote read the computed line-height and the authored value. Fail if the authored value has a unit (px, rem) rather than a unitless number, or if the computed ratio to font-size is outside 1.3-1.7. For article/long-form containers (more than about 300 words) require >= 1.5.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Set line-height as a unitless number (about 1.5 for body, higher for short lines, never a px value) on the root text style.

rules.statement: Headings that wrap to two or more lines use a unitless line-height of 1.35 or less, and lower than the body line-height.
rules.why: USWDS says headings can use line-height 1 to 1.35 and body reading text at least 1.5; GOV.UK heading styles pair 48/50, 36/40 and 24/30 px (ratios about 1.04-1.25) against 19/25 for body.

check.how: For h1-h3 and display text, read computed line-height / font-size; fail if > 1.35 or if it is >= the body ratio. Skip single-line headings.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Give large headings a tight unitless line-height (about 1.1-1.25) so wrapped lines read as one unit.

rules.statement: All text sizes come from a defined scale of named tokens with at most 8 distinct sizes in use on a page (a fluid token counts once, not per viewport).
rules.why: web.dev tells designers to build a typography scale into the design system; GOV.UK defines 7 scale points with line heights that are multiples of 5px and says to align any new style to an existing point; Utopia generates a named scale (the example in its post uses 5 steps up and 2 down). The count 8 is derived from those two (7 and 8 steps) and is our threshold.

check.how: Collect computed font-size of all rendered text nodes at 1280px, round to 0.5px, and count distinct values. Fail above 8. Then confirm the sizes map to named tokens (custom properties) in the CSS.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Define 6-8 type-size tokens up front, give each a role (caption, body, lead, h3, h2, h1, display), and use only those.

rules.statement: Long-form content shows at most three visually distinct heading levels, and the size step between adjacent levels is small enough that a heading is not mistaken for display text.
rules.why: Butterick says to use no more than three heading levels (two is better), to raise size only slightly and to emphasize with space; GOV.UK's default pairing uses just three heading styles (l, m, s) for h1-h3, with a larger fourth only for long-form pages.

check.how: In article/long-form containers, list the distinct computed (font-size, font-weight) pairs of h1-h6. Fail if more than three look distinct. Manual: confirm each level is distinguishable from the next by size, weight or space.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Style at most three heading levels in articles and separate them mainly with space above and below.

rules.statement: Headings and button labels are written in sentence case and are not set in all caps when longer than one short line.
rules.why: GOV.UK says to write headings in sentence case; Butterick advises against title case and against all-caps headings that are full sentences, allowing caps only for text shorter than one line.

check.how: Extract heading text; flag headings where most words are capitalized (title case) for manual review. Flag any heading with computed text-transform: uppercase that wraps to more than one line.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write headings as sentences in sentence case and reserve uppercase for short labels and eyebrows.

rules.statement: Body text and any text under 24px uses font-weight 400 or heavier; weights of 300 or lighter appear only at display sizes (24px and above).
rules.why: Apple HIG says to avoid Ultralight, Thin and Light because they are hard to see at small sizes; WCAG 1.4.6 notes thin fonts render fainter due to anti-aliasing so a thicker font or a stronger color pair is advised; Butterick says heavier black/ultra weights are for display, not body. The 24px cut-off is WCAG's large-text size and our threshold.

check.how: Collect computed font-weight and font-size of every text node. Fail where weight <= 300 and size < 24px. Variable fonts: check the computed value, not the file.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Use weight 400-600 for text below 24px and reserve light and thin weights for large display lines.

rules.statement: The page uses at most two font families (plus an optional monospace for code), with hierarchy built from size, weight and color within them.
rules.why: Apple HIG says to minimize the number of typefaces because many faces obscure hierarchy and hurt readability; web.dev notes each added font file increases load time. The figure of two is our own threshold: neither source states a number.

check.how: Collect distinct computed font-family first entries across all rendered text, ignoring generic fallbacks and monospace on code/pre. Fail above two.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Pick one family (or one pair) and create hierarchy with size, weight and color instead of adding another typeface.

rules.statement: No font-size is set in vw, vh or vi alone. Text that must reach 200% on zoom (body, UI, and headings you cannot afford to clip) uses rem sizes stepped at em or rem breakpoints, with the smallest step at least 40% of the largest. A clamp() with a vw term is allowed only for decorative display type, and only after you measured that it still grows at 200% zoom.
rules.why: web.dev says never to use vw alone and to combine it with rem/em/ch in calc(), clamping with rem bounds; MDN says the maximum should be a relative unit at least twice the minimum so text can reach 200% (WCAG 1.4.4); Roselli shows `clamp(1.5rem, 5vw, 3rem)` growing from 64px only to about 68px at 200% zoom in a 1024px window, so the vw term can still fail 1.4.4 even when max = 2x min; Utopia cites the same warning and says to test before production. Our own measurement (content/learn/measurements/type-zoom-2026-11-05.json, Chrome): viewport-unit and clamp(rem + vw) sizes did not reach 200% at 200% zoom, because the vw term shrinks as the viewport in CSS px shrinks; stepped rem sizes with a small size of at least 40% of the large size did. The rule therefore prefers stepped rem and no longer recommends clamp(rem + vw) for text that must scale.

check.how: Static: reject any font-size value that is a bare vw/vh/vi length or a clamp() with px bounds. Dynamic: at a 1024px-wide window measure the computed size of fluid headings, then emulate 200% and 300% browser zoom (viewport halves/thirds) and confirm the on-screen size at 200% is close to double; flag headings whose size grows by far less (Roselli's example: 6.25%) for manual review. Mark a clamp() with a vw term as failing for any text larger than 24px unless the measured size at 200% zoom is at least 1.5 times the 100% size.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Set headline sizes in rem and step them at em/rem media queries (for example 3rem, 4rem, 7rem), keeping the smallest at least 40% of the largest; do not use clamp(rem + vw) for text that must scale; test at 200% zoom and 320 px.

rules.statement: Headings, captions and short display text set text-wrap: balance, and long paragraphs set text-wrap: pretty, with no layout depending on either.
rules.why: MDN says balance evens line lengths but browsers apply it only to blocks of six lines or fewer in Chromium and ten or fewer in Firefox (so it suits headings, captions, blockquotes), and pretty uses a slower algorithm to reduce orphans for body copy. MDN's text-wrap page lists Baseline Widely available (March 2024) while the text-wrap-style page lists Baseline 2024 newly available (October 2024), so treat it as progressive enhancement. Only MDN was read, so this is labeled our-take.

check.how: Check computed text-wrap-style on h1-h3, figcaption, blockquote (expect balance) and on long p (expect pretty). Confirm nothing breaks when the declaration is removed.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Add text-wrap: balance to headings and captions and text-wrap: pretty to long paragraphs as a progressive enhancement.

rules.statement: Text set in uppercase or small caps has letter-spacing between 0.05em and 0.12em.
rules.why: Butterick: capitals are designed to sit next to lowercase and look too tight set together, so add 5-12% letterspacing (CSS 0.05-0.12em), always for all caps; the 12% upper end also matches the WCAG 1.4.12 override value of 0.12 x font size that layouts must survive.

check.how: Select elements with computed text-transform: uppercase or font-variant-caps small-caps (or text that is all uppercase); fail when letter-spacing / font-size is below 0.05 or above 0.12.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Whenever you uppercase a label, eyebrow or button, add letter-spacing of about 0.06-0.1em.

rules.statement: Uppercase text is limited to strings shorter than one line (labels, eyebrows, buttons, short headings); no paragraph or multi-line block is uppercase.
rules.why: Butterick: all caps is harder to read at body sizes because readers recognize lowercase word shapes, suits text shorter than one line, and whole paragraphs set in caps get skimmed; emphasize with rules, a label-style heading or a larger size instead.

check.how: Find elements with text-transform: uppercase (or uppercase source text) and compute rendered line count; fail when any has two or more lines or more than about 40 characters (40 is our review threshold).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Use uppercase only for short labels and set anything longer than a line in sentence case.

rules.statement: Body paragraphs in lowercase text keep letter-spacing at normal (0); added tracking on body text is limited to small text, and large display headlines may be tightened but not widened.
rules.why: Butterick: lowercase usually needs no letterspacing, text smaller than about 9pt may benefit from slight added spacing, and large lowercase headlines are often tightened.

check.how: For p, li and td at 16px or more, fail if computed letter-spacing is not 'normal' or 0 (allow within +-0.01em). For text 24px and above, flag positive letter-spacing on lowercase headlines for review.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Leave letter-spacing at normal on body text and use small negative tracking, if any, only on large headlines.

rules.statement: Multi-line body paragraphs are start-aligned (left in LTR); none is center-aligned or justified, except justified text that also has hyphens: auto and a declared lang.
