rules.why: Butterick left-aligns web text because browser justification is crude, says justified text must be hyphenated, and says to use centered text sparingly; WCAG 1.4.8 (AAA) asks that users can avoid full justification because it can make reading harder for some people. Butterick's remark that CSS hyphenation support is inconsistent is undated and may be stale.

check.how: For paragraphs with 3 or more rendered lines, fail if computed text-align is center or justify (for justify, pass only if hyphens is auto and html has lang).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Left-align paragraphs of three lines or more and center only short headlines, taglines and single-line captions.

rules.statement: Inline emphasis uses either bold or italic on a run of text, never both, and is limited to short phrases; underline is reserved for links.
rules.why: Butterick: use bold or italic, not both, only sparingly, because both are harder to read than regular text and stacking leaves no room for further emphasis; do not underline text except possibly web links.

check.how: Find inline em/strong/b/i/span runs with both font-weight >= 600 and font-style italic; find text-decoration: underline on non-link elements; flag emphasized runs over about 12 words for review (12 is our threshold).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Emphasize a phrase with bold or italic, not both, and never underline anything that is not a link.

rules.statement: Primary body text reaches at least 7:1 contrast against its background, and secondary or muted text at least 4.5:1.
rules.why: WCAG 1.4.6 (AAA) sets 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text); Apple HIG says 4.5:1 minimum and 7:1 for custom foreground/background colors, especially small text. The 4.5:1 floor for secondary text is WCAG 1.4.3 AA (already covered by a11y-contrast-text); this rule only adds the 7:1 target for primary text, which is AAA and so advisory.

check.how: Compute the WCAG 2.x contrast ratio of the main body text color against its actual background in both light and dark themes; fail the target if under 7:1, and list muted text under 4.5:1 as a failure of a11y-contrast-text.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Choose a near-black (or near-white in dark mode) body color that reaches 7:1 and keep muted text at 4.5:1 or better.

rules.statement: Text placed over photos, video or gradients keeps 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) against the worst-case backdrop beneath each line of text, using an overlay or scrim where needed.
rules.why: WCAG 1.4.3 Understanding says background images that fail to give sufficient contrast with text are a failure, and contrast is judged on the color pairs actually adjacent; no gradient-specific method is given, so sampling the lightest/darkest backdrop pixel is our reading of it. This refines the existing a11y-contrast-text for hero imagery.

check.how: Screenshot each section with text on imagery at 375, 768 and 1440 px (and at the video's brightest frame). Sample the backdrop under each text line's bounding box, take the pixel closest to the text color, compute the WCAG ratio. Fail below 4.5:1 (3:1 for 24px+ or 18.66px+ bold).

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Put a solid or gradient scrim behind any text that sits on a photo or video and verify the contrast on the brightest area.

rules.statement: Colors are defined once as named role tokens (text, secondary text, background, surface, border, accent/link, focus, error, success) and components reference the tokens; literal color values appear only in the token definitions.
rules.why: GOV.UK says to reference functional colours by name, not hex, so palette updates propagate, and lists role colours such as text, secondary text, border, focus, error and success; web.dev's theming module stores colors in custom properties redefined for dark mode; Apple HIG prefers semantic colors over hard-coded values.

check.how: Parse the CSS: collect hex/rgb/hsl/oklch literals outside :root, [data-theme] and @media (prefers-color-scheme) token blocks. Fail if components contain literals; confirm the token set includes at least text, background, border, accent, focus, error and success.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Declare role-named color custom properties first and write every component color as var(--role).

rules.statement: A color that signals interactivity or a state (link/accent, focus, error, success, warning) is not reused for non-interactive decoration or for a different state.
rules.why: GOV.UK says to use functional colours only in their intended context, to reserve the focus yellow for keyboard focus and to use the error colour only for errors; Apple HIG says not to use the same color for different meanings, for example a brand color that marks a button as interactive should not style non-interactive text.

check.how: List the computed colors of links, buttons, focus rings, error and success messages. Fail if any of those exact colors also appears as text or fill on non-interactive elements, or if error and success use the same hue. Confirm by reading the token definitions.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Give links and primary buttons one accent color and never use that accent, or the error or success colors, as pure decoration.

rules.statement: If the site has a dark theme, it declares color-scheme (meta tag before stylesheets and CSS) and follows prefers-color-scheme by default, so scrollbars, form controls and canvas render in the matching scheme.
rules.why: MDN: color-scheme makes the browser adjust canvas, scrollbar and form control colors, the meta tag placed before stylesheets avoids a flash of wrong colors, and prefers-color-scheme (Baseline widely available since Jan 2020) is what styles the rest; light-dark() (Baseline 2024) only works when color-scheme is set. web.dev's theming module redefines custom properties in the dark media query. Apple HIG says to avoid an app-specific appearance setting that overrides the system choice.

check.how: Emulate colorScheme 'dark' and 'light'. Confirm getComputedStyle(html).colorScheme includes the scheme, a <meta name='color-scheme'> exists in head before stylesheets, native inputs/scrollbars are dark in dark, and no first-paint flash of the light theme occurs (screenshot at DOMContentLoaded).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Set color-scheme and the matching meta tag, define theme tokens for light and dark, and let prefers-color-scheme pick the default unless the brand is deliberately single-theme.

rules.statement: In the dark theme every text and UI color pair is re-checked against the same contrast thresholds (4.5:1 text, 3:1 large text and UI components), and the palette is not made by inverting or filtering the light one.
rules.why: Apple HIG: dark colors are not simple inversions, keep 4.5:1 in every appearance and test with Increase Contrast; web.dev's theming module redefines each token for dark and darkens photos with `brightness(.8) contrast(1.2)` rather than inverting; WCAG 1.4.3 thresholds apply to the page as rendered. White-background images should be dimmed so they do not glow (Apple).

check.how: Run the contrast audit (text 4.5:1, large 3:1, UI components 3:1) twice, once per emulated color scheme, over all pages and states (hover, focus, disabled excluded). Fail any pair that passes light but fails dark. Flag use of `filter: invert()` on the page root.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Author the dark palette as its own set of tokens, check contrast in both themes, and dim bright images instead of inverting anything.

rules.statement: Tints, shades and state variants (hover, active, disabled) of a brand color are generated from one base by changing lightness with hue and chroma held fixed (OKLCH, color-mix() or relative color syntax) instead of hand-picked unrelated hex values.
rules.why: web.dev: in OkLCh changing hue does not change perceived lightness or saturation, which makes adjustments predictable; MDN lists lightness ramps and theming variants from one base as use cases and gives oklch() Baseline Widely available since May 2023; USWDS shows the payoff of lightness-ordered grades, where a grade gap of 40/50/70 predicts WCAG AA large/AA/AAA (written for WCAG 2.0). Contrast must still be computed with the WCAG 2.x formula; OKLCH lightness is not a contrast guarantee.

check.how: Inspect the color tokens: for each ramp, confirm hover/active/tint values are derived with oklch()/color-mix()/relative color from one source token, or that their OKLCH hue differs by less than about 5 degrees and chroma follows a smooth curve (our tolerance). Still run the WCAG ratio on each text pairing.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Derive every tint and state color from the base token by changing OKLCH lightness only, then verify contrast numerically.

rules.statement: Contrast pass/fail is decided with the WCAG 2.x ratio (4.5:1 text, 3:1 large text and UI); APCA Lc values may be reported as extra information but never override a failing WCAG 2 ratio.
rules.why: The W3C status page calls WCAG 3 an incomplete draft that is not expected to be a standard for a few more years and says meeting WCAG 2.2 is the best preparation; the Working Draft dated 10 Sep 2026 leaves the contrast algorithm as a placeholder ('yet to be determined') and does not name APCA in the part read. Myndex's own docs describe APCA as a candidate (author's opinion, not W3C's), with Lc 75 as a body-text minimum and Lc 90 as preferred on that page.

check.how: Contrast reports must be computed with the WCAG 2.x relative-luminance ratio; if an APCA value is also shown, check the pass/fail column is still WCAG 2. Fail if a pair below 4.5:1 is marked as passing because of an APCA score.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Validate colors with the WCAG 2.x ratio and treat APCA only as a second opinion for borderline thin or small text.

rules.statement: Custom components stay legible under prefers-contrast: more and forced-colors: active (visible borders, focus and state) and the site strengthens borders or text colors when prefers-contrast: more is set.
rules.why: web.dev's media-features module: prefers-contrast: more lets you strengthen colors and borders, Windows contrast themes replace page colors so custom components need fixing under forced-colors, and forced-color-adjust: none is for elements where color carries meaning; its accessibility module says to test with the OS increased-contrast setting. Apple HIG: custom colors need an increased-contrast variant with significantly more differentiation.

check.how: Emulate forcedColors: active and contrast: more. Screenshot key pages; confirm buttons, inputs, cards, tabs and focus rings keep a visible boundary and no text disappears. Confirm a @media (prefers-contrast: more) block exists that raises border/text contrast.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Give borders and focus rings a token that increases contrast under prefers-contrast: more and test the page with forced colors on.

rules.statement: All margin, padding and gap values come from one spacing scale defined as tokens on a single base unit, with at most 12 distinct non-zero spacing values in use on a page.
rules.why: web.dev: pick a spacing system (a fixed gutter or a multiple of em) and store values as custom properties; GOV.UK defines units 0-9 in 5px steps up to 15px then larger; USWDS tokens are multiples of 8px with 4px half-steps; Utopia builds a named space palette and prefers as few sizes as possible. Base units differ (5px, 8px, em multiples), so any consistent base is acceptable. The cap of 12 is our threshold (GOV.UK has 9 non-zero units).

check.how: At 1280px collect computed margin, padding, row-gap and column-gap (block/inline) of all elements, round to 0.5px, ignore 0 and 1-2px borders, and count distinct values; fail above 12 or when a value is not a multiple of the base unit (4 or 8, or the project's token base). Confirm values come from spacing custom properties.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Define a spacing token scale (for example 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96) first and use only those values for padding, margin and gap.

rules.statement: Section-level spacing (section padding, page gutters, large gaps) is smaller on a 360px viewport than on a 1280px viewport, while the smallest steps stay constant.
rules.why: GOV.UK's responsive scale keeps units 0-3 the same at every size and lets units 4-9 grow above 640px (unit 9 is 40px on small screens and 60px on large); Utopia interpolates its named space steps between a small and large viewport so layouts breathe without per-breakpoint rules.

check.how: Measure the computed vertical padding/margin of the main section containers at 360 and 1280 px; require the 1280 value to be greater. Measure small component gaps (4-16px) and require them to be unchanged within 2px.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Scale section padding with clamp() or a breakpoint step so it grows with the viewport while small gaps stay fixed.

rules.statement: Space between items inside a group (label and field, heading and its paragraph, card contents) is smaller than the space between groups or sections.
rules.why: Apple HIG: group related items with negative space, container shapes or separators and keep unrelated items visually distinct; alignment and indentation tell people what is related. Only this one source was read for this claim (the sources.json gestalt-secondary page was not re-read), so it is labeled our-take.

check.how: For each heading, compare its margin/padding above with below; for each card or form group, compare the internal gap with the gap to the neighbouring group. Fail where the internal gap is greater than or equal to the external gap. Visual review of screenshots for ambiguous groupings.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Keep items in a group close together and put clearly larger gaps between groups, with each heading nearer to its own content than to the previous block.

rules.statement: Layout breakpoints are written in em/rem at the widths where the content breaks, not at named device widths, and the page has no overflow, clipped content or line-length violation at any viewport width between 320px and 1920px.
rules.why: web.dev: set breakpoints from your content rather than popular device sizes, use em/ch for text-based content, and prefer intrinsic grid rules (auto-fill/minmax(15em, 1fr)) and container queries over a ladder of media queries; GOV.UK says to design for a range of screen sizes rather than specific devices and to start with one column on small screens.

check.how: Automated: resize one loaded page from 320 to 1920 px in 40px steps and fail at any width where the document scrolls sideways (scrollWidth > clientWidth); list the px media-query breakpoints of the readable stylesheets and flag any matching device presets (375, 414, 768 and 1024 px) for review. A person checks what the audit does not: no element overlapping its sibling's box, the measure rule at each width, and that breakpoints are written in em or rem where the content breaks.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Build the layout with fluid grid rules first and add a breakpoint in em only where you can see the content break.

rules.statement: Page content sits in a centered container with a maximum width of 1400px or less; only backgrounds and full-bleed media may exceed it.
rules.why: GOV.UK's default maximum page width is 1020px (wider only when content needs it) and USWDS names widths up to desktop 1200px and widescreen 1400px. These are the two design systems' own choices; neither states the number as a universal rule, so the rule is advisory.

check.how: At a 1920px viewport, measure the bounding box of the main content wrapper(s): fail when text, cards or controls span wider than 1400px or touch both viewport edges; allow elements flagged full-bleed (backgrounds, images, video).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Wrap content in a centered container with max-inline-size of 1200-1400px and let only backgrounds and media run edge to edge.

rules.statement: Every img and video element has width and height attributes or a CSS aspect-ratio, so its box is reserved before the file loads.
rules.why: web.dev: always include width and height so the browser reserves the right space and avoids layout shift even when CSS scales the image; MDN: `aspect-ratio: auto 3/2` keeps the ratio before load and the natural one after (Baseline Widely available since Sept 2021). This is the cause-level rule behind the existing perf-cls metric.

check.how: For every img, video, iframe: fail if it lacks both (width and height attributes) and a computed aspect-ratio other than auto. Run with images blocked and check CLS stays at or below 0.1.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Put the intrinsic width and height on every image tag and keep height: auto in CSS.

rules.statement: No image is shown stretched or squashed: its rendered aspect ratio matches its natural ratio unless object-fit: cover or contain crops or letterboxes it, and crops that lose the subject on small screens use object-position or a different crop via picture.
rules.why: web.dev: block-size: auto keeps the ratio, forcing another ratio with aspect-ratio can squash or stretch, and object-fit avoids distortion; MDN: the default fill stretches content while cover crops and contain letterboxes; web.dev's picture module says to serve a different crop, not a smaller copy, when an image loses impact at small sizes.

check.how: For every img/video compute renderedW/renderedH and naturalWidth/naturalHeight. If computed object-fit is fill (or none specified) and the ratios differ by more than 2%, fail. For object-fit: cover images in hero/portrait slots, screenshot at 375 px and confirm the subject (face, product) is inside the visible area.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Fit images with object-fit: cover and an object-position that keeps the subject in view, and never set both width and height that change the ratio.

rules.statement: All UI icons come from one family with a single stroke weight, corner style and fill treatment, are drawn on a shared size grid, and their stroke weight visually matches adjacent text.
rules.why: Apple HIG: use the same size, level of detail, stroke weight and perspective across all interface icons, and match icon weight to adjacent text weight; web.dev: icons are part of the brand identity so their style should match the rest of the site.

check.how: Extract all inline SVG icons; collect distinct stroke-width, stroke-linecap/linejoin, fill-vs-outline treatment and viewBox sizes. Fail if more than one stroke-width or more than one outline/filled style is mixed in the same context. Manual: confirm icons beside text look the same weight.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Pick one icon library and one stroke weight and draw or import every icon from it, sized from a small set of steps.

rules.statement: UI icons are vector (inline SVG or SVG sprite) that take their color from currentColor or theme tokens, so hover, focus and dark-theme changes apply to them; no raster icons are used for UI controls.
rules.why: web.dev: inline SVG can be styled with CSS (fill set to match button text, hover and focus changes applying to icon and text together) while SVG background images are harder to recolor, and SVG fill/stroke can follow the theme custom properties; Apple HIG: use vector formats so icons scale and adapt, with dark-mode variants when needed.

check.how: List all icon elements: fail any PNG/JPG/GIF used as a control icon; for inline SVG, fail hard-coded fill/stroke hex values instead of currentColor or var(--token). Toggle dark theme and hover state and confirm icon color changes with the text.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Inline the SVG icons with fill or stroke set to currentColor and size them with em or rem so they follow the text.

rules.statement: An icon, chip or picture set inside a line of text is centred on the capital height of that text, about 1em square, with the space before it equal to the word space after it; it never sits on the baseline below the letters.
rules.why: A text-less inline-flex or inline-grid box aligns its bottom edge with the text baseline, so the chip hangs below the capitals and the line looks broken; the owner spotted this in the whata.design statement within seconds (2026-11-17). web.dev sizes icons in em so they follow the text.

check.how: For each img, svg or element without its own text inside an h1 to h3 or p: compare its vertical centre with the centre of the capitals of the surrounding text (baseline minus half the cap height, from a Range rect of a capital letter or font metrics). A difference over 8% of the font size, or a left gap differing from the right gap by more than 0.1em, is a finding.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Make the inline chip display: inline-block, width and height 1em (or the cap height), vertical-align: middle or a measured -0.1em to -0.15em offset; centre any icon inside with its own flex box; set margin-inline so the gaps match the word space.

rules.statement: Functional UI transitions (hover, press, toggle, dropdown, tooltip, modal, drawer) last between 100ms and 400ms and none exceeds 500ms.
rules.why: NN/g: about 100 ms for simple feedback, 200-300 ms for large screen changes, 100-400 ms as the general range, 400 ms only for big movements, and over 500 ms starts to feel like a drag; Material 3 tokens run from 50 ms (short1) to 1000 ms (extra-long4) with duration growing with the area or distance covered, so longer values exist for large transitions. Sources differ at the top end; the rule follows the stricter NN/g figure for functional UI and leaves narrative or hero motion to its own review.

check.how: Collect computed transition-duration (+ delay) and animation-duration of interactive elements and overlays (button, a, input, nav, dialog, menu, tooltip, accordion). Fail durations under 100 ms (except color changes under 100 ms, review) or over 500 ms; flag 401-500 ms for review.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Set interface transitions to 150-300ms (100ms for tiny state changes) and keep anything over 400ms for rare, large movements.

rules.statement: Elements entering the screen use a decelerating curve (ease-out or equivalent), elements leaving use an accelerating curve (ease-in), and linear easing is limited to non-spatial changes (opacity, color) and continuous or looping motion.
rules.why: NN/g: linear motion looks unnatural, ease-out is the usual default for entrances, ease-in suits exits, and exits should be slightly shorter than entrances (for example about 300 ms in, 200-250 ms out); Material 3 tokens pair standard-decelerate cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0, 1) with entering and standard-accelerate cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 1, 1) with exiting motion, and keep a linear token for simple non-stylized motion.

check.how: For transitions that animate transform, top/left or height, read transition-timing-function: fail 'linear' on those properties. For overlays, menus and drawers, check the open state uses ease-out/decelerate and the close state ease-in/accelerate and has a duration no longer than the open duration.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Use cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1) style ease-out for things appearing, an ease-in for things leaving, and keep exits a bit faster than entrances.

rules.statement: Animations on frequently repeated interactions (hover, press, toggle, menu open, tab change) are 200ms or shorter and never block input: the next click, key press or scroll works while the animation is running.
rules.why: NN/g: the more often users see an animation, the shorter and subtler it should be, with about 100 ms for simple feedback; Apple HIG: avoid adding motion to frequently used interactions, keep feedback brief, and let people cancel motion so they do not wait for it to finish. The 200 ms ceiling combines NN/g's 100 ms feedback and 200-300 ms large-change figures.

check.how: Automated: collect durations of hover/active/focus/toggle transitions and fail above 200 ms. Manual/scripted: trigger an animation (open menu) and immediately click the next target, press Escape or scroll; fail if the input is ignored or delayed until the animation ends.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Make hover and press feedback about 100-200 ms and keep every control interactive while its animation plays.

rules.statement: Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, large spatial motion (parallax, scroll-linked movement, large translate or scale, autoplaying loops) is removed or replaced with opacity or color changes, while essential and feedback animations remain in a gentler form.
rules.why: web.dev's accessibility module: limit scaling and movement, color changes and opacity or cross-fades are generally acceptable; its media-features module: keep reduced-motion alternatives free of the problematic movement and do not remove meaningful feedback entirely; web.dev's reduced-motion article lists parallax, autoplaying video, animated images and attention-grabbing motion as things to reduce and says essential movement is outside the preference; NN/g says to remove or minimize animations; Apple HIG says custom motion should respect accessibility settings. This refines the existing a11y-reduced-motion by saying what to do under the preference.

check.how: Emulate reducedMotion: reduce. List computed transform/animation on elements that move more than about 20px or scale more than 5% (our review thresholds); fail if any remains. Confirm state changes (open, selected, error) still show a visible, non-spatial cue such as opacity or color. Confirm autoplay media and GIF/WebP loops are stopped or static.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Wrap movement in a no-preference media query and give reduce users opacity or color feedback instead of travel and scale.

check.how: At the 1440 px viewport, for each top-level section at least 240 px tall, take the left and right edges of its text (measured with a text range, not the block width) and of its images, controls and media. Flag when the content covers less than 40% of the width and the empty gaps on the two sides differ by 25% of the width or more. A person decides whether the space is meant.

rules.label: our-take
rules.statement: At desktop widths no section keeps all its content to one side and leaves a wide empty region next to it, unless the space is meant (a deliberate margin, a sticky rail, a pause between sections).
rules.why: Found when reviewing a real redesign: an accordion sat in a narrow left column at 1440 px and left the right side blank, which read as unfinished next to full-width sections. No source gives a number; the 40% content width and the 25%-of-width asymmetry limits are our own working thresholds, and the result is for a person to judge, not a fail.
rules.generate_hint: Give a section that is narrower than the page a reason: center it, balance it with a second column or an image, or let it span the grid.

check.how: At 1440x900 and 390x844 take each img, video and canvas of 80 px or more that starts in the first screen. Sample a 5 by 5 grid of points over its box and count the points where the element itself is on top (elementFromPoint) and inside the screen. Flag when fewer than 40% show. A person decides whether the cover is meant.

rules.label: our-take
rules.statement: Images in the first screen are at least 40% visible at desktop and mobile widths: not covered by another element and not cut off by the screen edge, unless the layering is the design and enough of each image still shows to read it.
rules.why: Found when reviewing a real redesign: on a phone the hero's scatter of frames sat mostly behind the text plate, so the mobile page lost the personality the desktop page had. No source gives a number; the 40% visible limit is our own working threshold, and the result is for a person to judge, not a fail.
rules.generate_hint: At mobile width show fewer, larger frames or move the text off them; do not let the lead images hide behind the headline plate.

rules.statement: Before building, a written direction file exists that names 4 to 6 colours with roles, the display, body and (if used) mono font roles, a radius scale, and the subject-derived lead element of the hero, and every colour, font family and border-radius value in the shipped CSS appears in that file.
rules.why: Four independent practitioner sources recommend fixing tokens up front (a 4 to 6 colour plan; exact tokens instead of adjectives like 'modern and clean'), and Impeccable ships rules that flag a font, colour, radius or font size outside a DESIGN.md. Vague adjective prompts are said to return the statistical average.

check.how: Read the direction file. Extract distinct computed colours, font-family primaries, border-radius values and font sizes from the built page's CSS. Fail any value that is absent from the file (allow neutrals derived from the stated ramp). Confirm the file names the hero's lead element and why it fits the subject.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write the direction file first, then use only the colours, faces, radii and sizes it names.

rules.statement: Every use of a flagged default in this family (overused font, purple/cyan palette, gradient text, glow, glass, cream+terracotta, identical card grid, eyebrow labels, marquee) is listed in the direction file with a subject-specific reason.
rules.why: The tells are defaults, not banned techniques; Capital & Compute and Laith's tool both provide an explicit way to mark an intentional use, and Impeccable offers inline ignores. An unrecorded use is indistinguishable from a reflex.

check.how: Run the automated checks of the other distinct- rules. For each finding, confirm the direction file records the reason. Findings without a recorded reason fail.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: When you choose a common default on purpose, write down why it fits this subject.

rules.statement: The primary font-family of the display headings (h1 to h3) is not on the overused list (inter, roboto, open sans, lato, montserrat, arial, helvetica, fraunces, instrument sans, instrument serif, geist, geist sans, geist mono, mona sans, plus jakarta sans, space grotesk, recoleta) unless it is the brand's own face or the direction file justifies it; the body face may be a neutral sans.
rules.why: Six independent groups of sources name default faces as the top typographic tell; Impeccable's list was current as of 2026-11-05. The list is contested (one local skill recommends Geist; Google ranks Inter 5th in popularity), so the stable rule is a chosen and recorded face, not membership of a list.

check.how: In a headless browser, read getComputedStyle(fontFamily) for h1, h2, h3 and body; take the first non-generic family, lowercase it, ignore spaces, hyphens and underscores, and compare with the list. Flag a match on display headings that is not recorded as an exception.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Pick the display face from the subject and brand, say why, and avoid the face most generated pages use.

rules.statement: The rendered type roles (body, h3, h2, h1) contain at least one step of 1.25x or more between neighbours, and headings are visibly separated from body by size or by weight (at least 200 weight units heavier for at least 80% of headings).
rules.why: Impeccable flags a flat hierarchy when heading and body roles differ by less than 1.25x at every step (it needs at least 3 roles) and weight does not separate them. Other sources push stronger contrast (prg.sh suggests size jumps of 3x or more and extreme weights); those numbers come from one blog.

check.how: For h1 to h3 and p, li, td, blockquote read computed font-size and font-weight. Compute the largest ratio between neighbouring size roles and the share of headings at least 200 weight units heavier than the body weight. Fail if every step is below 1.25 and fewer than 80% of headings clear the weight gap.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Make at least one type step visibly larger than the 1.25x floor and give headings real weight contrast.

rules.statement: The hero h1 is no larger than 6rem (96 px), is not both 72 px or larger and 40 characters or longer, uses letter-spacing no tighter than -0.04em, and wraps within about 45 characters per line.
rules.why: Impeccable's detector flags h1 at 72 px or more with 40 or more characters and its craft floor caps display type at 6rem with a tracking floor of -0.04em; Laith's wiki gives 30 to 45 characters per line and about -0.03em at 48 px or more. These thresholds conflict with very large, short headlines only when the headline is long.

check.how: At 1440 px and 390 px viewports, read the hero h1 computed font-size, letter-spacing (in em), text length, and the longest rendered line length in characters. Fail any threshold above; review one-to-three-word headlines as allowed.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Keep the headline short enough that its type size stays under 6rem and the line stays near 45 characters.

rules.statement: No gradient stop or primary accent has a hue between 260 and 310 degrees (purple, violet, indigo), and no cyan accent sits on a near-black ground, unless the brand is that colour and the direction file says so.
rules.why: Six independent source groups name purple-to-blue gradients as the most recognised tell. Impeccable tests purple text at hue 260 to 310 (and treats a declared colour as purple within 250 to 320). The Reddit-mining dataset (3,214,533 posts scanned, 3,033 comments) ranks the 'AI purple' gradient among its top tells; that measures what people complain about, not cause.

check.how: Parse all gradients and accent colours in computed styles; convert stops to HSL or OKLCH hue; flag any in 260-310 degrees with meaningful saturation, plus Tailwind classes from/to purple, violet, indigo. Flag cyan accent text or fills on a background with very low luminance.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Derive the accent hue from the brand or subject and avoid default violet-to-blue gradients.

rules.statement: A warm cream or beige page background (minimum channel 209 or higher, red at least green at least blue, red minus blue between 6 and 48) combined with a terracotta or clay accent and a serif display face is used only when the direction file gives a subject reason.
rules.why: Impeccable has a rule for the cream surface; Anthropic's skill names cream with a terracotta accent near #D97757 as a default to avoid; Capital & Compute reports it as the second-wave cluster that appears after purple is banned; the local design-taste skill bans a family of cream, brass and espresso hexes for premium-consumer briefs. These are all one lineage plus one local skill, so the evidence is thin.

check.how: Read body and main-section background colours; test the cream condition above; if true, also check for a terracotta/clay accent (hue roughly 10-30 degrees, moderate saturation) and a serif display face. Report all three together as one finding and require an exception record.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Choose the page background from the subject's world, not from the safe warm off-white.

rules.statement: No text (headings, metrics, body) is filled with a gradient: no element combines background-clip: text with a gradient background-image.
rules.why: Gradient text appears in the Impeccable detector as its own rule, in wystack and the Reddit dataset, in Laith's list and in the local skills; emphasis can come from weight or size instead.

check.how: Query all elements; flag those whose computed -webkit-background-clip or background-clip is text and whose background-image contains a gradient function.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Set emphasis with weight, size or a solid colour, not a gradient fill.

rules.statement: No h1 or h2 sets one word or a short run (up to three words and under half of the heading's characters, not a link or code) apart from the rest of the heading by italic, a different colour, a different font family or a weight 200 or more units away (for example "Taste your AI can read." with the accent colour on "read."). One such heading per page is allowed only as a recorded exception with a subject reason.
rules.why: The single italic or accent-coloured word in a serif display headline is a stock move of generated hero sections: the owner named it on 2026-11-17 as one of the tells that made our own mock-ups read as AI-made, and the local design-taste skill bans the line-broken italic headline as a default move and mixed-family emphasis. Emphasis that the sentence needs can come from wording and order; the three-word and half-heading limits are our own thresholds.

check.how: For every visible h1 and h2 with two or more words, compare each descendant element (skipping links, code, sup, sub, images and runs of 1 px or less) whose text is three words or fewer and under half the heading's characters with the heading's computed style: font-style italic or oblique versus normal, colour (summed RGB channel difference over 48, a hue shift over 30 degrees between chromatic colours, or chromatic versus neutral), primary font family, and font-weight 200 or more apart. Report one finding per heading; any finding fails unless it is recorded as an exception.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Write a headline that carries its own emphasis; if one word must stand out, change the sentence, not the word's colour or slant.

rules.statement: No element has a chromatic box-shadow or text-shadow with zero offset and blur of 3 px or more; no chromatic radial-gradient halo (a saturated stop fading to transparent, on an element or its ::before/::after) sits behind the hero or a section, on a dark page at any size or on a light page at 160 x 160 px or larger; and no blurred colour blob (a textless element of 120 px or more with a chromatic fill and filter: blur of 20 px or more) is used, unless the glow or halo encodes a state (focus, selection, live status).
rules.why: Five independent source groups call glows and halos a default AI look. Impeccable's detector uses a minimum glow strength of 3 px and, for radial halos, a minimum effective alpha of 0.14 and contrast of 1.30 on the surface. One lineage's numbers; treat as indicative. The light-page halo (a soft peach or pink radial glow behind a centred hero) was added on 2026-11-17 after the owner named it as one of the tells that made our own hero mock-ups read as AI-made; the 160 px floor is our own threshold so a small button sheen does not count.

check.how: Parse computed box-shadow and text-shadow lists: flag entries with 0 horizontal and vertical offset, blur at or above 3 px and a saturated colour. Flag background-image radial-gradient (on the element or its ::before/::after) with a saturated stop and a stop under 0.3 alpha: on a dark page at any size, on a light page when the box is 160 px or more both ways. Flag textless elements of 120 px or more with a chromatic background and filter blur of 20 px or more. A halo that encodes a state is recorded as an exception.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Use neutral elevation shadows and a flat or subtly shifted background instead of coloured glow.

rules.statement: Every element using backdrop-filter blur is listed in the direction file with its function (for example nav over media, overlay separation), has a solid-colour fallback, and glass is not the default style of cards.
rules.why: Impeccable and Capital & Compute flag decorative glass; the Reddit dataset indicates users rarely complain about glassmorphism, and trend articles disagree on whether it has peaked. No source gives a numeric limit, so this is a judgement call.

check.how: Count elements with computed backdrop-filter containing blur. For each, confirm a recorded function and that text on it passes contrast against the worst-case content behind it (see a11y-contrast-text). Check a @supports fallback exists.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Use blur only where it separates a layer from content that changes behind it, with a solid fallback.

rules.statement: Small labels used as ornament stay rare: tracked uppercase or small-caps labels directly above headings plus small (14 px or less) uppercase, small-caps or monospace labels anywhere in the first viewport that are not links, buttons, navigation, form, table or code text (corner labels such as "SHEET 01" or "MEASURED ON RENDER") number at most ceil(sections / 3) on the page and at most one in the first viewport; none sits above the hero headline unless recorded as an exception; and numbered markers (01, 02, 03) appear only where the content is a real sequence.
rules.why: Impeccable bans a kicker above a heading outright and flags the hero chip; Anthropic's skill and Capital & Compute list tracked all-caps eyebrows and numbered markers; Noqta flags excess tracking on uppercase eyebrows; the local skill sets 'at most one per three sections'. The strict source and the lenient source disagree; this rule checks the lenient threshold. Corner and caption labels in the first viewport were added on 2026-11-17: the owner named decorative all-caps mono labels as a tell in our own mock-ups, and the local skill bans the mono-caps decoration strip at the hero bottom. The one-per-first-viewport limit is our own threshold.

check.how: Find elements with text-transform uppercase (or small-caps), positive letter-spacing and length of 40 characters or fewer that are the previous sibling of a heading (eyebrows). Separately, in the first viewport, find elements whose own text is 2 to 40 characters at 14 px or less, set uppercase, small-caps, literal capitals (two or more words, or six or more letters) or a monospace family, outside a, button, nav, label, form fields, footer, code, pre, table and headings (ornament labels). Fail if eyebrows plus ornament labels exceed ceil(section count / 3), if eyebrows in the first viewport plus ornament labels exceed 1, or if an eyebrow sits above the h1. Flag numeric prefixes in eyebrows where the section list is not an ordered process.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Let each heading stand alone, and drop corner labels, sheet numbers and mono captions that only decorate; keep a label only when it tells the reader something.

rules.statement: No section is built mainly from three or more same-size sibling cards that each hold an icon (or rounded icon tile), a heading and a short paragraph; the most important item gets more space than the others.
rules.why: Five independent source groups name the three-column icon-card feature row and the icon tile above a heading; Impeccable lists both as rules. Laith's tool lets you waive it when the product truly has three equal pillars.

check.how: In the DOM find sibling groups of 3 or more elements with widths within 5% of each other that each contain an svg/img icon, a heading and a paragraph. Report groups; a reviewer accepts a group only when the content is genuinely parallel and recorded as an exception.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Give the lead feature more room or show it as a real example instead of a row of identical cards.

rules.statement: No bordered, shadowed or tinted card container sits inside another such container.
rules.why: Impeccable has a nested-cards rule and wystack lists cards inside cards; Laith flags stacking shadow, border and tint on one card; the local skill allows cards only where elevation signals hierarchy. Flattening with spacing and dividers is the common fix.

check.how: For each element with a visible border, box-shadow, or non-transparent background different from its parent plus radius at or above 4 px, check whether an ancestor within the same section also qualifies. Report depth 2 or more.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Use spacing, rules and type to group content instead of boxes inside boxes.

rules.statement: No rounded element (radius 4 px or more) has a chromatic border on a single side wider than 1 px.
rules.why: Impeccable calls the thick coloured one-sided border on a card the most recognisable tell and sets 4 px radius as the point where it reads as a rounded card; Noqta makes the same claim. Square callouts with a severity rule are an older convention and are not flagged.

check.how: For each element, compare computed border widths per side. Flag where exactly one side is above 1 px, its colour is chromatic, and the two corners away from that side have radius at or above 4 px.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Mark emphasis with a background tint or an icon, not a thick coloured edge on a rounded card.

rules.statement: The CSS defines a named radius scale and a named elevation scale, each element role (button, input, card, badge, image) maps to a documented value, a single radius of 16 px or more is not applied to all roles, and no row of three or more cards pairs a hairline border with a shadow blur of 32 px or more.
rules.why: Noqta recommends a named scale (24 px everywhere versus a 6 px card example), Laith flags 16 to 24 px on everything and stacked border-shadow-tint, Impeccable flags rows of cards with a hairline border and a shadow of at least 32 px blur. The local design-taste skill asks for one consistent scale, so the compromise is a documented role map.

check.how: Collect computed border-radius for buttons, inputs, cards, badges and images; fail when all share one value at or above 16 px. Collect box-shadow blur on card rows: fail when 3 or more adjacent cards have a visible 1 px border and blur at or above 32 px. Confirm radius/shadow tokens exist in the direction file.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Define radius and shadow tokens per element role and use each token the same way everywhere.

rules.statement: The first viewport shows a real, subject-specific element (the product UI, work, place or object) and does not match the stock skeleton: at most two of these six signals appear together (centred headline, badge or eyebrow above it, exactly two buttons, a logo row within the next section, a three-card feature row as the following section, a stats strip of three or more big numbers in one row below the headline or as the following section).
rules.why: Five independent groups describe the same skeleton; Capital & Compute lists it as 'stock page order'. A centred hero alone is common and conventional, so this rule scores the whole skeleton plus whether real subject content leads. The stats strip was added as the sixth signal on 2026-11-17: the owner named the centred stack of eyebrow, headline, sub, pill button and stats row as the shape of our own AI-looking mock-ups.

check.how: At 1440 px, score the six signals from the DOM and computed styles. A big number is an element whose own text is a number of 10 characters or fewer (with an optional unit, %, x, + or currency) at max(28 px, 1.6 x body size); three or more with tops within 16 px and different left edges, below the h1 in the hero's section or anywhere in the next section, form a stats strip. Fail at three or more signals. A reviewer confirms the hero's dominant visual is real subject content (not a gradient blob or a div mock-up).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Open with the most characteristic real element of the subject and compose the hero around it.

rules.statement: Section paddings or heights are not all identical, no layout family is used for more than two consecutive sections, and a page of 8 sections uses at least 4 different layout families.
rules.why: Four independent groups flag uniform spacing and repeated section shapes (Impeccable's monotonous-spacing rule; Laith's uniform section rhythm). The numbers 4 of 8 and 2 in a row come from one local skill only.

check.how: Measure each top-level section's computed padding-block and height; flag a coefficient of variation near zero. Classify each section's skeleton (full-bleed, split, grid of N, list, quote) and count runs and distinct families.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Vary section structure and spacing on purpose, with one anchor section per screen of content.

rules.statement: Motion is one authored sequence plus responses to user action: the same entrance animation is not applied to every section, no easing overshoots (cubic-bezier with y outside 0 to 1, or elastic/bounce), no infinite animation exists that does not encode a state, and at most one auto-scrolling marquee exists.
rules.why: Five independent groups describe motion on everything and bounce easing; Impeccable treats bounce as advisory and any auto-scrolling marquee as a tell, while the local skill allows one marquee per page. Awwwards Sites of the Day are heavily animated (GSAP on 19 of 31), so the tell is sameness and lack of purpose, not motion itself. See also a11y-reduced-motion, a11y-pause-stop-hide and ux-minimal-motion.

check.how: Collect CSS animations and transitions: flag identical keyframe names applied to 4 or more sibling sections; flag cubic-bezier with a coordinate outside 0 to 1 on y; count animation-iteration-count infinite and marquee patterns. A reviewer records the purpose of each remaining animation (hierarchy, story, feedback, state).

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Design one signature motion moment and make every other animation answer a user action.

rules.statement: No pulsing status dot and no 'Live', 'New', 'Beta' or version pill appears unless it is bound to real changing state or a real release, and no pill chip sits above the hero heading.
rules.why: Noqta, Impeccable (pulsing-dot, hero-eyebrow-chip), the redesign skill and the design-taste skill all flag decorative liveness badges. Reserving pulse for live data is the stated fix.

check.how: Find small elements (aspect ratio 1.5 or less) with an infinite pulse animation; find pill-shaped elements (radius at or above half the height) whose text is new, live, beta, alpha, or matches a version pattern, within the first viewport; flag unless linked to data attributes or a release record.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Show a status label only when it reports something true and current.

rules.statement: Shipped copy contains no lorem ipsum, no placeholder people or brands (John Doe, Jane Smith, Acme, Globex, Initech), none of the filler words streamline, empower, supercharge, unlock, elevate, seamless, unleash, world-class, enterprise-grade, next-generation, cutting-edge, game-changer, and every statistic is traceable to a source or removed.
rules.why: Five independent groups list invented round numbers, placeholder names and filler verbs; Impeccable has a buzzword rule and Laith names the stat pattern (for example 10x, 99.9%, 10,000+). The existing guideline set already covers plain tagline and objective language (ux-tagline-specific, ux-objective-language, ux-descriptive-labels); this rule adds the mechanical list check.

check.how: Extract visible text and alt text. Regex for the list above (case-insensitive), lorem ipsum, and standalone round statistics (10x, 99.9%, \d{1,3},000+). For every statistic, require a data-source or footnote in the content brief; flag otherwise.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write what the product literally does with real numbers, and delete any figure you cannot source.

rules.statement: No more than two links or buttons end in an arrow glyph, no more than one meta string uses middle-dot separators, and em-dashes stay below saturation (fewer than 8 in total, or less than one per 500 characters of body text).
rules.why: Anthropic's skill and Laith list arrows on links and buttons; the Anthropic skill and the local skill ration middle-dot strings; Impeccable's em-dash rule is advisory and only fires at 8 or more em-dashes near one per 500 characters. The 'two' and 'one' limits are our own working thresholds. The local skill's total em-dash ban is not shared by any other source.

check.how: Count link and button labels ending in an arrow character (arrow, chevron); count text nodes with 2 or more middle-dot separators; count em-dashes and body-text length.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Write plain button and link labels and separate metadata with layout instead of dots and arrows.

rules.statement: No img uses a placeholder or stock-demo host, the product is not shown as a mock-up built from empty div rectangles (live interface built from real text, controls and states is fine), no hero-sized inline SVG scene is assembled from primitive shapes, no emoji or Unicode pictograph stands in for an icon, and icons come from one family at one stroke weight.
rules.why: Five independent groups flag stock or machine-made imagery, emoji icons or default icon sets; Impeccable has a shape-assembled-illustration rule (advisory) and bans glyph icons in its craft floor; the local skill suggests picsum placeholders only while developing, so they must be replaced before shipping. Existing rule ux-informative-imagery already asks for imagery that informs. When no real screenshots or photos exist yet, show the product as live HTML/CSS with real text and states (not empty boxes), or leave the imagery out and mark the gap; never ship a placeholder host or stock demo image. For physical goods there is no interface to show, so the offer itself (price, seats, dates, a calculator or booking control built from real HTML), type set large as the image, or an omitted and marked gap are the honest options; real photographs have to be commissioned.

check.how: List img and background-image sources and flag placeholder hosts (picsum, placehold, via.placeholder, unsplash source URLs used as demo); regex visible text and button labels for pictographic emoji used as icons; flag svg elements above half the viewport width built from at least a handful of primitive shapes; compare icon svg stroke widths. A reviewer confirms the hero image is real.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Use real photos or screenshots and one consistent icon set, never emoji or placeholder images; with no screenshots yet, build the product view as live HTML with real text and states, or omit it. For a physical product with no photographs, the offer itself can be the live object (price, seats, dates, a calculator, a booking control), or a measurement or price can be set large as real text, or leave the imagery out and mark the gap; do not draw the product from shapes in code (recipe no-photography-physical-goods).

rules.statement: Component-library defaults (for example shadcn/ui tokens or Tailwind palette values) are customised: the shipped radius, colour and font variables differ from the library's init output.
rules.why: The Reddit dataset ranks the default shadcn/Tailwind look as its top specific tell; the local design-taste skill says never ship default state. Two groups, one of them an informal proxy of opinion.

check.how: Generate the library's default theme in a scratch project; diff its CSS variables for radius, background, foreground, primary and font against the shipped CSS; flag when radius, primary and font all equal the defaults.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Set your own radius, colour and type tokens before using any library component.

rules.statement: With the logo and name replaced by a competitor's, a reviewer can still tell which site is which from the hero, type, colour and imagery alone.
rules.why: Only Noqta states this test; Prg.sh's call for personality and a clear point of view is related. Treat as a judgement heuristic.

check.how: Screenshot the first two viewports, swap the logo and brand name with a competitor's, and ask a reviewer who did not build it to identify the site and say what the design idea is. If they cannot, record a finding.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Anchor the design in one idea that only this subject could carry.

rules.statement: A page rebuilt after a reference site ("make it like X") takes the reference's structure, proportions, sizes and motion, and none of its brand: not its name, copy, logo, illustrations or signature object, not a paid font it licenses, and not screenshots or pictures of its own product. Its signature object is replaced by one made from the subject's own world, and its picture slots hold the subject's own or properly credited material.
rules.why: Structure and rhythm are craft anyone may learn from; the name, words, art and licensed fonts are the reference's property, and a picture of the reference's own product on another site reads as an advertisement for it (the owner caught exactly that on the whata.design home, 2026-11-17). Replacing the reference's object with one from the subject's world (a keychain of interface parts on a site about interface design) is what made the rebuild read as the subject's own.

check.how: Put the rebuilt page beside the reference. List every name, sentence, logo, illustration, font family and picture on the rebuilt page that also appears on the reference, or that shows the reference's own product; each one is a finding. Then ask what the hero object is made of: if it is the reference's object recoloured, it is a finding.

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Measure the reference into the library first (get_sections, get_section) and copy its numbers, order and motion beats; draw the hero object from the subject's own parts; fill pictures from the subject or the library with credit; use a free or owned font with the same role.

rules.statement: Before shipping, the page is reviewed against the four published Awwwards criteria (Design 40%, Usability 30%, Creativity 20%, Content 10%) with one piece of evidence recorded per criterion, and any criterion without evidence is treated as failing.
rules.why: Awwwards publishes these weights and states that at least 18 jurors score each nominee; Webby lists seven criteria (including accessibility and speed under Visual Design and Functionality) without weights; CSS Design Awards gives only thresholds. Using a public rubric makes the review explicit; the evidence requirement is our own.

check.how: Score Design, Usability, Creativity and Content on 1 to 10 with a cited screenshot or report per score; compute 0.4*Design + 0.3*Usability + 0.2*Creativity + 0.1*Content; optionally also check the Webby list (content with a point of view, structure and navigation, visual design, functionality, interactivity, innovation, overall experience).

rules.label: our-take
rules.generate_hint: Keep a one-line piece of evidence for design, usability, creativity and content before calling the page done.

rules.statement: The homepage says who you are, what you offer and how you differ, quickly, in the audience's own words.
rules.why: When the purpose is not visible at a glance, potential customers leave.

check.how: Five-second test: show the first screen and ask what the site is for; compare answers with the brief.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Say in the first screen who you are, what you offer and how you differ, in the audience's words.

rules.statement: Use a plain, specific tagline and headline instead of generic welcome messages or jargon.
rules.why: Users scan and spend most of their time at the top; vague text wastes it.

check.how: Read the headline without the logo: could any competitor say the same?

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Write a specific headline and tagline; no generic welcome text or jargon.

rules.statement: Images carry information about the offer or brand rather than serving as decorative stock.
rules.why: Decorative imagery adds weight without meaning.

check.how: For each major image ask what it communicates that the text does not.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Use images that carry information about the offer, not decorative stock.

rules.statement: Show specific samples of real content (products, articles, projects) instead of only generic category links.
rules.why: Concrete examples reveal what the site offers.

check.how: Check that the first two screens show actual items, not only labels.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Show real samples of products, work or articles, not only category links.

rules.statement: Links and buttons have specific descriptive labels, not "Click here" or "Learn more".
rules.why: Users scan, and screen reader users hear links out of context.

check.how: List every link and button label out of context.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Label links and buttons with the result ('Book a demo'), not 'Learn more' or 'Submit'.

rules.statement: Make text scannable: meaningful subheadings, short paragraphs with one idea each, lists, and the conclusion first.
rules.why: In NN/g's study (Nielsen, 30 Sep 1997; sample size not stated) 79% of users always scanned and 16% read word by word. Concise text scored +58%, scannable layout +47% and the combined version +124% on usability, relative to a promotional-writing control.

check.how: Read only headings, first sentences and bold text; the page should still make sense.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Use meaningful subheadings, short paragraphs with one idea, lists and the conclusion first.

rules.statement: Prefer plain factual statements to boastful marketing language.
rules.why: Objective language scored +27% on usability relative to a promotional control (Nielsen, 30 Sep 1997; sample size not stated); users spend effort filtering out hype.

check.how: Highlight superlatives and claims; each should be backed by a fact or removed.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Prefer plain facts to boastful marketing language; back claims with proof.

rules.statement: Put the most important information in the first screens and the first two paragraphs; begin headings, bullets and paragraphs with meaningful words.
rules.why: Eyetracking of 232 users found a rough F-shaped pattern (Nielsen, 16 Apr 2006; a later study 11 years on reportedly confirmed it); it is a shape, not a law. In a 2018 study (Fessenden, 15 Apr 2018; 120 participants, over 130,000 fixations) 57% of viewing time was above the fold and 74% in the first two screenfuls.

check.how: List the top three things a visitor must learn and check they appear in the first two screens.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Put the most important information in the first screens and the first words of headings and paragraphs.

rules.statement: The primary call to action is visible without scrolling, with visual hierarchy built around the top task.
rules.why: Attention drops sharply after the fold: 57% of viewing time was above the fold in 2018 versus 80% in 2010; 74% fell in the first two screenfuls (NN/g, 15 Apr 2018, 120 participants).

check.how: Automated: find the primary call to action (the first visible link or button in the hero, else in main, that starts with an action verb or is drawn as a button; else the first button-like element on the page) and fail when its bounding box is not fully inside the first viewport at 1440x900 and 390x844. The evidence names the element it took and why (for example 'first filled button in the hero'). When the page's main action is something else (a board of rows, a form, a single link), mark that element with a data-primary-cta attribute: it overrides the heuristic and its bounding box is measured instead. A person confirms the element found is the page's top task and that the visual hierarchy is built around it.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Show the primary action in the first viewport and repeat it where natural.

rules.statement: Avoid false floors: signal that there is more below, for example with cut-off content.
rules.why: Minimalist layouts can look finished before they are.

check.how: Look at the first screen: does anything suggest more content below?

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Let the next section peek in at the bottom edge so the first screen does not look finished.

rules.statement: The logo links to the homepage and sits where people expect it (top-left in left-to-right languages); the homepage looks distinct from interior pages.
rules.why: Easy access to the starting point is a basic orientation need.

check.how: Click the logo from several pages.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Link the logo to the homepage in a findable place, top-left in left-to-right layouts.

rules.statement: Show primary navigation on desktop; on mobile show four or fewer top-level links, and use a menu only for more.
rules.why: In a study with 179 participants on 6 live sites (Pernice and Budiu, 26 Jun 2016), navigation was used in 27% of desktop tasks when hidden versus 48% visible and 50% combined; hidden navigation cut content discoverability by more than 20%. On mobile the article suggests showing four or fewer top-level links, otherwise hiding some.

check.how: Check whether the main sections are visible without opening a menu.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Show primary navigation links on desktop; on mobile show four or fewer, otherwise use a disclosure menu.

rules.statement: Use conventional layouts and patterns where the user's goal is practical, so existing mental models apply; depart from convention deliberately.
rules.why: Users bring expectations from other sites. NN/g recommends standard layouts for homepages.

check.how: Ask whether each unconventional choice is worth its cost, and write the reason down.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Use conventional patterns for practical goals and break convention deliberately, with a written reason.

rules.statement: Keep labels, components and behavior consistent within the site and with common conventions.
rules.why: Heuristic 4 (consistency and standards); GOV.UK says "consistent, not uniform".

check.how: Audit repeated components and labels across pages.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Reuse the same labels, components and behavior for the same function.

rules.statement: Prefer a single static hero to a rotating carousel. If you use a carousel: five frames or fewer, controls inside it with a clear current state, no auto-advance on mobile, timing based on reading speed (about 3 words per second), and the important content repeated elsewhere.
rules.why: Users often scroll past carousels and miss frames after the first. This is a 2013 article (reviewed 2026) with no stated sample size, so the guidance is guideline-level, not study-level.

check.how: Check frame count, controls, auto-rotation and whether any critical message exists only inside the carousel. APG carousel pattern: an auto-rotating carousel has a stop/start button as its first tab stop (its label changes, so no aria-pressed), rotation stops when focus enters or the mouse hovers, and previous and next buttons are required.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Prefer one static hero; if you use a carousel keep it to five frames, controls inside, no autoplay on mobile, and repeat key content elsewhere.

rules.statement: If you use a mega menu: group options with short front-loaded labels, show each option once, keep the search visible, make it work with a keyboard and screen reader, and use hover intent (pointer still for about 0.5 s before opening).
rules.why: Prevents flicker and lost context.

check.how: Test with mouse, keyboard and screen reader.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: For mega menus group options with short labels, use hover intent, keep search visible and support keyboard and screen readers.

rules.statement: Do not style important content like an ad (banner shapes, right-rail boxes, animated strips).
rules.why: Users ignore elements they perceive as ads, including content nearby and large distinct images (NN/g, 22 Apr 2018, 26 participants in the latest eyetracking study). One participant's gaze on one page gave the right rail 33 times fewer fixations than its size suggested (1 of 132 content-area fixations); that is an illustration, not a statistic.

check.how: Check that key messages are not in banner-like containers.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Do not style important content like banners, right-rail boxes or animated strips.

rules.statement: Avoid popups and splash screens on the homepage, except where legally required (cookie consent, age checks).
rules.why: They are among the most disliked web design elements, per NN/g.

check.how: Load the page fresh; note anything that interrupts the first view.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Avoid popups and splash screens on the homepage except legally required consent or age checks.

rules.statement: Keep motion minimal on the homepage; moving elements are often mistaken for ads, and the logo, tagline and headline should stay static.
rules.why: Motion draws attention away from the message and can look like advertising.

check.how: Watch the first 10 seconds with and without motion.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Keep motion minimal near the headline and primary action; keep logo, tagline and headline static.

rules.statement: Keep forms as short as possible: remove fields that can be derived, collected later or dropped; limit optional fields to one or two and label them.
rules.why: Fewer fields mean higher completion.

check.how: List every field and justify it.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Ask only for fields you need; at most one or two optional fields, labeled.

rules.statement: Use a single column with labels close to their fields (above on mobile); only short related fields share a row.
rules.why: A single column keeps people moving down the form.

check.how: Check layout at desktop and mobile widths.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Use one column with labels close to their fields (above on mobile).

rules.statement: Do not use placeholder text as the label or as the only instruction.
rules.why: NN/g reports usability problems with placeholders; the text disappears on input.

check.how: Check every field has a visible, persistent label.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Never use a placeholder as a label; keep a visible label.

rules.statement: Use radio buttons instead of dropdowns for two or three options; size inputs to the expected value; state format rules up front; avoid Reset and Clear buttons.
rules.why: Reduces hidden options and accidental data loss.

check.how: Review each control type.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Use radio buttons instead of dropdowns for two or three options; state formats up front; avoid Reset buttons.

rules.statement: Signal errors with several cues, not color alone; explain the problem specifically; keep what the user typed.
rules.why: Users must understand and fix errors without redoing work.

check.how: Submit invalid data and read the messages.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Signal errors with more than color, say what is wrong and keep the user's input.

rules.statement: Largest Contentful Paint is 2.5 seconds or less at the 75th percentile of page loads, for mobile and desktop separately.
rules.why: Reflects whether the page feels like it is loading. NN/g cites a Google finding that bounce likelihood rises 32% as load time goes from 1 to 3 seconds; the method is not given, so treat it as secondary evidence.

check.how: Check field data (CrUX) and lab data (Lighthouse). LCP candidates are img, image in svg, video (poster load or first frame, whichever is earlier), url() background images (not gradients) and block-level text.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Keep LCP at 2.5 s or less: make the LCP image discoverable in HTML, never lazy-load it, set fetchpriority high, keep head scripts and CSS small.

rules.statement: Interaction to Next Paint is 200 ms or less at the 75th percentile.
rules.why: Reflects whether the page feels responsive.

check.how: Check field data; lab tools only approximate it.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Keep interaction responses at 200 ms or less: avoid long main-thread tasks, animate with transform and opacity, debounce handlers.

rules.statement: Cumulative Layout Shift is 0.1 or less at the 75th percentile.
rules.why: Reflects whether the page feels stable.

check.how: Check field and lab data. Common fixes: width and height or aspect-ratio on images and video, reserved space for late content, font-display: optional with a close fallback, animate transform instead of top, left or box-shadow.

rules.label: standard
rules.generate_hint: Reserve space for images, video, embeds and late content; keep layout shift at 0.1 or less.

rules.statement: Core content loads immediately and does not depend on a heavy effect layer; build effects on top of working content.
rules.why: Progressive enhancement keeps the page usable when effects fail or are slow.

check.how: Disable JavaScript and throttle the network; the message and navigation should still appear.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Build core content and navigation as HTML that works without JavaScript; layer effects on top.

rules.statement: Test usability with about five people per audience group per round, fix problems, and test again; several small rounds beat one large one.
rules.why: Nielsen (18 Mar 2000): the first user finds about a third of problems (31% averaged over projects studied), five users find about 85%, and three rounds of five beat one round of fifteen; test 3 to 4 users per group for two groups and at least 3 per group for three or more. Norman (2013, ch. 6) also advises five and iterating.

check.how: Run the planned rounds; record problems and fixes.

rules.label: evidence
rules.generate_hint: Plan about five people per audience group per round, fix problems and test again.

rules.statement: Start from real user needs and test assumptions with real people from the beginning.
rules.why: GOV.UK and the U.S. Web Design System both list it as their first principle.

check.how: Check the brief cites research, not only internal opinion.

rules.label: craft-consensus
rules.generate_hint: Start from real user needs and test assumptions with real people.

recipes.title: Dark, neon and atmospheric palettes that stay readable
recipes.summary: Keep the near-black canvas and the glowing accents. Make text sit on solid surfaces, use neon for large or graphical elements only, and give focus its own bright, high-contrast ring.
recipes.keep: Dark canvas, neon accents, glow, grain and gradients as atmosphere.
recipes.avoid: Neon text for body copy; accents as the only sign of state; thin low-contrast hairlines; strobing glows.

contrast.pair: neon green accent on background (UI, large text)
neon pink accent on background (UI, large text)
dark text on neon green button
white text on 55% black scrim over gradient stop #3B1E8F
white text on 55% black scrim over gradient stop #D946EF
white text on 55% black scrim over gradient stop #FDE68A

steps.title: Name palette roles and check pairs
steps.do: Define colors as named roles, and check every text and surface pairing before choosing accents. Body text and muted text use the first two roles; neon is for large text, icons, borders and buttons with dark text on top.
steps.how: Use the verified pairs in this recipe as the starting palette; change a color only after recomputing its contrast.
steps.label: craft-consensus

steps.title: Solid scrim under text
steps.do: Put text on a solid or semi-opaque surface, never directly on a gradient, glow, grain or image. Grain and noise sit on the background layer only. Over a gradient, a 55% black scrim keeps white text at 4.5:1 or better on every tested stop (#3B1E8F, #D946EF, #FDE68A), where unscrimmed white on #FDE68A fails.
steps.how: Layer order: background gradient and grain, then a scrim or surface, then text.
steps.label: craft-consensus

steps.title: Bright dedicated focus ring
steps.do: Give focus a distinct bright ring that works on both background and surface, and never remove the outline without a replacement.
steps.how: Use :focus-visible (Baseline widely available since March 2022) so the browser decides when the ring shows. MDN: the indicator needs at least 3:1 contrast (WCAG 1.4.11) and must not simply be removed. In forced-colors mode outline-color and border-color are forced to system colors and stay visible, but box-shadow is forced to none, so draw the ring with outline (as below) and do not rely on box-shadow alone. MDN advises against building a separate forced-colors design; do not use forced-color-adjust to override users' colors. Cyan #5CE1FF measures 3:1 or better on both dark roles.
steps.label: craft-consensus

steps.title: Show state beyond color
steps.do: Show state (selected, error, success) with more than a color shift: an icon, underline, weight or text.
steps.how: WCAG techniques: put the information in text (G14) or add another visual cue (G182); failures include required or error fields identified by color alone (F81). Inline links need 3:1 against surrounding text or another cue. WCAG lists color-vision simulators for checking; a grayscale view is a quick approximation.
steps.label: craft-consensus

steps.title: Keep glow static or slow
steps.do: Keep glow static or slow. Never flash: content passes WCAG 2.3.1 if it flashes no more than three times per second.
steps.how: WCAG 2.3.1: no more than three general or red flashes in any one second passes without a tool; otherwise the flashes must stay below the thresholds (opposing luminance change of at least 10% with the darker state below 0.80 is a general flash; area limit about 341×256 px at 1024×768). Prefer a still box-shadow glow; if you pulse, keep it slow and respect reduced motion.
steps.label: craft-consensus

steps.title: Show toggle state beyond color
steps.do: Style toggles from [aria-pressed=true] and add a knob position or check icon, not only a color change.
steps.how: Grayscale screenshot of both states; confirm still distinguishable. Check CSS selectors key off aria-pressed/aria-checked/:checked. (Derived from the rule; see its sources.)
steps.label: craft-consensus
steps.status_note: generated from a craft-consensus rule; the technique itself was not separately verified

steps.title: Scrim behind text on media
steps.do: Put a solid or gradient scrim behind any text that sits on a photo or video and verify the contrast on the brightest area.
steps.how: Screenshot each section with text on imagery at 375, 768 and 1440 px (and at the video's brightest frame). Sample the backdrop under each text line's bounding box, take the pixel closest to the text color, compute the WCAG ratio. Fail below 4.5:1 (3:1 for 24px+ or 18.66px+ bold). (Derived from the rule; see its sources.)
steps.label: craft-consensus

steps.title: Re-check contrast in dark mode
steps.do: Author the dark palette as its own set of tokens, check contrast in both themes, and dim bright images instead of inverting anything.
steps.how: Run the contrast audit (text 4.5:1, large 3:1, UI components 3:1) twice, once per emulated color scheme, over all pages and states (hover, focus, disabled excluded). Fail any pair that passes light but fails dark. Flag use of `filter: invert()` on the page root. (Derived from the rule; see its sources.)
steps.label: craft-consensus
