Chrome demo: the close button is a button with aria-label "Close window", measures at least 44 by 44 px once its open transition finishes and shows a solid 3px outline on keyboard focus. WCAG 2.5.8 requires 24 by 24 px or spacing.
steps.label: standard

recipes.generate_hint: State the accent hue and why in the direction file, use flat accents on graphite (orange, lime, amber, green) or a solid committed purple with an exception record, draw depth with hairlines and neutral shadows, bind any status text to real data, and measure the contrast of text under scanlines.

recipes.title: No photography exists (physical goods or services): the offer as the live object, type as image, or an honest gap
recipes.summary: When no photographs exist (a physical product with no photos yet, or a service with none you can use), do not draw the subject from shapes and do not use stock. Make the offer itself the live object when it has state (price, seats, slots, dates, a calculator, a booking control or self-check), let a large measurement, price or fact be the image, present the catalogue or fee table as a menu or run sheet where there are rows to list, or leave the imagery out and mark the gap, and plan the real photographs. For a service, np-offer-live-object applies when there is state to show, np-type-as-image and np-mark-the-gap always apply, np-menu-and-run-sheet only when the service has rows to list, and np-pieces-only-limit is for goods.
recipes.keep: A first object made of real controls and real numbers; type set large as real text; tables and run sheets with specific rows; an honest, listed gap.
recipes.avoid: Shape-assembled drawings of the product; stock or placeholder images; emoji icons; a decorative texture that starts to depict the product; unconfirmed prices or hours shown as facts; claiming the live object replaces photographs for a pieces-only shop.

steps.title: Make the offer the first object
steps.do: When the offer has state to show (seats left, time slots, dates, sizes, bundles, a price that changes with a choice), make the offer itself the first object on the page: a booking or price control built from real HTML controls with real numbers and real states, placed where a product photo would normally sit.
steps.how: In the pilot, a ceramics studio selling six seats at a stated price per workshop used a ring of six native checkboxes that totals the price and writes the booking email, instead of a photograph. It works because the offer is seat-limited; it does not work for a pieces-only shop, which has no state to show (see np-pieces-only-limit). The numbers on the page must be the owner's: mark any you do not have with the assumption marker from the protocol (3.2). For a service: it applies when the service has state to show (free slots, a waiting time, opening hours, a self-check or calculator); a self-check was the live object in a tenant-rights advice pilot. If the service has no state, use np-type-as-image.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Derived from one pilot (a model designing a ceramics-studio homepage on the lean track); no user was shown the page and no conversion was measured. Only structural checks were run (no img, svg or canvas, no emoji).

steps.title: Live object from native controls
steps.do: Build the live object from native controls (checkbox, radio, select, button, number input) with visible labels, a fieldset and legend for a group, keyboard operation for free, and a total that updates in an output element so the change is announced without moving focus. State is never carried by colour alone: selected seats also differ by fill, ring or text.
steps.how: WCAG 4.1.3 asks that status messages can be announced without taking focus; the Understanding page lists role=status and live regions as the techniques. Using native controls follows the ARIA practice 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA'. Not measured with a screen reader here: test it with VoiceOver or NVDA before launch.
steps.label: standard

code.text:
Pick your seats

Total: 0

steps.status_note: The requirement (status messages announced without focus) was read in the WCAG Understanding page. The markup pattern is general engineering knowledge and was not tested with a screen reader.

steps.title: Let type carry the image
steps.do: Let type carry the image: set a measurement, a date, a price, a capacity or a name large as the visual, in the display face, as real text. Never export the type as an image.
steps.how: WCAG 1.4.5 (images of text) is the reason it stays real text: it resizes, reflows and can be read by assistive technology. Which fact to set large is a design judgement: choose the one that answers the visitor's first question about the product (how big, how many, how much, when).
steps.label: craft-consensus
steps.status_note: The images-of-text requirement was read in the WCAG Understanding page. That type can stand in for a product image is our design judgement, with no study behind it.

steps.title: Catalogue as a table or list
steps.do: Present the catalogue, price list or run sheet as a menu: a real table or definition list with one row per item (name, size or detail, price, availability, how to get it) in plain text. Vary the structure of the sections below the hero: a run sheet in one, a price list in another, a measurements table in a third.
steps.how: Specific rows (a size, a price, a firing or delivery time) inform the way a photograph would, and a list is not an image-card grid. Each figure must be a fact the owner gave or be marked unconfirmed. Judgement: whether visitors who buy by looking accept a text catalogue is not tested here. For a service: use it only when there are rows to list (a fee table, opening hours, the steps of a process); in the advice pilot it did not fit.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Derived from one pilot (a model designing a ceramics-studio homepage on the lean track); no user was shown the page and no conversion was measured. Only structural checks were run (no img, svg or canvas, no emoji).

steps.title: Mark the missing photography
steps.do: If none of the above fits, leave the imagery out and mark the gap: in the design notes and in design/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md write that photographs are missing, which shots are needed, and that the page is not finished without them. Do not use a placeholder host, a stock demo image, an emoji, or a picture of the product assembled from shapes in code.
steps.how: A faint decorative gradient or texture that does not depict the product is ornament and the rule does not flag it. One that starts to depict the product (grooves that read as a pottery wheel, a glaze, a bowl) is an illustration: remove it or commission it as a file. The rule's detector flags hero-sized inline SVG scenes assembled from primitives; a drawn bowl or cross-section is that.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Derived from the wording of `distinct-real-imagery-and-icons` and one pilot. The line between ornament and illustration is a judgement call and is not measured.

steps.title: Plan the photo shot list
steps.do: Plan the real photographs: a shot list (hero object, scale, detail, in use), who takes them, licence and alt text, reserved width and height for each image slot, and the likely LCP image set with fetchpriority high and not lazy-loaded when it arrives. Put the plan in assets and in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.
steps.how: Reserving dimensions now prevents layout shift later; alt text describes what the photograph conveys in context. The shot list is our suggestion, not a tested checklist.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: A planning step, not a measured technique.

steps.title: Limits when selling single pieces
steps.do: If the business sells individual pieces and the offer has no state to show (no seats, slots or sizes to choose), the live object cannot replace a photograph. Say so in the notes, use the menu form and type as image, and record the missing photographs as the main launch risk.
steps.how: The pilot's own conclusion: the live object worked only because the studio sold a seat-limited class. People often buy a piece by looking at it, so a page without images may read as unfinished; this is a risk to state to the owner, not a measured effect. This step is for goods. A service has its own version of the problem only when nothing about it can be shown as state or as a fact; then use np-type-as-image and np-mark-the-gap, and photographs of people need their consent.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Derived from one pilot (a model designing a ceramics-studio homepage on the lean track); no user was shown the page and no conversion was measured. Only structural checks were run (no img, svg or canvas, no emoji).

recipes.generate_hint: No photos (goods or a service)? Build the offer as the live object with native controls when it has state (or set the key fact, measurement or price large as real text), show a fee table or catalogue as a table or run sheet when there are rows, mark the photograph gap in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, and never draw the subject from shapes in code. Services: skip the pieces-only limit; the menu step only if there are rows to list.

recipes.title: Urgent help routes on public-service and crisis pages: the emergency line once, a real phone route with hours, and the primary action still on the first screen
recipes.summary: For audiences who may be in danger, in debt, ill or facing a deadline, put the urgent route where it is read first, but keep it small. State the emergency-services boundary once, give a phone number as a tel: link with its hours and an out-of-hours route, carry the meaning in words, a border and position rather than red alone, and measure that the band does not push the page's primary action below the first screen at 390x844. Use plain labels in the reader's words.
recipes.keep: One short urgent band, first in reading order; a visible phone number that is a tel: link; hours as text and a stated out-of-hours route; the emergency-services line written once; the primary action inside the first phone screen.
recipes.avoid: Red as the only signal; the emergency line repeated in every section; a sticky or modal urgent bar that covers content or focus; a pop-up, a timer or an auto-opening chat; a phone number only as an image; hours or numbers the owner has not confirmed shown as facts; labels such as 'crisis escalation' that the reader would not use.

palette.name: Urgent band, computed (WCAG 2 relative luminance); the colours are an example, the cue is the text, the border and the position

steps.title: Urgent route first in order
steps.do: Decide the one urgent route for this audience and put it first in reading order, before the page's main content, as a short band: one heading, one or two sentences, one phone link. Put the page's primary action directly after it. The urgent route is not the page's primary action unless the service itself is a helpline.
steps.how: Code order equals reading order, so a screen-reader or keyboard user meets the route first and a sighted reader meets it first too. Keep it to a band, not a section, so it does not take over the page. Which route comes first (the emergency line, the helpline, the service's own number) is the owner's call and depends on the service.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Derived from one fictional-service pilot (a model designing a homepage for a UK tenant-rights advice service on the sprint track) and general practice; no user, screen-reader or phone test was run on the pattern.

steps.title: State emergency boundary once
steps.do: State the emergency-services boundary once, in plain words, at the top: say who to call if someone is in danger now (for example 'If someone is in danger now, call 999, the emergency services') and that this service is not one. Do not repeat it in every section or in the footer. 999 is the UK number and an example: the owner must confirm the number for the service's country (112, 911 ...).
steps.how: Said once, the line is read and acted on; repeated, it dilutes the page, frightens people who are not in danger and is read aloud again at every repeat by a screen reader. Whether the boundary line is also legally or professionally required for this service is for the owner to confirm. This is a design judgement, not a tested result.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Derived from one fictional-service pilot (a model designing a homepage for a UK tenant-rights advice service on the sprint track) and general practice; no user, screen-reader or phone test was run on the pattern.

steps.title: Phone number as a tel link
steps.do: Show the phone number as real text inside a tel: link whose visible text includes the number and a verb ('Call us: 020 7946 0000'), at least 44 by 44 CSS px, with the country code in the href. Show the same number as text on desktop, where there may be no calling app.
steps.how: The visible text is the accessible name, so voice-control users can say what they see (label in name). The tel: scheme is standard HTML; a desktop browser with no calling app may do nothing, which is why the number stays visible as text. Not tested on real phones here. The number in the example is from the UK range set aside for fiction; the owner's number, or the visible assumption marker (protocol 3.2) until it is confirmed, goes in its place.
steps.label: craft-consensus

code.text:
If someone is in danger now

Call 999 for the emergency services. We are not an emergency service.

Call us: 020 7946 0000

Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm. Outside those hours, use the call-back form and we reply the next working day.

steps.status_note: The accessible-name and target-size requirements are WCAG 2.5.3 and 2.5.8 (quick reference); the markup is ordinary HTML. No phone, desktop-without-app or voice-control test was run.

steps.title: Hours and out-of-hours route
steps.do: Write the opening hours as text next to the number and say what to do outside them: another number, a form with the reply time, or where to leave a message. Promise only a reply time the service keeps. Hours, reply times and numbers the owner has not confirmed carry the visible assumption marker (protocol 3.2) and are listed in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.
steps.how: A phone line that is closed with no other route is a dead end for a person in a hurry. A live 'open now' badge from JavaScript is optional and must not replace the text, because the core content has to work without JavaScript.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Derived from one fictional-service pilot (a model designing a homepage for a UK tenant-rights advice service on the sprint track) and general practice; no user, screen-reader or phone test was run on the pattern.

steps.title: Urgency beyond red alone
steps.do: Carry the urgency in words, position and a border, not in red alone. The band starts with a plain sentence, has a visible border, has text at 4.5:1 and its boundary at 3:1 (check with check_contrast, role text and ui), and keeps its meaning in forced-colors mode and for a reader who cannot tell the colour. Keep red for errors so the two do not mean the same thing.
steps.how: WCAG 1.4.1 says colour is never the only way to show information. The palette above is computed with the WCAG 2 formula; amber is an example, not a requirement. The band's text works on its own, so removing the colour loses nothing.
steps.label: standard
steps.status_note: The requirement was read in the WCAG Understanding page and the ratios were computed. How the band reads under forced colors or to people with colour-vision differences was not tested.

steps.title: Band and action above the fold
steps.do: Stack the band with the primary action and check it at 390x844: the primary action's bottom edge must be inside the first viewport. Keep the band compact (a heading and one line, or one line with the phone link), do not make it sticky or a full-height overlay, and trim the page's own heading before the band if they compete. If the action still falls below, shorten the band before you shrink the action.
steps.how: A sticky or fixed bar costs the first screen on every scroll position and can cover focused elements (WCAG 2.4.11). Measure, do not guess: the audit's primary-action check and a screenshot at 390x844 both work. In the pilot an amber band took about a quarter of the phone's first screen and put the main button at 858 px, below the 844 px fold; the audit found it and the layout was changed. Any height budget (for example 'a fifth of the viewport') is our rule of thumb, not a standard.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Derived from one fictional-service pilot (a model designing a homepage for a UK tenant-rights advice service on the sprint track) and general practice; no user, screen-reader or phone test was run on the pattern. The snippet measures one element's box; it does not replace looking at the screenshot.

steps.title: Labels in the reader's words
steps.do: Write every label in the reader's words and in plain language: 'Call us', 'Call 999 if someone is in danger now', 'I have been given an eviction notice', not 'Crisis escalation', 'Urgent triage' or the service's internal names. Put the verb first, spell out acronyms, state what a call costs if the reader may have to pay, and aim at the lower reading target for stressed, ESL or low-literacy readers (see copy-reading-grade).
steps.how: People under stress read less and take in less (the COGA guidance lists stress and low literacy among the groups it covers); plain, literal wording is the cheapest fix. No reading test was run on the example wording.
steps.label: craft-consensus
steps.status_note: The wording guidance follows the plain-language and COGA sources behind the cited rules; the examples were not read-tested with real readers.

steps.title: No pop-ups for the urgent route
steps.do: Keep the urgent route in the page, not in a pop-up, a timed banner, a modal or an auto-opening chat. It exists in the HTML at load, does not move, and does not take focus.
steps.how: A person in distress should not have to dismiss something to reach the content, and a banner that disappears on a timer can vanish before it is read. This is an application of the cited rules, not a measured result.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Applies the cited rules to this case; not measured.

steps.title: Observed example, not verified
steps.do: Observed example only, not verified: the pilot for a fictional UK tenant-rights service put a flat amber band above a board of five first-person situations ('What is happening to you?'), with the 999 line once and the service's phone number as a link, and a call-back form below. Use it as one shape to compare against, not as the answer.
steps.how: The pilot's own account: the band was the first thing on the page, the five rows were the primary action, and the phone-first screenshot needed a change after the audit found the button below the fold. No person looked at the page, nobody called the number, and the advice text was a draft that lawyers had not checked. Whether this shape helps people in distress is untested.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: One pilot, one model, no users.

recipes.generate_hint: Public-service or crisis page: put one compact urgent band first (the emergency-services line once, the phone number as a tel: link with hours and an out-of-hours route, meaning carried by words and a border, not red alone), use plain labels, and screenshot 390x844 to confirm the primary action is still on the first screen.

recipes.title: Forms with no backend: a mailto fallback, an honest success message, a privacy line and a rule for sensitive text
recipes.summary: A small site with no server can still offer a callback or enquiry form: native fields with native required as the no-JS fallback, a mailto: form action, and JavaScript that validates and then opens a prefilled email. Say plainly that nothing is sent until the visitor presses send in their mail app and that email is not private. Put a short privacy line next to the button, tell people not to write bank details in a free-text box, show errors and success as text in live regions, and offer a phone number as another route.
recipes.keep: Visible labels; native required, type, inputmode and autocomplete; a working form with JavaScript off; a success message that says what really happened; a privacy line of five short facts; a phone link beside the form.
recipes.avoid: Claiming 'Message sent' when only a mail app was opened; placeholder text as a label; a type=number phone field; asking for bank, ID or health details in free text; an example email address shipped as real; moving focus onto the error message; a privacy line that promises something the owner has not confirmed.

steps.title: Native single-column fields
steps.do: Build the form from native fields in one column: a visible label above each, a fieldset with a legend for radio groups, native required, and the right type, inputmode and autocomplete tokens: name (autocomplete="name"), phone (type="tel" inputmode="tel" autocomplete="tel"), email (type="email" autocomplete="email"), postcode (autocomplete="postal-code"). Three required fields at most. Never use a placeholder as the label, and never type=number for a phone number.
steps.how: WCAG 1.3.5 asks that fields collecting personal data declare their purpose with autocomplete; 3.3.2 asks for labels or instructions. type=tel and inputmode=tel bring up the phone keypad; type=number would add spinners and drop leading zeros. The tokens are HTML autofill tokens; check them in a browser, which is not done here.
steps.label: standard

code.text:
Do not write bank details, passwords or ID numbers here.

...

steps.status_note: The requirements were read (the labels-instructions Understanding page); the autocomplete and inputmode values are standard HTML and were not tested on devices. The example address is an example domain: replace it with the owner's real address, or mark it with the visible assumption marker until it is confirmed.

steps.title: Mailto form as no-JS fallback
steps.do: With no backend, use the native form as the no-JS fallback: action="mailto:...", method="post", enctype="text/plain", with native required on the fields. Layer JavaScript on top: on submit, validate, then build a mailto: link with the subject and body encoded (encodeURIComponent) and open it. Beside the form always show the phone link and the plain email address as other routes. Keep the body short: some mail apps cut a very long mailto: link (not measured here).
steps.how: The form works with JavaScript off because the browser's own required and mailto: handling remain; JavaScript adds nicer validation and a readable prefilled body. mailto: depends on the visitor having a mail app set up (a webmail-only user may get nothing), so the phone link and the written email address are not optional extras. The core content works without JavaScript, as the guide requires.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Derived from one pilot (the fictional tenant-rights service) and general practice. The mailto: handoff was not opened in a real mail app in the pilot, and no cross-client behaviour was measured.

steps.title: Honest mailto success message
steps.do: Never write 'Message sent' or 'Thank you, we have your request' for a mailto: form. Say what really happened in a role=status region that exists empty at load: your email app should open with the message ready; nothing is sent until you press send there; if it does not open, here is the phone number and the email address. Say the same on the page before submit, in one line next to the button.
steps.how: WCAG 4.1.3 asks that status messages are announced without taking focus; the Understanding page names role=status as a technique, and an empty live region that already exists is announced more reliably than one inserted with its text. The honest wording is our design judgement; it protects people from believing a request was made when it was not.
steps.label: standard
steps.status_note: The status-message requirement was read in the WCAG Understanding page. How screen readers announce this exact region was not tested.

steps.title: Errors next to fields, with summary
steps.do: Show each error as text next to its field, say what is wrong and how to fix it, keep what the user typed, and use more than colour (an icon or the word 'Error' and a border). Put a summary in the role=alert region that exists empty at load, fill it on a failed submit, do not call focus() on it, and move focus to the first invalid field. Errors stay until fixed. Native required alone gives browser-styled bubbles that vary by browser, so validate with your own text when JavaScript runs.
steps.how: This resolves a tension between comp-alert-no-focus-no-autodismiss (do not move focus to a message) and the common error-summary pattern that moves focus to the summary: the summary is announced by the live region, and focus goes to the first field that needs fixing. Resolution is our judgement; it was used in one pilot and not tested with a screen reader.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Our resolution of a rule tension; one pilot, no screen-reader test.

steps.title: Five-question privacy line
steps.do: Put a short privacy line next to the button, answering five questions in plain words: what we ask for, why, who sees it, how long we keep it, who to contact. Name the law only as an example of what applies (for example 'UK GDPR' for a UK service) and say that the owner must confirm which law, which legal basis and which retention period apply: this is not legal advice. Link to the full privacy notice if one exists. For the mailto: route add that email is not private on its way.
steps.how: Example copy for the owner to confirm: 'We use your name and phone number only to call you back about your case. Two advisers can see them. We delete them after 30 days. Questions: privacy@example.org. By email, your message is not private on the way.' The 30 days, the two advisers and the address are placeholders to confirm; until the owner confirms them they carry the visible assumption marker, and a lawyer or data-protection adviser should check the final wording before launch.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: A drafting pattern, not legal advice and not a compliance claim. No lawyer reviewed it.

steps.title: Warn against sensitive free text
steps.do: Rule of thumb for a free-text box: do not ask for sensitive data you do not need, and tell people what not to write directly under the label ('Do not write bank details, passwords or ID numbers here'), tied to the field with aria-describedby. Ask for health, immigration, financial or identity details only if the service cannot work without them, and then in a channel the owner has chosen for it, not in an email.
steps.how: With a mailto: form everything typed goes by ordinary email, which is not private and stays in two mailboxes. The cheapest protection is not to collect it. The wording is plain on purpose, so low-literacy and ESL readers can follow it.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: A rule of thumb from the pilot and general privacy practice; not tested.

steps.title: No example domains as real addresses
steps.do: Do not ship example domains (example.org, .example) as real addresses. Until the owner supplies the real address and phone number, show them with the visible assumption marker (protocol 3.2), list them in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, and let realize-launch stop the release.
steps.how: A form that opens an email to a dummy address looks finished and sends nothing; this is the form case of the guide's rule against invented facts.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Applies the guide's launch gate to forms.

recipes.generate_hint: No backend? Use a native form with required as the no-JS fallback, a mailto: action and JS that validates then opens a prefilled email, plus a phone link; say that nothing is sent until the user presses send and that email is not private; add a five-part privacy line and 'do not write bank details here'; show errors and success in live regions without moving focus onto them; set type=tel, inputmode and autocomplete.

recipes.title: Real data as the picture: the product's own true numbers as the hero or section visual
recipes.summary: When the product's strongest image is something it measured or specifies, make that the visual: a measured index (every item placed by its real score), a ruler of real values (a type scale, spacing steps, prices, distances), or a spec set beside the screenshot it describes. The numbers are true, sourced and dated, set as real text in HTML or SVG, and the picture still works for people who cannot see it, at 320 px, at 200% text and without motion. It replaces the gradient glow and the row of three big numbers, it does not decorate them.
recipes.keep: One composed picture made of the product's own data: a measured index, a ruler of real values, or a spec beside its screenshot, in the page's own type and tokens.
recipes.avoid: Invented or rounded-up numbers; a row of three big numbers under the hero (the stats strip); data drawn as a raster image or as decoration with no labels; colour as the only key; count-up animations that hide the final value; a chart with no text alternative or source.
recipes.generate_hint: Use the product's own measured or specified numbers as the visual (an index, a ruler, a spec beside its screenshot), set as real text with a source and date, a text alternative and a table behind it; never a stats strip or a decorative chart.

steps.title: Only true, sourced numbers
steps.do: Draw the picture only from numbers the product really has: a measurement you ran, a value in a source file, a published spec. Record where each comes from and when (a data-source attribute, a visible note under the picture, and the source in design/assets.md). Numbers you do not have are left out, never estimated or rounded up to look better.
steps.how: distinct-no-filler-copy fails round statistics with no data-source; the honesty rules in the protocol (3.2) forbid invented numbers and mark unconfirmed facts with the .assumed marker. Read the values from the file or tool that produced them at build time (a JSON the site already reads, a measurement script) so the picture cannot drift from the truth.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Written 2026-11-17 from the owner's review of hero mock-ups (the tells were a centred stack with a stats strip, a glow, an accent word and decorative labels); not yet built as a demo or audited, so the markup is general engineering knowledge.

steps.title: One composed picture, not a strip
steps.do: Compose the data as one picture with its own structure (items placed on a scale, ticks on a ruler, callouts beside a screenshot), large enough to be the lead object of the first screen or the section. Do not set three or four big numbers in a row under the headline: that is the stats strip of distinct-hero-not-template.
steps.how: The audit counts a row of three or more numbers at 28 px or 1.6 times body size or larger, below the h1 or in the next section, as a stock hero signal. A measured index or ruler reads as the product's own work; give it the space a product photo would take and no glow behind it.
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Written 2026-11-17 from the owner's review of hero mock-ups (the tells were a centred stack with a stats strip, a glow, an accent word and decorative labels); not yet built as a demo or audited, so the markup is general engineering knowledge.

steps.title: Labels and values as text
steps.do: Set every label and value as real text: HTML, or SVG text elements in the page's fonts, never a raster image of the chart. Tick labels, values and units scale with the user's text size.
steps.how: WCAG 1.4.5 asks for text rather than images of text where the presentation can be achieved with text; text in HTML or in SVG text elements can be resized, translated and selected. Size SVG text in CSS units relative to the root size so it follows a 200% text setting, and check it with the audit's stress pass.
steps.label: standard
steps.status_note: The requirement was read in the WCAG Understanding pages listed. Written 2026-11-17 from the owner's review of hero mock-ups (the tells were a centred stack with a stats strip, a glow, an accent word and decorative labels); not yet built as a demo or audited, so the markup is general engineering knowledge.

steps.title: Name the takeaway, keep the table
steps.do: Give the picture a text alternative that states its takeaway in one sentence (role="img" with aria-labelledby on an SVG, or a figure with a figcaption), and make the underlying values available as a real table or list: visible below, or in a details element. Purely decorative ticks and gridlines are aria-hidden.
steps.how: WCAG 1.1.1 asks that non-text content has a text alternative that serves the same purpose; for a chart the purpose is the finding, and the data itself belongs in a table with th and scope (see comp-data-table-semantics). Write the takeaway, not a description of the shapes ("40 sites by measured contrast, from 2.1:1 to 17:1").
steps.label: standard
steps.status_note: The requirement was read in the sources listed; the markup was not tested with a screen reader here. Written 2026-11-17 from the owner's review of hero mock-ups (the tells were a centred stack with a stats strip, a glow, an accent word and decorative labels); not yet built as a demo or audited, so the markup is general engineering knowledge.

code.text: All 40 values...

steps.title: Shape and label carry meaning
steps.do: When marks fall into groups or one item is highlighted, tell them apart by label, shape or position as well as colour; marks that must be seen to read the picture reach 3:1 against their background and all text 4.5:1 (3:1 at large size).
steps.how: WCAG 1.4.1 forbids colour as the only visual means of conveying information, and 1.4.11 asks 3:1 for graphical objects required to understand the content. Check each mark and text colour against the background with check_contrast (role ui for marks, text for labels).
steps.label: standard
steps.status_note: The requirements were read in the sources listed. Written 2026-11-17 from the owner's review of hero mock-ups (the tells were a centred stack with a stats strip, a glow, an accent word and decorative labels); not yet built as a demo or audited, so the markup is general engineering knowledge.

steps.title: Reflow or scroll its region
steps.do: At 320 px the picture either reflows (a horizontal ruler becomes vertical, an index becomes a ranked list) or scrolls inside its own labelled region; the page itself never scrolls sideways.
steps.how: WCAG 1.4.10 exempts content that needs two-dimensional layout for meaning, such as data tables and some charts, but the rest of the page must still reflow. A scrolling region needs tabindex="0", a role and an accessible name so keyboard users can scroll it. Check with the audit CLI's widths command at 320, 390 and 320 at 200% text.
steps.label: standard
steps.status_note: The requirement was read in the source listed. Written 2026-11-17 from the owner's review of hero mock-ups (the tells were a centred stack with a stats strip, a glow, an accent word and decorative labels); not yet built as a demo or audited, so the markup is general engineering knowledge.

steps.title: Final values without motion
steps.do: The final values are in the HTML and visible without JavaScript and with reduced motion. If marks draw in or numbers count up, that runs once, briefly, only without prefers-reduced-motion, and never starts from zero in the markup.
steps.how: A count-up that starts from 0 in the HTML shows false numbers to crawlers, screen readers and anyone whose script fails. Render the true values server-side and animate from them only as an enhancement inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference).
steps.label: our-take
steps.status_note: Written 2026-11-17 from the owner's review of hero mock-ups (the tells were a centred stack with a stats strip, a glow, an accent word and decorative labels); not yet built as a demo or audited, so the markup is general engineering knowledge.

principles.name: Good design is innovative
principles.statement: Innovation grows with technology and is never pursued for its own sake.
principles.apply: Use a new technique only where it serves the message.
principles.check: Can you state what the new technique gives the visitor?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Good design makes a product useful
principles.statement: A product meets functional, psychological and aesthetic needs, without distractions.
principles.apply: Cut elements that do not help the visitor's job.
principles.check: Does each element serve the primary action or a stated need?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Good design is aesthetic
principles.statement: Everyday objects shape well-being, so how they look matters, and beauty depends on quality of execution.
principles.apply: Spend effort on alignment, spacing and detail.
principles.check: Are spacing, alignment and type consistent with the tokens?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Good design makes a product understandable
principles.statement: Its structure should be clear, ideally needing no explanation.
principles.apply: Make the page's purpose and next step obvious without instructions.
principles.check: Five-second test: can people say what it is and what to do?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Good design is unobtrusive
principles.statement: Products are tools: restrained, leaving room for the user.
principles.apply: Keep decoration from competing with content.
principles.check: Does motion or ornament compete with the headline or the action?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Good design is honest
principles.statement: A product does not claim more innovation, power or value than it has.
principles.apply: Make claims you can support; show proof.
principles.check: Is every claim backed by a fact on the page?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Good design is long-lasting
principles.statement: Avoiding trends keeps a design from looking dated.
principles.apply: Use a trend as one element with a reason; keep structure and type timeless.
principles.check: If the trend disappears, does the design still work?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Good design is thorough down to the last detail
principles.statement: Nothing is left to chance; care shows respect for the user.
principles.apply: Design states, errors, empty cases and edge widths.
principles.check: Are hover, focus, error, empty and small-screen states designed?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Good design is environmentally friendly
principles.statement: It conserves resources and reduces pollution across its life.
principles.apply: Keep pages light: fewer bytes, fewer requests, no pointless autoplay.
principles.check: Is the page weight within the budget set in assets?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: As little design as possible
principles.statement: Focus on what is necessary and strip away the rest.
principles.apply: Remove an element and see whether the page loses anything.
principles.check: Could any section be removed without loss?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Visibility of system status
principles.statement: Keep users informed about what is happening with timely feedback.
principles.apply: Show loading, success and error states.
principles.check: Does every action give feedback quickly?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: Match between system and the real world
principles.statement: Use the users' language and conventions, not internal jargon.
principles.apply: Use the audience's words in labels and headlines.
principles.check: Would a first-time visitor understand each label?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: User control and freedom
principles.statement: Provide clear exits for unwanted actions.
principles.apply: Offer cancel, back and undo where actions are costly.
principles.check: Can the visitor leave every state?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: Consistency and standards
principles.statement: Words and actions mean the same thing throughout; follow conventions.
principles.apply: Reuse components and labels; follow platform conventions.
principles.check: Do identical functions look and read the same everywhere?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: Error prevention
principles.statement: Prevent problems or confirm before users commit.
principles.apply: Use constraints, defaults and confirmations for costly actions.
principles.check: Can the visitor make a costly mistake without warning?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: Recognition rather than recall
principles.statement: Make options visible so people need not remember them.
principles.apply: Show choices; avoid hidden gestures and hover-only options.
principles.check: Does anything require remembering what is not on screen?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: Flexibility and efficiency of use
principles.statement: Let experts speed up tasks while novices stay supported.
principles.apply: Provide shortcuts that supplement visible controls.
principles.check: Is there a fast path that does not hide the slow one?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: Aesthetic and minimalist design
principles.statement: Remove information that competes with what matters.
principles.apply: Focus visuals on the primary goal.
principles.check: Does extra content distract from the primary action?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors
principles.statement: Error messages explain the problem and suggest a fix.
principles.apply: Write errors in plain language with a next step.
principles.check: Does each error say what happened and how to fix it?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: Help and documentation
principles.statement: The system should need little explanation, but help should be easy to find.
principles.apply: Put help in context and make it searchable and task-focused.
principles.check: Can the visitor find help from where they are stuck?
principles.label: evidence

principles.name: Discoverability and understanding
principles.statement: Two key qualities of good design: people can find out what actions are possible, and understand how it works.
principles.apply: Make actions visible and meaning clear.
principles.check: Can a new visitor find and understand the main action?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Signifiers show where action is possible
principles.statement: Affordances define what is possible; signifiers tell people where and how.
principles.apply: Make links and buttons look and read as such.
principles.check: Is every clickable element signalled, and is anything signalled that is not clickable?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Feedback
principles.statement: Communicate the result of an action clearly and promptly.
principles.apply: Show a response to every action.
principles.check: Is there a visible response within a moment of each action?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Conceptual model
principles.statement: People form a simple mental model of how something works; design should support an accurate one.
principles.apply: Keep structure and wording consistent with one clear model.
principles.check: Can the visitor explain how the site is organized?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Observe, ideate, prototype, test, repeat
principles.statement: Human-centered design iterates observation, idea generation, prototyping and testing.
principles.apply: Loop the process; do not treat it as linear.
principles.check: Has each stage fed back into the previous one at least once?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Perceivable
principles.statement: Information and interface components can be perceived by users.
principles.apply: Provide text alternatives, captions, adaptable content and sufficient contrast.
principles.check: Run the perceivable Quality Bar rules.
principles.label: standard

principles.name: Operable
principles.statement: Interface components and navigation can be operated, including by keyboard.
principles.apply: Everything works by keyboard; allow enough time; avoid seizure triggers; make navigation easy.
principles.check: Tab through the page.
principles.label: standard

principles.name: Understandable
principles.statement: Information and operation are understandable: readable, predictable, with help avoiding mistakes.
principles.apply: Use plain language, predictable behavior and clear errors.
principles.check: Is behavior predictable and are errors explained?
principles.label: standard

principles.name: Robust
principles.statement: Content works with current and future tools, including assistive technology.
principles.apply: Use native HTML and correct names, roles and values.
principles.check: Does the accessibility tree match what is shown?
principles.label: standard

principles.name: Recognize exclusion
principles.statement: Acknowledge bias and notice where products fail because of mismatches between people and experiences.
principles.apply: List who the design could exclude.
principles.check: Is there a written list of who might be excluded and what the design does about it?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Learn from diversity
principles.statement: Keep people at the centre; varied perspectives produce insight.
principles.apply: Include people with different abilities in research.
principles.check: Were different users consulted?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Solve for one, extend to many
principles.statement: Designing for people with permanent disabilities benefits everyone.
principles.apply: Treat accessibility needs as design constraints that improve the product.
principles.check: Which accessibility feature also helps everyone?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Start with user needs
principles.statement: Research users and data first; what people ask for is not always what they need.
principles.apply: Write the need before the solution.
principles.check: Does the brief cite evidence about users?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Do the hard work to make it simple
principles.statement: Make it genuinely easy to use even when the underlying system is complex.
principles.apply: Absorb complexity in the design, not in the visitor's effort.
principles.check: Where does complexity land: on the page or on the visitor?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Iterate, then iterate again
principles.statement: Start small, test with real users, refine or scrap what does not work.
principles.apply: Plan several small test rounds.
principles.check: Is a second test round planned?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: This is for everyone
principles.statement: Build inclusive, accessible services, especially for people who struggle most.
principles.apply: Test with people who struggle most.
principles.check: Have the hardest-case users been considered?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Be consistent, not uniform
principles.statement: Use shared language and patterns where possible, as guidance to be improved.
principles.apply: Reuse patterns but adapt where users need it.
principles.check: Are differences deliberate and explained?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Proximity
principles.statement: Elements close together are seen as a group.
principles.apply: Group related items; separate unrelated ones with space.
principles.check: Is spacing within groups smaller than between groups?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Similarity
principles.statement: Elements that look alike are seen as related.
principles.apply: Style items of the same kind the same way.
principles.check: Do similar-looking items have similar roles?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Closure
principles.statement: We complete incomplete shapes and perceive wholes.
principles.apply: Use implied shapes carefully; avoid ambiguity.
principles.check: Is any implied grouping accidental?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Good continuation
principles.statement: We follow smooth paths and alignments.
principles.apply: Align elements along clear lines to guide the eye.
principles.check: Does the eye path follow the intended reading order?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Layers: meaning, presentation, behavior
principles.statement: Start from well-structured HTML everyone can use, then enhance by capability.
principles.apply: Build core content first; layer effects on top.
principles.check: Does content work with JavaScript off and CSS failing?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: Design parts and whole together
principles.statement: Check components in the context of the page; revise parts when a page fails.
principles.apply: Test components inside real pages.
principles.check: Have components been reviewed in context?
principles.label: craft-consensus

principles.name: The grid is an aid, not a guarantee
principles.statement: A grid supports order and readability; it does not make a design good.
principles.apply: Use a grid to align, and break it with intent.
principles.check: Is each break from the grid deliberate?
principles.label: craft-consensus

trends.status_evidence: Among the 31 Awwwards Sites of the Day from 2026-10-06 to 2026-11-05, 14 carry the Three.js tag, 11 the 3D tag and 10 the WebGL tag. Of the 31 Sites of the Year up to 2025-11-17, 19 carry 3D and 14 WebGL; the 2025 winner (Lando Norris, 2025-11-17) is tagged 3D, WebGL, GSAP. Commercial-side pages are more cautious: Framer Websites (2026-03-28) puts 3D and WebGL under 'approach with caution', Muzli's store page warns of an overuse wave, StudioMeyer (2026-09-30) says 3D/WebGL underdelivered for client work. So it is peak among award sites and cooling for ordinary commercial homepages. Based on a handful of pages, not data.
trends.good_for: Showcase and brand-led pages where the object is the product: automotive, hardware, games, agencies, portfolios, launches.
trends.do_well: Keep real text, nav and the primary call to action in HTML that paints without the 3D layer; lazy-load the scene after first paint; provide a static poster for reduced motion and for low-power devices; make rotation or drag operable by keyboard and by single tap; have the 3D show what the product is or does.
trends.slop_version: A floating abstract blob or glossy primitive behind a centred headline with a purple-blue gradient, loading 5+ MB before the headline appears, with no fallback.
trends.confidence: medium for award sites, low for commercial sites

trends.status_evidence: 19 of the 31 latest Sites of the Day carry the GSAP tag, 21 carry Animation, 9 Storytelling, 8 Transitions (2026-10-06 to 2026-11-05). Sites of the Month: Storytelling 13, Scrolling 11, GSAP 10 of 31. Digidop (updated 2026-10-06) dates the enabling events: Webflow made GSAP free on 2025-04-30 and Figma Motion launched in June 2026, which makes it cheap, which is a saturation signal. Webflow (Dec 2025) frames the 2026 shift as scroll as navigation (progress indicators) rather than only narratives.
trends.good_for: Storytelling, portfolios, product walk-throughs, long editorial or launch pages where order carries meaning.
trends.do_well: Content visible by default and enhanced by script, never hidden until a trigger fires; one authored sequence that reveals meaning in order; native scroll preserved (no scroll-jacking that traps wheel or keyboard); progress indicators for long pages; a reduced-motion path that shows everything statically.
trends.slop_version: The same fade-and-slide-up applied to every section, count-up stat tiles, bounce easing, and a marquee strip, with nothing explaining what changed.

trends.status_evidence: Named in Figma (bold typography), Framer Websites (bold typographic layouts, 2026-03-28), Line25 (oversized type as the hero, 2026-04), Webflow (dynamic text treatments), Muzli store (kinetic type is now an expected baseline rather than a differentiator), Muzli feed. Awwwards 'Typography' tag appears on 10 of 31 latest Sites of the Day but only 4 of 31 Sites of the Year. The Muzli store 'baseline' claim and the multi-source repetition point to peak.
trends.good_for: Brand-led and short-copy pages: studios, launches, cultural and editorial brands; hero that works with no image.
trends.do_well: Real text (not images of text); fluid sizing with clamp that survives 200% zoom and 320 px width; tracking tightened only to the point letters keep their shape; short headings (the Impeccable detector flags headlines >= 72 px with >= 40 characters); balanced line breaks; kinetic effects only on a few words and with a static fallback.
trends.slop_version: A long full-sentence headline at 7rem+, with one italic or gradient-filled word, an all-caps tracked eyebrow above it, and a typewriter or rotating-word animation that never stops.

trends.status_evidence: Typewolf Site of the Day, 45 entries from 2025-01-17 to 2025-12-14: by my reading of the font names about 26 pair a serif display (Cardinal, Editorial Old, Tobias, Arizona Flare, Martina Plantijn, GT Super and similar) with a neutral grotesk (Soehne, Neue Montreal, Founders Grotesk, Diatype). Webflow (Dec 2025) names vintage and classical art references as a trend. At the same time Capital & Compute and Impeccable name the cream + serif + terracotta combination and the italic serif hero as the second-wave AI default, and Google metadata ranks Fraunces 82 and Instrument Serif 79 by popularity. I read this as peak in curated design and saturated in generated sites. The Typewolf feed stops at 2025-12-14, so this is a 2025 snapshot.
trends.good_for: Editorial, cultural, hospitality, luxury, publications, studios, consultancies, DTC with a story.
trends.do_well: Choose a serif with a reason tied to the subject (heritage, authorship, publication), pair it with a neutral grotesk for UI and body, keep one display voice, self-host with font-display swap and size-adjusted fallbacks, and state the pairing in the direction file.
trends.slop_version: Fraunces or Instrument Serif in italic as the hero headline on a cream background (#F4F1EA family) with a terracotta accent, a tracked mono eyebrow above and numbered section labels, for a product that has no editorial reason.
trends.confidence: medium (type), low (status of the AI-default part)

trends.status_evidence: Typewolf Site of the Day 2025: about 10 of 45 entries add a mono (DM Mono, Diatype Mono, Favorit Mono, Suisse Int'l Mono, Soehne Mono, Monument Grotesk Mono, GT Flexa Mono, Azeret Mono, GT Alpina Typewriter). Webflow (Dec 2025) and Muzli feed cite ASCII/pixel treatments. Impeccable has a rule against mono used only as a costume for 'technical' and a rule against decorative blinking cursors; Capital & Compute lists mono small labels and tracked eyebrows as template chrome. Saturation inferred from the Typewolf share plus the slop catalogues naming it, not measured.
trends.good_for: Data, code, specs, captions, measurements, timestamps, developer tools and products that really show code.
trends.do_well: Use mono where the content is code, data or measurement; keep tabular figures aligned; size at least 14 px for functional text (Impeccable flags functional text under 11 px).
trends.slop_version: Tiny uppercase mono eyebrows over every heading, 'A / B / C' meta strings, section numbers, and a fake blinking cursor in the hero.

trends.status_evidence: Listed by Line25, Framer Websites, Muzli feed and uiuxshowcase; StudioMeyer (2026-09-30) says it 'held up' for content prioritisation; the Reddit dataset ranks bento near the bottom of tells people complain about. Awwwards has no 'bento' tag, so I could not count it. Line25's 45% adoption figure is unsourced and not used. Several sources describe an anti-grid counter-trend (brutalist, broken-grid) as a reaction to its ubiquity. Peak, possibly turning saturated; low confidence.
trends.good_for: Product overviews with unlike content (UI shot, stat, quote, integration), dashboards-in-marketing, feature summaries on SaaS homepages.
trends.do_well: One cell per real piece of content (no empty tiles); tile size encodes importance; DOM order matches reading order; at 320 px collapse to one column in meaningful order; vary tile backgrounds with real imagery or product UI.
trends.slop_version: Six same-colour cards with a small icon and one line each, a decorative empty tile, all with the same radius and soft shadow.

trends.status_evidence: Framer Websites (2026-03-28) and Line25 (2026-04) and Muzli feed list dark-first; StudioMeyer says dark mode 'held up' when fully checked. The 2025 Awwwards Site of the Year page lists palette #D2FF00 on #111112. At the same time Impeccable, wystack, Capital & Compute and the Reddit dataset name cyan-on-dark, purple glows and neon glows as top tells. Saturated as a default, still winning when motivated.
trends.good_for: Media-forward, gaming, music, developer, security and automotive brands; products used in low light.
trends.do_well: Design the dark theme as its own system (not an inversion), keep body text at 4.5:1 or better, avoid pure black behind large white text for halation, and choose the accent from the subject; one theme per page unless a deliberate switch.
trends.slop_version: Near-black with cyan or violet glow, gradient text, radial halos and glass cards on every section.

trends.status_evidence: Webflow (Dec 2025) calls it a shift from one accent colour to full colour systems; Figma lists vibrant saturated palettes (Y2K, 'dopamine design'); Muzli feed predicts a move away from beige but admits it is not yet widespread. In Awwwards data the 'Colorful' tag is on 9 of 31 Sites of the Month and 9 of 31 Sites of the Year but only 1 of 31 of the latest Sites of the Day, so award-site evidence is mixed. Several sources are predictions. Emerging, low confidence.
trends.good_for: Consumer, kids and family, food and drink, events, creative tools, brands whose identity is energy.
trends.do_well: Define a named palette with roles and use every colour with a rule; verify pairings at 4.5:1 for text; keep one dominant hue; do not communicate state by colour alone.
trends.slop_version: A random rainbow gradient wash or mesh blob behind a centred hero, with pastel text on pastel backgrounds.

trends.status_evidence: Muzli store (cyberbrutalism: ASCII, pixel art, repurposed system UI), Line25 (brutalism and anti-design 'for authenticity'), Muzli feed (retro and brutalism as a reaction to AI-polished visuals), Figma (neo-brutalism and collage), StudioMeyer (a missed counter-movement, 'author's observations, not backed by independent data'). Awwwards: 'Experimental' on 7 of 31 latest Sites of the Day and 4 of 31 Sites of the Month. Impeccable treats hard offset shadows as a review prompt outside a real neobrutalist concept. Rising, from the repeated 'reaction to sameness' framing; low confidence.
trends.good_for: Studios, artists, independent publications, cultural institutions, developer tools with a rebellious voice. Not suggested for finance, healthcare or enterprise B2B (Muzli store).
trends.do_well: Keep structure and focus order intact under a deliberately raw surface; keep navigation findable; commit to one rule set (grid lines, type, one colour pair) and apply it everywhere.
trends.slop_version: Hard offset block shadows and thick black borders applied as a costume to an otherwise ordinary SaaS template.

trends.status_evidence: Webflow (Dec 2025) names two linked trends: proprietary visual systems (its example: illustrative visuals across Anthropic's site) and 'art converging with advanced UI' (vintage illustration, painted or ASCII backdrops behind product UI). Muzli feed (Prince Pal, 2026-01-18) lists narrative illustration replacing stock photos. Awwwards 'Illustration' tag: 2 of 31 latest Sites of the Day, 4 of 31 Sites of the Month, 7 of 31 Sites of the Year. Capital & Compute notes that the Anthropic-style warm editorial look has itself become an AI-default cluster. Emerging with a saturation risk.
trends.good_for: SaaS and AI products that want to look made by people, consumer brands, education, non-profits; any brand needing a recognisable image language.
trends.do_well: Commission or draw a consistent illustration system; keep product UI readable as real, live text and screenshots; give meaningful images alt text and decorative ones empty alt; keep file weight low.
trends.slop_version: AI-generated plastic illustrations, stock 'diverse team' photos, or hero-sized SVG scenes built from circles and polygons.

trends.status_evidence: Webflow (Dec 2025) lists minimalism in copy and a TL;DR experience (pitch-deck-style overview in the nav) as two of its 8 trends. Muzli feed lists content-first layouts (2026-01-18). Awwwards 'Clean' tag appears on 12 of 31 latest Sites of the Day, 'Minimal' on 4. Impeccable catalogues an 'aphoristic cadence' copy tell, which shows that short punchy copy is itself becoming a template. One vendor source for the specific trend; emerging, low confidence.
trends.good_for: Complex B2B services, consultancies, fintech, anything with a clear value proposition that can be stated in a line, with the details one click deeper.
trends.do_well: Say what it is in plain words in the first screen; offer a structured overview (what, for whom, proof, next step) with deeper pages behind it; make every remaining word load-bearing.
trends.slop_version: Manufactured contrast one-liners ('Not a feature. A platform.') repeated section after section, with no explanation of what the product does.

trends.status_evidence: Muzli store (volumetrics: restrained glass, 3D hero objects, textured type; cites Apple Liquid Glass in iOS 26), Digidop (2025's glow becoming shader-based; Apple Liquid Glass dated 2025-06-09; advises one material effect per page), Line25 (glassmorphism 2.0 as a controlled return; peaked originally around 2021). Framer Websites (2026-03-28) says glassmorphism has peaked and hurts readability and rendering; StudioMeyer says it overpromised; Impeccable flags it when decorative; the Reddit dataset says people rarely name it. Multiple sources saying 'peaked' or 'use sparingly' suggest saturated, fading as a default.
trends.good_for: Overlays and navigation above imagery or video, premium consumer and OS-adjacent products, where depth must show layering.
trends.do_well: Use it on one or two functional surfaces; keep text at 4.5:1 against the worst-case content behind it; give a solid-fill fallback for reduced transparency and forced colors; test on mid-range phones.
trends.slop_version: Frosted cards with a glow border on every section over a purple-blue gradient.
trends.confidence: medium (that it has peaked), low (exact stage)

trends.status_evidence: Figma (experimental navigation: radial menus, hidden drawers, interactive maps, nonlinear paths), Muzli store (nav that appears on scroll, hidden nav, single-screen layouts, framed as conversion experiments; suggests a two-week no-nav test), IONOS countertrends (hamburger menus vs nostalgic styles). Awwwards 'Unusual Navigation' tag: 1 of 31 latest Sites of the Day, 2 of 31 Sites of the Month, 3 of 31 Sites of the Year, so it stays rare. Emerging and niche; low confidence.
trends.good_for: Showcase sites, single-screen launches, portfolios, and experiments where exploration is the point.
trends.do_well: Keep a visible, labelled route to the main sections (or a menu button with a text label); full keyboard and screen reader support; test whether people find a section within seconds.
trends.slop_version: A mystery-icon or gesture-only menu that hides primary links on desktop for a page whose job is conversion.

trends.status_evidence: Single source: Webflow (Dec 2025) names 'the infinite canvas' (dot grids, node lines, open space) for creation and generative tools, with Flim as an example. No second source and no Awwwards tag exists for it. Impeccable lists decorative grid-line backgrounds as an advisory tell unless the surface really is a canvas or a measuring tool. Hypothesis only.
trends.good_for: Tools whose product is a canvas, node editor or workspace.
trends.do_well: Use the grid or canvas only where the product is one; show the real product on it.
trends.slop_version: A dot-grid or hairline grid background behind a generic SaaS hero with no canvas in the product.

trends.status_evidence: Dated 2026-11-06. In UK government and public-service sites this style is documented and long established: the GOV.UK design principles, type scale, layout and clear-language guidance (all read; see sources) describe plain words, one thing per page, sentence case and left-aligned text on a restrained palette. Status `saturated` applies only inside that niche and is inferred from the guidance being a published standard, not from a count of sites. Whether non-government services (charities, advice services, local services) are adopting it is unmeasured; one pilot (a fictional UK tenant-rights service, model-built, 2026-11-06) chose it, which is not evidence of a trend.
trends.good_for: Advice, benefits, housing, health information and any service whose visitors are stressed, reading in a second language or in a hurry, and whose first job is to get them to the right next step.
trends.do_well: Write in the reader's words at a low reading level, put the one next step and a phone route in the first screen, use visible focus and real labels, then add one lead element that comes from this service (the question as the interface, a live self-check, a number that matters) so the page is not a clone. See the recipes `urgent-help-route` and `form-no-backend-and-privacy`. Never imitate a government's crest, colours or name.
trends.slop_version: A pale header, a blue 'Start now' button and grey 'Related content' links on a private or charity service that has no service-specific content; every line hedged and nothing a person could act on; no phone number or hours; or a copy of a government's branding to borrow its trust.
trends.confidence: low (inferred from published guidance, not counted)

trends.status_evidence: Dated 2026-11-06. A description of a template, not a measured trend: no count of charity sites was made. It is named as an anti-goal in one pilot brief (a fictional UK tenant-rights service, 2026-11-06) and recognised from general familiarity with the sector. Treat `saturated` as a judgement that this is the page a reader expects from a charity, so copying it gives no distinction; re-check against real sites before relying on it.
trends.good_for: Fundraising pages whose job is a donation and whose story is real, named and consented to.
trends.do_well: Lead with what the service does and for whom, in plain words; use a real number or a real, consented case with a source; keep one donate action, not five; show where the money goes; if you have no photographs, say so and use type or a live object instead (recipe `no-photography-physical-goods`).
trends.slop_version: A full-bleed photo of a smiling person under a warm overlay, a heart icon, 'Together we can make a difference', a donate button in the header, the hero and every section, impact counters with no source, three icon cards, a row of stock volunteers, and a story with no name or date.

trends.status_evidence: Dated 2026-11-06. A description of a template, not a measured trend: no count of law-firm sites was made. It is named as an anti-goal in one pilot brief (a fictional UK tenant-rights service, 2026-11-06) and recognised from general familiarity with the sector. `saturated` means a reader expects this page from a law firm, so copying it gives no distinction; re-check against real sites before relying on it.
trends.good_for: Firms whose clients expect formality and whose proof is real (named areas of practice, regulated status, years of practice that can be checked).
trends.do_well: Say what you do for whom in plain words, put the phone number and the first step in the first screen, show real people and real credentials that can be checked (regulator, registration), explain legal terms where they appear, and carry the formality in clear structure rather than in navy and gold.
trends.slop_version: Navy and gold, a serif logotype with a scales or pillar icon, a courthouse or handshake photograph, 'Trusted legal counsel' and 'decades of experience' with no named case or checkable credential, a gold 'Free consultation' button, a three-column grid of practice areas with icons, a row of partner headshots in suits, and the disclaimer in small grey text.
